body.p: Adam and Havah (Eve)

Adam was the first man, the father of the human race. God created the first couple in his image to populate the earth and rule the created order (Gen 1:26-31). God made Adam from the earth and breathed life into him (2:7); he was to cultivate the garden in which God placed him (2:15), name the animals (2:19-20), and follow God’s instructions (1:28; 2:16-17).

God created the first woman as a companion and helper for Adam (2:18-22). Havah’s creation from Adam’s rib portrays the unity that God intended for man and woman in marriage (2:23-25). She is honored as “the mother of all who live” (3:20).

After the serpent deceived Havah into rejecting God’s rule, Adam also rebelled (3:1-6). Their willful disobedience disrupted their relationship (3:7) and separated them from God. God looked for Adam after his rebellion; he and Havah were hiding among the trees, already aware of the alienation (3:8). When God questioned him, Adam blamed Havah and, by implication, God (3:12). Their rebellion brought pain, strained relationships, hardship in governing the earth, and death—physical and spiritual (3:16-19, 22-24). Nonetheless, God provided animal skins to cover Adam and Havah (3:21), and promised that Havah’s offspring would defeat Satan (3:15; see Rom 16:20; Rev 12:1-9; 20:1-10).

Adam was a historical individual (Gen 4:25; 5:1-5; 1 Chr 1:1; Hos 6:7; Luke 3:38; Rom 5:14; 1 Cor 15:22, 45; 1 Tim 2:13-14; Jude 1:14) who also represents humanity as a whole. God’s mandates (Gen 1:26-30) and curses (3:16-19) affected not only Adam and Havah, but the entire human race. Adam represents separation from God, which all humanity experiences.

The apostle Paulos (Paul) contrasted those represented by Adam, the first man, with those who follow Christ, the “last Adam” (Rom 5:12-21; 1 Cor 15:45-50; see also Rom 8:5-11, 20-22). Those represented by Adam live only after his example—they partake of his sin, his alienation from God and God’s creation, and his spiritual death. By contrast, those who follow Christ live by faith in him. They are recreated in Christ’s image and become “new people” who partake of a new creation (see Rom 8:29; 1 Cor 15:49; 2 Cor 5:17; Gal 6:15). The barriers Adam and Havah raised are removed by Christ (Rom 5:1; 2 Cor 5:19; Gal 3:27-28; Eph 2:14-16); Christ restores what they lost.
Passages for Further Study
Noah

Noah was the son of Lemek (Lamech), a descendant of Shet (Seth) (Gen 5:3-29). Lemek might have hoped that Noah (whose name means “rest” or “relief”) would ease the curse of hardship in working the ground. Instead, God used Noah to help relieve the world of evil.

God intended to destroy creation because of pervasive human wickedness (Gen 6:1-7; see Matt 24:37-39; Luke 17:26-27), but he decided to preserve Noah (Gen 6:8). God gave Noah, a righteous and blameless man (Gen 6:9), precise instructions for building the ark in which only the eight people of his family would be saved, along with every kind of creature (Gen 6:14–8:19). When Noah and his family finally emerged from the ark after the flood, Noah pleased God by building an altar and sacrificing burnt offerings. God promised that he would never again flood the whole earth or disrupt the sequence of the seasons, despite human sin (Gen 8:20–9:17).

Noah’s sons were Shem, Ham, and Yefet (Japheth). All the nations of the earth descended from them (Gen 9:18-19). When Noah became drunk on wine from his vineyard, his sons and their descendants were cursed or blessed in accord with how they responded to him (Gen 9:20-27). Noah lived for 950 years, including 350 years after the flood (Gen 9:28-29). He is an example of righteousness, obedience, courage, and faith (see Ezek 14:12-20; Heb 11:7; 2 Pet 2:5).
Passages for Further Study
Malki-Tsedek (Melchizedek)

Malki-Tsedek is a mysterious biblical personality whose name means “king of righteousness.” He was a Kena’ani (Canaanite) priest and king; there is no record of his family or of the beginning or end of his life.

Avraham (Abraham) met Malki-Tsedek after defeating four Mesopotamian kings. The Mesopotamians had raided Sedom (Sodom) and Amorah (Gomorrah) and captured Avraham’s nephew Lot (Gen 14:1-16). When Avraham returned from battle, Malki-Tsedek, king of Shalem (Salem) (=Yerushalem (Jerusalem); see Ps 76:2 and footnote there), was with the grateful kings of the Dead Sea confederacy. When Malki-Tsedek gave Avraham bread, wine, and his blessing, he was acting as “a priest of God Most High” (Gen 14:18), the true God who created heaven and earth (see Pss 7:17; 47:2; 57:2; 78:56). Malki-Tsedek correctly understood that Avraham worshiped the true God, and he praised God for giving victory to Avraham (Gen 14:19-20). Avraham received Malki-Tsedek’s gifts and gave him a tithe, which demonstrated the prominence of Malki-Tsedek (see Heb 7:4-10).

While Genesis gives genealogies for many of its characters, Malki-Tsedek appears suddenly without any such record, and he disappears just as quickly. Much later in Yisrael’s (Israel’s) history, King David was perhaps reflecting on this when he said that the Messiah is “a priest forever in the order of Malki-Tsedek” (Ps 110:4; cp. Heb 7:15-25). The book of Hebrews picks up on this notion that Malki-Tsedek had no genealogical record and uses it to compare the temporary Levitical priesthood with the eternal priesthood of Christ. The book of Hebrews also explains that Malki-Tsedek is remembered as “resembling the Son of God” (Heb 7:3), but was not himself the Son of God. His priesthood lasts forever as an archetype that prefigures the Messiah’s priesthood. Like Malki-Tsedek (but unlike the kings of Yisrael), Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) is a king who also fulfills priestly functions.

Malki-Tsedek, a royal priest, was superior to Levi, the ancestor of Yisrael’s priests. In the same way, the Messiah, Yeshua Christ, is a better priest than the descendants of Aharon (Aaron). Yeshua provides permanent atonement for sins and direct access to his Father (Heb 7:24-28). He guides his people by the Spirit rather than by law (Heb 8:7-13) and lives forever as priest and king for those who trust in him.
Passages for Further Study
Hagar

Hagar was the Mitsri (Egyptian) servant of Saray (Sarai), Avram’s (Abram’s) wife. When God commanded Avram to leave Mesopotamia, he promised him a multitude of descendants who would be given a new land (Gen 12:2, 7). After ten childless years in Kena’an (Canaan), Saray followed a customary Mesopotamian practice by giving Hagar to Avram as his concubine; any son born of the union of husband and concubine was considered the wife’s child (cp. 30:1-8).

Hagar got pregnant and became disrespectful to Saray during her pregnancy. Saray responded by dealing harshly with her, and Hagar fled into the desert (16:4-6). The angel of Yahweh appeared to her at a desert well, telling her to return to Avram’s house and submit to Saray.
Hagar bore a son, Yishmael (Ishmael), when Avram was eighty-six years old (16:1-16).

Fourteen years later, God gave Avraham (Abraham) and Sarah their promised son, Yitshak (Isaac). When Yitshak was weaned (at about three years), a traditional feast was held. At this event, Yishmael mocked Yitshak (21:9), so Sarah insisted that Avraham send Hagar and Yishmael away. God affirmed this action (21:12), so Hagar and Yishmael were sent away to wander in the wilderness of Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba). When their water was gone, God miraculously rescued them and assured Hagar that Yishmael would father a great nation (21:17-19).

Paulos (Paul) made an analogy (Gal 4:22-31) in which Hagar represents Mount Sinay (Sinai), where the old covenant was formed, while Sarah represents the heavenly Yerushalem (Jerusalem), the community of those who receive salvation by faith in Christ. As Yitshak was Avraham’s son by faith in the divine promise, Christians who are free of the law are spiritual children of Sarah.
Passages for Further Study
Yishmael (Ishmael)

Yishmael was Avraham’s (Abraham’s) first son, born of Hagar, Sarah’s Mitsri (Egyptian) servant. The boy was born near Hevron (Hebron) when Avraham was eighty-six years old (Gen 13:18; 16:16). God had promised to make a great nation of the childless Avraham (12:2) and assured him that he would have a son to be his heir (15:4). Yishmael was born in Avraham’s attempt to fulfill God’s promise by human means (see 16:1-16; Gal 4:23), but God would nevertheless accomplish his purposes through Sarah (see Gen 17:15–18:15; 21:1-7).

When God announced that Sarah would have a son to fulfill the promise (17:15-16), Avraham asked God to accept Yishmael (17:17-18). Yishmael was not the promised son—the covenant would be established with Yitshak (Isaac) (17:19)—but God did bless Yishmael and make him the father of a great nation (17:20-21).

At age thirteen, Yishmael was circumcised in accordance with God’s covenant with Avraham (17:9-14, 23-27). Later, at Yitshak’s weaning celebration (when Yishmael was about seventeen), Yishmael made fun of Yitshak (21:9), and Avraham sent Yishmael and Hagar away with provisions. The angel of God helped Hagar survive in the wilderness, and Yishmael became a wild game hunter. He settled in the wilderness of Paran and married an Mitsri woman (21:20-21). He assisted in Avraham’s burial (25:9-10), gave his daughter Mahalat (Mahalath) in marriage to Esav (Esau) (28:9), and died at age 137 (25:17). His twelve sons are named in Genesis 25:13-15.

Paulos (Paul) alluded to Yishmael when urging the Galatians to put their faith in God rather than in the law (see Gal 4:21-31). Those who trust the law will not inherit the kingdom, just as the slave woman’s son did not inherit with the son of the free woman (Gal 4:30).
Passages for Further Study
Sarah

Sarah was Avraham’s (Abraham’s) wife and half sister (Gen 11:29; 20:12). She accompanied Avraham from Ur to Haran to Kena’an (Canaan) (11:31; 12:5). On two occasions, in Mitsrayim (Egypt) (12:10-20) and Gerar (20:1-18), Avraham asked Sarah to say that she was his sister rather than his wife because he was afraid that he would be killed as her husband. In both cases, despite Avraham’s lack of faith, God protected Sarah, thus preserving the chosen line through whom he promised to multiply the Israeli (Israelite) nation (12:2; 17:19).

Sarah is one of several women in Scripture who were barren but miraculously bore a son (see also Gen 30:22-24; 1 Sam 1:9-20; 2 Kgs 4:14-17; Luke 1:5-25). After a series of promises from God, Sarah eventually conceived and gave birth to Yitshak (Isaac). Because Sarah was ninety years old when this happened (cp. Gen 17:17; 21:1-5), she testifies to God’s ability to do what is humanly impossible. Her name Saray (Sarai) was changed to Sarah on one of the occasions when Yitshak’s birth was promised (17:15-16). Sarah is honored for her faithfulness, even though she laughed at the prediction of Yitshak’s birth (18:10-15), twenty-five years after God’s original promise to Avraham.

Sarah died at age 127 and was buried in the cave that Avraham purchased (Gen 23) at Makpelah (Machpelah). She is known as the mother of the nation of Yisrael (Israel) (Isa 51:2), just as Avraham is its father. She is a key player in accounts of Avraham’s faith (see Rom 4:19). She represents the freedom that Christians have (as children of Sarah the free woman) through faith in Christ (see Gal 4:21-31). Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) cites her as an example of holy submission (1 Pet 3:5-6). The writer of Hebrews presents Sarah as an example of faith, for she believed in God’s ability to keep his promises (Heb 11:11-12). Her life demonstrates that God is indeed faithful, though his timing may not always match our expectations.
Passages for Further Study
Lot

Lot was Avraham’s (Abraham’s) nephew and the ancestor of the Moavim (Moabites) and Amonim (Ammonites). Like Avraham, Lot was born in Ur and accompanied Terah to Haran (Gen 11:27-32). After Terah’s death, he joined Avraham in journeying to Kena’an (Canaan) and Mitsrayim (Egypt).

When Lot and Avraham returned from Mitsrayim to Kena’an, their flocks and herds grew too numerous for them to live together, so Avraham gave Lot his choice of land on which to settle. Lot chose the fertile plain of the Yarden (Jordan) that was like “the garden of Yahweh” (Gen 13:10), and eventually he took up residence in Sedom (Sodom). Lot’s increasing involvement with the completely corrupt cities of the plain compromised him.

While Lot lived in Sedom, four Mesopotamian kings defeated the kings of five towns in the area; in the subsequent plundering, they carried off Lot, his family, and his possessions (Gen 14:1-12). When word of this reached Avraham, he launched a rearguard action against the invaders and recovered the prisoners and property (14:13-16).

Because of the wickedness of Sedom and the neighboring city of Amorah (Gomorrah), God decided to destroy these towns. He sent two angelic visitors to Lot in Sedom to encourage his departure from the doomed city (Gen 19:1-15). The city’s depravity became even more evident in an attempted homosexual attack on the visitors. Lot’s willingness to sacrifice his daughters, along with his reluctance to leave Sedom, shows how corrupt and compromised he had become. No one but his immediate family accompanied him, and his wife was destroyed when she turned back in disobedience. Soon after the destruction of Sedom, Lot’s daughters, despairing of having no husbands, got Lot drunk enough to have sexual relations with them. Their two sons, Moav (Moab) and Ben-Ami (Ben-ammi), were ancestors of the Moavim and Amonim (Gen 19:30-38), two nations that became inveterate enemies of Yisrael (Israel) (see Deut 23:3-6). Despite Lot’s waywardness, Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) declares that Lot was a “righteous man who was tormented in his soul by the wickedness he saw and heard day after day” (see 2 Pet 2:6-9). This analysis of Lot may stem from Jewish interpretive tradition, as it is difficult to see in the Genesis account.
Passages for Further Study
Yitshak (Isaac)

The name Yitshak means “he laughs,” reflecting the circumstances of his birth. When God promised that Yitshak would be born, both Avraham (Abraham) and Sarah first laughed in disbelief (Gen 17:15-19; 18:9-15). God had promised Avraham a son (15:4-6), but no son had come, and Avraham and Sarah were beyond childbearing age. So at Yitshak’s birth, they laughed for joy (21:6-7).

During Yitshak’s adolescence, God tested Avraham by telling him to sacrifice Yitshak (22:1-19). Avraham’s faith remained firm; he obeyed, and Yitshak submitted to his father. God then intervened to provide a sacrificial ram in Yitshak’s place. Avraham’s faith in God was rewarded with the promise of great blessings (22:15-18).

Yitshak married Rivkah (Rebekah) and was ready to carry on the chosen line, but Rivkah was unable to bear children (25:21). Rather than take matters into his own hands as his father had done (see 16:1-16), Yitshak “pleaded with Yahweh” and Rivkah bore twin sons. Yitshak favored Esav (Esau), the older son, while Rivkah preferred Ya’akov (Jacob). This favoritism led to Yitshak’s being deceived by his son Ya’akov when he was old and blind (27:1-40). Favoritism remained a problem among Yitshak’s descendants (see 29:30; 33:1-2; 37:4).

Yitshak followed his father Avraham’s example in relating to surrounding nations. When visiting another kingdom during a famine, he fearfully claimed that his wife was his sister (26:1-11; cp. 12:10-20; 20:1-18). Like his father, Yitshak became prosperous in that land and was asked to leave (26:12-16; cp. 12:16-20); he experienced conflict over water and land with other herdsmen (26:17-22; cp. 21:25-31); and he made a treaty with the king of the Pelishtim (Philistines) (26:26-31; cp. 21:22-32).

Yitshak was given the same promise that his father had received (26:2-5, 23-25; cp. 22:16-18), and he demonstrated his participation by carrying on the practice of circumcision, which signified the covenant (see Acts 7:8). As the child of promise, Yitshak represents all who are children of Avraham by faith in Christ and are thereby free to live as God’s children rather than as slaves (see Gal 4:21–5:1).
Passages for Further Study
Hitim (Hittites)

The Hitim were once unknown to secular history and thought to be a mythical people by some critics of biblical history. But information about the Hitim has been uncovered by archaeologists and historians, and they are now known to have had an empire centered in Asia Minor, with their capital at Hattusha (modern Baghazkoy). At times the empire extended over a much larger area without definite boundaries since it included city-states that were dependencies by treaty. They were of sufficient military strength to challenge the armies of Mitsrayim (Egypt) under the vainglorious Ra’meses (Rameses) II (1279–1213 BC) and fought him to a standstill at Kadesh on the Orontes (ca. 1274 BC). In patriarchal times, the Hitim held power in cities like Hevron (Hebron) in Kena’an (Canaan).

The progenitor of the Hitim, Het (Heth), is listed second among the sons of Kena’an in the “table of nations” (Gen 10:15; see also 1 Chr 1:13 and the textual footnote there). Most of the references to the sons of Het appear in the narrative of the purchase of the cave of Makpelah (Machpelah) by Avraham (Abraham) (Gen 23). Later, God commanded the people of Yisrael (Israel) to destroy all the Hitim living in the Promised Land (Deut 7:1-2), but Yisrael did not completely do so (1 Kgs 9:20-21). Some of David’s best warriors were from Hiti (Hittite) ancestry (1 Sam 26:6; 2 Sam 11–12), and Shelomoh (Solomon) engaged in trade with Hiti kings (1 Kgs 10:29–11:1). The Bible thus suggests that the Hitim were a people of great consequence.
Passages for Further Study
Rivkah (Rebekah)

Genesis 24 describes the mission of Avraham’s (Abraham’s) servant to find a wife for Yitshak (Isaac). At Avraham’s command, he went to Haran in Aram-Naharayim (Aram-naharaim) (northwest Mesopotamia), to Avraham’s relatives, because Avraham did not want Yitshak to marry a local Kena’ani (Canaanite). The servant prayed that the young woman God had selected to be Yitshak’s wife would answer his request for a drink by immediately giving it and watering his camels as well (24:12-14). This would not only serve to confirm God’s will in the matter but would also demonstrate her character, hospitality, and work ethic.
God decisively answered his prayer with Rivkah, the daughter of Betuel (Bethuel) (22:23; 25:20), the son of Avraham’s brother Nahor (24:24).

When Avraham’s servant described how God had led him (24:34-49), Rivkah’s family recognized it as God’s hand, but they were reluctant to let her go immediately (24:50-56). Rivkah, however, demonstrated faith in God’s plan; she was willing to leave her family without delay to marry Yitshak (24:57-58). Rivkah’s faith was richly rewarded; the blessing her family gave her in parting (24:59-60) came true when she bore to Yitshak the next generation of God’s chosen line.

Rivkah bore twins, Esav (Esau) and Ya’akov (Jacob) (25:20-26). She preferred Ya’akov, the younger son, who God had told her would be the stronger one and the leader of the two (25:23). Rivkah helped Ya’akov seize the blessing of the firstborn by deceiving Yitshak (27:1-40). Afterward, she arranged for Ya’akov to be sent to Haran to get away from his brother’s resulting anger (27:41–28:5). Rivkah’s deceptive scheme created a lasting schism in the family, and she apparently never saw her favorite son again. She was, however, buried with Yitshak in the family burial site (49:31), and she fulfilled God’s plan as the mother of Ya’akov, the founding father of Yisrael (Israel).
Passages for Further Study
Esav (Esau)

Esav, the son of Yitshak (Isaac) and Rivkah (Rebekah), was Ya’akov’s (Jacob’s) older twin brother (Gen 25:24-26), so named because his body was hairy at birth. His descendants were called Edomim (Edomites) (“Edom” meaning “red”) on account of his reddish color at birth (25:25), the red lentil stew he received from Ya’akov (25:30), and the reddish color of the land in which he settled (see study note on Gen 25:25).

Esav was a proficient hunter who brought tasty wild meat to his father. Yitshak enjoyed its strong flavor more than the mild meat Ya’akov provided from the family flocks. One day Esav returned home very hungry from an unsuccessful hunt, and Ya’akov persuaded Esav to surrender his birthright in exchange for food (25:29-34). Esav had little regard for his birthright and was controlled by his carnal desires (see Heb 12:16). He also married two local women who were not Avraham’s (Abraham’s) descendants (Gen 26:34-35), which may have fed into Rivkah’s favoritism toward Ya’akov and her idea about stealing the blessing of Yitshak that was intended for Esav (27:1-40). Esav’s anger on discovering his brother’s deception prompted Ya’akov to flee for Haran. The brothers were reunited twenty years later when Esav demonstrated gracious forgiveness (33:1-16).

Esav was born with Ya’akov grasping his heel; this omen was interpreted to mean that Esav’s descendants would be subject to Ya’akov’s offspring. The subservient relationship between the Edomim and the Israelis (Israelites) began in David’s time (2 Sam 8:11-15; 1 Chr 18:11-13) and continued until the reign of Yehoram (Jehoram) (2 Kgs 8:20-22; 2 Chr 21:8-10). Following a rebellion in 845 BC, the Edomim briefly gained their independence but were conquered again by Amatsyah (Amaziah) (796–767 BC). They regained their freedom in 735 BC and then remained independent of Yehudah (Judah).

In the New Testament, Esav represents the line of Avraham’s descendants who lacked the gift of faith and were rejected by God as recipients of his promised blessings (see Rom 9:6-24). Herodes (Herod) the Great was an Edomi (Edomite).
Passages for Further Study
Rahel (Rachel)

Rahel, Lavan’s (Laban’s) beautiful younger daughter, was Ya’akov’s (Jacob’s) favorite wife. He first met her as he arrived at Padan-Aram (Paddan-aram) in Haran, when he helped her remove the stone from a well and watered her father’s sheep (Gen 29:10). Ya’akov agreed to work seven years for Lavan in order to have Rahel as his wife, and the time seemed like only a few days because of his great love for her.

Lavan deceptively required Ya’akov to marry Le’ah (Leah), his older, less attractive daughter, before finally giving him Rahel. Unlike Le’ah, Rahel was barren in the early years of her marriage to Ya’akov (29:31; 30:1). She gave her servant Bilhah to Ya’akov in order to have children by her, and Dan and Naftali (Naphtali) were born (30:3-8). In time, Rahel conceived and bore Yosef (Joseph) (30:22-24), and soon after, Ya’akov took his wives, children, and possessions away from Haran.

Somewhere between Beyt-El (Bethel) and Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem), Rahel died while giving birth to Benyamin (Benjamin) (35:16-20). Ya’akov set up a pillar over her tomb that was a landmark even in Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) time (1 Sam 10:2). Rahel and Le’ah are highly regarded for having built up the house of Yisrael (Israel) (Ruth 4:11). In Jeremiah 31:15, Rahel is pictured as crying for her children being carried off into captivity, and Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios) recalls Yirmiyah’s (Jeremiah’s) words at Herodes’s (Herod’s) slaughter of the male infants around Beyt-Lehem shortly after Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) birth (Matt 2:16-18).
Passages for Further Study
Le’ah (Leah)
Le’ah was Lavan’s (Laban’s) first daughter, Ya’akov’s (Jacob’s) unloved first wife, and Rahel’s (Rachel’s) older sister.

After Ya’akov deceived his father Yitshak (Isaac) into giving him the blessing intended for Esav (Esau) (Gen 27:1-40), Ya’akov went to his uncle Lavan in Mesopotamia to escape Esav’s revenge and find a wife (27:41–28:5). He fell in love with his cousin Rahel and arranged with her father to marry her after seven years of work (29:17-20). After the wedding feast, Lavan deceived Ya’akov by giving him Le’ah instead of Rahel (29:21-25), claiming that custom required the older daughter to marry first (29:26). Le’ah was less attractive than her sister (29:17), and Ya’akov did not love her (29:30-35).

Ya’akov’s love for Rahel induced him to work another seven years to marry her. Because Ya’akov favored Rahel, the Lord blessed Le’ah with six sons and a daughter (Re’uven (Reuben), Shim’on (Simeon), Levi, Yehudah (Judah), Yisakar (Issachar), Zevulun (Zebulun), and Dinah) before Rahel was able to conceive (29:31–30:22). At one point Rahel bargained with Le’ah for some mandrakes, a plant believed to ensure conception, in exchange for conjugal rights. Le’ah then conceived and bore her fifth son (30:14-17), increasing her advantage in her rivalry with Rahel.

Le’ah was the mother of two tribes that played particularly significant roles in Israeli (Israelite) history. The tribe of Levi was the tribe of the priesthood, and the tribe of Yehudah became the tribe of royalty through which the promised seed (Gen 3:15; 12:2-3; 2 Sam 7:16; Matt 1:1) came in the person of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ.
Passages for Further Study
Yosef (Joseph)

Yosef is known for his dreams and for the beautiful coat his father, Ya’akov (Jacob), gave him. He is an example of faith, prudence, and administrative ability. Despite overwhelming difficulties, Yosef saved Kena’an (Canaan), Mitsrayim (Egypt), and his own family from starvation during seven years of drought.

Yosef was Ya’akov’s eleventh son, the first child of Ya’akov’s favorite wife, Rahel (Rachel). Yosef’s name means “may he add,” expressing Rahel’s desire that God give her another son (Gen 30:24). Rahel later died at the birth of Benyamin (Benjamin), Yosef’s only full brother.

Yosef’s brothers resented him because of his dreams. They sold him to a passing caravan and led Ya’akov to believe an animal had killed him. In Mitsrayim, Yosef quickly rose in prominence, until he was jailed when his master’s wife falsely accused him. In prison he correctly interpreted dreams for fellow inmates and was later summoned when Par’oh (Pharaoh) couldn’t understand his own dreams. Yosef interpreted Par’oh’s dreams—which were about an upcoming famine—with insight and wisdom, so Par’oh released him (thirteen years after he had been brought to Mitsrayim as a slave) and appointed him to lead the nation in preparation for the famine. When Yosef’s brothers had to buy grain in Mitsrayim, they appeared before him, but they did not recognize him. Later, their remorse and Yehudah’s (Judah’s) intercession provoked Yosef to disclose his identity. The family was reconciled and reunited when Ya’akov came to live in Mitsrayim.

Because Ya’akov blessed Yosef’s sons, Efrayim (Ephraim) and Menasheh (Manasseh), and took them as his own (48:5-20), each was considered a separate tribe later in Yisrael (Israel). Efrayim, whom Ya’akov put first and to whom he gave the birthright (48:17-20), became one of the strongest tribes of Yisrael and the leading tribe in the northern kingdom after the division during Rehav’am’s (Rehoboam’s) reign (see 1 Kgs 11:26–12:33). Several of the prophets refer to the northern kingdom under the names Efrayim (e.g., Ezek 37:15-19; Hos 5:3-5) and Yosef (e.g., Obad 1:18).

Yosef had faith that the Israelis (Israelites) would someday return to the land God had promised them, so his dying wish was that his bones be buried in Kena’an when they left Mitsrayim (Gen 50:24-26; see Exod 13:19; Josh 24:32). Yosef’s story dramatizes the life of a man of faith and godly character who fulfilled God’s plan. His name is mentioned frequently in Scripture, showing that he was highly regarded by later Israelis. His story is summarized in the Psalms (Ps 105:16-22) and in Stefanos’s (Stephen’s) speech just prior to his martyrdom (Acts 7:9-14).

Yosef’s life confirms God’s control of the long course of history even when bad things happen (Gen 50:20). God expresses his sovereign power through his provident, faithful love for his people. Yosef also models for us a firm faith in the sovereign God and personal integrity in the face of adversity.
Passages for Further Study
Yehudah (Judah)

Yehudah is remembered most often as the ancestor of King David and of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ. Despite his birth as a middle child and his sins as an adult (Gen 38), God chose Yehudah to carry the line of King David (1 Chr 2:1-17; 3:1-24) and of the Messiah (Gen 49:8-12; Matt 1:1-16; Luke 3:23-34).

Yehudah was the fourth of Ya’akov’s (Jacob’s) twelve sons (Gen 35:23; 1 Chr 2:1). Le’ah (Leah), overjoyed to have borne her fourth son, named him Yehudah, meaning “praise” (Gen 29:35). Yehudah fathered five sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah by Bathshua, a woman from Kena’an (Canaan) (Gen 38:1-5; 1 Chr 2:3); and the twins, Perets (Perez) and Zerah, by his daughter-in-law Tamar (Gen 38:27-30; 1 Chr 2:4). God killed his first two sons, Er and Onan, in Kena’an for disobedience (Gen 46:12). Yehudah eventually settled his family in Mitsrayim (Egypt) with his father and brothers (Exod 1:1-2).

Though reckless in his behavior with Tamar (Gen 38:6-30), Yehudah took personal responsibility for Benyamin’s (Benjamin’s) safety in Mitsrayim and interceded with Yosef (Joseph) for his brothers (44:14-34). When Ya’akov gave his dying blessing, he granted Yehudah a position of leadership; the future kings of Yisrael (Israel) would come through Yehudah’s offspring (see 49:10).
Passages for Further Study
Avraham (Abraham)

“By faith . . . Avraham obeyed when God called him to leave home and go to another land. . . . He went without knowing where he was going. . . . By faith . . . Avraham offered Yitshak (Isaac) as a sacrifice when God was testing him” (Heb 11:8, 17). These key events in Avraham’s life illustrate the faithful obedience for which he is best known.

God called Avram (Abram) from the city of Ur to become the patriarch of God’s people. Avram’s family relationships are recorded in Genesis 11:26-32. Terah had three sons: Avram, Nahor, and Haran. Terah left Ur with Avram, Avram’s wife Saray (Sarai), and Lot, whose father, Haran, had died. On his way to Kena’an (Canaan), Terah settled in the city of Haran (11:31). God had called Avram to a new land while he was still in Ur (Acts 7:2-4). God told Avram, “Leave your native country, your relatives, and your father’s family, and go to the land that I will show you” (Gen 12:1). God blessed Avram by making a covenant with him that included promises of great blessing, numerous descendants, and a new land (12:1-3). These promises later saved Yisrael (Israel) from destruction when they repeatedly failed to keep their covenant with God (see Lev 26:40-45).

Avram left Haran at age seventy-five. Entering Kena’an, he went first to Shekem (Shechem), a Kena’ani (Canaanite) city between Mount Gerizim and Mount Eyval (Ebal). God appeared to Avram near the oak of Moreh, likely a Kena’ani shrine. Avram built altars there and near Beyt-El (Bethel) (Gen 12:6-8), proclaiming the one true God at these centers of false worship. Avram later moved to Hevron (Hebron) by the oaks of Mamre, again building an altar to worship God (13:18).

When God again promised blessings to Avram in a vision (15:1), Avram exclaimed that he was still childless because Saray was barren (11:30) and that Eliezer of Damesek (Damascus) was his heir (15:2). This obscure statement is clarified by the Nuzi documents, discovered at the site of the ancient Mesopotamian city of Nuzi. According to Hurrian custom, a childless couple of means could adopt an heir, often a slave who would be responsible for their burial and mourning. However, a natural son born after the slave-heir’s adoption would supplant him. Apparently Avram had adopted Eliezer in this manner, but God promised that Avram’s own son would be his heir (15:4).

The hallmark of Avram’s life was that he believed the Lord, and the Lord considered him righteous because of his faith (Gen 15:6; see Rom 4:3; Gal 3:6; Jas 2:23). Avram was declared righteous not because he was sinless. On several occasions he failed to do what was right—twice he lied about Saray out of fear, and he took the provision of a son into his own hands with Hagar rather than continuing to wait for God to act (Gen 16:1-5). But he consistently returned to faith as the fundamental principle of his life before God.

Avram was eighty-six years old when Yishmael (Ishmael) was born to Saray’s servant Hagar. When Avram was ninety-nine, the Lord appeared to him and reaffirmed his covenant promise of a son and of blessing (Gen 17), adding circumcision as the mark of the covenant relationship (17:9-14). God also changed Avram’s and Saray’s names to Avraham and Sarah (17:5, 15). Avraham laughed at the promise of another son (17:17). Shortly afterward, the Lord appeared again to Avraham (18:1-15) and again announced the promised son. This time, Sarah was caught laughing in disbelief (18:10-15). Avraham was one hundred years old and his wife was ninety when the Lord did “exactly what he had promised” (21:1). The long-promised son was born and was fittingly named Yitshak (“he laughs!”).

The supreme test of Avraham’s faith came when God commanded him to sacrifice Yitshak (22:1-19). Avraham obeyed faithfully, trusting that God would not thwart his own purposes (see Heb 11:17-19). Just as the knife was about to fall, the angel of God stopped Avraham and provided a ram for him to sacrifice in Yitshak’s place. Avraham’s faith was complete (22:10-13).

Christians understand the sacrifice of Yitshak as prefiguring God’s provision of his only Son, Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ, as a sacrifice for the sins of the world. God has fulfilled his covenant with Avraham through Yeshua Christ, through whom the blessing of salvation is extended to all who have faith (Rom 4:16-17), making believers Avraham’s spiritual descendants (Gal 3:29). Avraham’s life shows that God is faithful and worthy of belief and obedience. The full import of God’s promise was realized when the gospel was preached to all nations and people from all families of the earth responded in faith (see Gal 3:6-9).

Avraham was called God’s friend (2 Chr 20:7; Jas 2:23). All who live by faith are challenged to live as he did, daily venturing into the unknown with trust in God’s guidance and sustenance. Avraham is one of many great “witnesses” to a life of faith (Heb 12:1; see Heb 11), inspiring believers to persevere in faith because we know God is faithful.
Passages for Further Study
Ya’akov (Jacob)

Ya’akov, the younger twin son of Yitshak (Isaac) and Rivkah (Rebekah), struggled with his twin brother Esav (Esau) in the womb and was born grasping Esav’s heel (Gen 25:21-26). God told Rivkah that the boys represented two nations and that the older son would serve the younger (Gen. 25:23).

Yitshak favored Esav, an outdoorsman; Rivkah preferred Ya’akov, who was happier at home. Once, Esav returned famished from hunting and Ya’akov bought his birthright with some red stew he had cooked (Gen 25:27-34; see Heb 12:16). Some time later, Yitshak asked Esav to prepare wild game so he could eat and bless him (Gen 27:1-4; cp. 25:28). But Rivkah sent Ya’akov to deceive Yitshak into blessing him instead, and her ploy was successful (27:5-29). Ya’akov’s ruse was soon discovered (27:30-35), but legally, valid blessings were irrevocable promises (27:33). So Yitshak gave Esav a lesser blessing (27:36-40), and Esav plotted to kill Ya’akov (27:41). Rivkah convinced Yitshak to send Ya’akov away to her brother Lavan (Laban) so that Ya’akov would marry among relatives (27:42-46).

So Yitshak transferred the covenant promises to Ya’akov and sent him to Haran (28:1-5). Along the way, God appeared to Ya’akov in a dream and affirmed the promises of land and descendants that he had given to Avraham (Abraham) and Yitshak (28:10-15). Ya’akov worshiped the Lord and named the place Beyt-El (Bethel) (“house of God”).

At Haran, Ya’akov began to serve his uncle Lavan (Gen 29–31). Ya’akov loved Lavan’s daughter Rahel (Rachel) and worked seven years to marry her, but Lavan deceived him by substituting his older daughter Le’ah (Leah) on Ya’akov’s wedding night. Ya’akov worked seven more years for Rahel and an additional six years to acquire flocks for himself (30:25-43; see also 31:38-42). Despite many hardships, he had thirteen children and became very prosperous.

After twenty years, God told Ya’akov to return to Kena’an (Canaan) (31:3). Fearing reprisals from Lavan and his sons (31:1-2), Ya’akov organized his caravan and left while Lavan was away (31:4-21). Lavan gave chase, but God prevented him from harming Ya’akov (31:22-24, 29). Lavan instead upbraided Ya’akov for leaving stealthily and for stealing his idols (31:25-30). Ya’akov let Lavan search his tents, but the idols were not found (31:33-35), and Ya’akov became angry (31:36-42). Though their conflict remained unresolved, the two men made a peace covenant (31:43-54); the location formed a lasting boundary between Yisrael (Israel) and Aram.

Ya’akov now faced Esav and God. When Esav came to meet him with four hundred men, Ya’akov sought God’s protection and sent gifts to pacify his estranged brother (32:3-21). Meanwhile, that night, in an event that symbolized his whole life, Ya’akov wrestled with a man who dislocated his hip and gave him the blessing he sought (32:22-32). God also changed his name to Yisrael (“God fights”).

In the morning Ya’akov met Esav and the two were reconciled (33:1-11); Esav was gracious and forgiving, and Ya’akov shared some of his blessing. Esav then returned to Se’ir (Seir) while Ya’akov continued to Kena’an. In Shekem (Shechem), Ya’akov bought land and built an altar (33:18-20), then moved to Beyt-El and expelled all foreign idols from his household (35:1-8). God reaffirmed Ya’akov’s new name, Yisrael, and renewed his promises of land and descendants (35:9-15).

Ya’akov’s favoritism for Rahel extended to her son Yosef (Joseph) (37:1-3). Yosef’s brothers became filled with jealousy and hatred toward Yosef—further fueled by Yosef’s dreams (37:4-11)—and they sold him as a slave (37:12-28). For over twenty years Ya’akov believed Yosef was dead. Only after letting Benyamin (Benjamin) go to Mitsrayim (Egypt) in Yehudah’s (Judah’s) care did Ya’akov learn that Yosef was alive and would be the source of famine relief for his family (43:1-14; 45:24-28). Ya’akov’s spirits revived, and he moved to Mitsrayim and joyously reunited with his favorite son at Goshen (46:28-30), where he prospered for seventeen more years.

When Ya’akov approached death at age 147, he arranged for the future of his family. He made Yosef swear to bury him in Kena’an (47:29-31; 49:29-32). He gave Yosef’s sons his prime blessing (48:1-20) and put Efrayim (Ephraim), the younger son, first. He gave assurance that the family would return to Kena’an (48:21-22), then blessed each of his sons and prophesied the future of their descendants (49:1-28). He died and was buried at the cave of Makpelah (Machpelah), accompanied by his sons and a large Mitsri (Egyptian) procession (49:33–50:13). His death marked the end of the patriarchal age and the beginning of Yisrael’s growth as a nation in Mitsrayim until they returned to live again in the Promised Land (see Exodus—Yehoshua (Joshua)).

The name “Ya’akov” became synonymous with the nation of Yisrael (see Num 23:7, 21; 24:5; Hos 12:2). God called the nation to serve him as their forefathers had done (Hos 12:3-14). He promised Yisrael the same love that he had shown toward Ya’akov (Mal 1:2). And he promised that a conquering ruler would come from Ya’akov’s descendants (Gen 49:8-12; Num 24:17-19).
Passages for Further Study
Mitsrayim (Egypt)

Mitsrayim was already a great and ancient civilization when Yosef (Joseph) rose to power (Gen 39–41) and Ya’akov’s (Jacob’s) family traveled there for food (chs 42–46; cp. 12:10-20). Its unique location and geography gave it security from invaders (with the harborless Mediterranean Sea to the north, the rugged Sinay (Sinai) peninsula to the east, and a great desert to the west) and made it an attractive refuge for foreigners during times of drought.

Mitsrayim has been called “the gift of the Nile,” and no other river has been so vital to the history of the nation through which it flows. To the Mitsrim (Egyptians) it was simply “the River.” The Nile is more than just the longest river in the world. Without its water, civilization would have been impossible in Mitsrayim—the Nile is Mitsrayim’s lifeblood, and the Mitsrim worshiped it for the life and fertility that it provided. The river’s annual floods constantly brought new and fertile soil for crops, and its waters provided food from its abundance of fish and waterfowl as well as fresh water for drinking and cleaning. It also functioned as the main means of travel, trade, and communication. During times of drought, when the surrounding nations were in danger of famine, the Nile gave Mitsrayim a reliable supply of fresh water. The Nile defined every aspect of life in Mitsrayim and made Mitsrayim what it was.

Mitsrayim figured significantly in biblical events. Avraham (Abraham) lived there in a time of famine (Gen 12:10-20). Yosef was sold into slavery in Mitsrayim and rose to a position equivalent to that of prime minister (Gen 37–41). Yosef’s family then came to reside in the eastern delta region of Goshen during another time of famine (Gen 42–50). Their descendants were later enslaved (Exod 1), and God’s rescue of his people in the exodus from Mitsrayim would become the central defining story of the Jewish people (Exod 2–15).

Later, during Yisrael’s (Israel’s) monarchy, Mitsrayim was continually involved in the struggle for international power (e.g., 1 Kgs 14:25-28). After the Babylonians destroyed Yerushalem (Jerusalem) in 586 BC, a group of Yehudim (Jews) moved to Mitsrayim to escape Bavel’s (Babylon’s) influence (Jer 43:6-7).

At the opening of the New Testament, Mitsrayim once again served as a refuge, this time for Yosef, Maria (Mary), and Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) as they fled the assassination attempts of Herodes (Herod) the Great (Matt 2:13-23).
Passages for Further Study
Aharon (Aaron)

Mosheh’s (Moses’) older brother, Aharon (see Exod 6:20; 7:7), played a crucial role in founding Yisrael (Israel) and its institutions, particularly the priesthood. He first appears after Mosheh’s calling at the burning bush (Exod 3:1–4:17). Mosheh was reluctant to accept his divine commission, claiming that he was unfit to lead the Israelis (Israelites) out of Mitsrayim (Egypt) because his words tended to “get tangled” (Exod 4:10). Despite God’s assurances, Mosheh continued to object until God appointed Aharon to be Mosheh’s mouthpiece. Thereafter, Aharon was often at Mosheh’s side, speaking to the Israeli (Israelite) leaders and demanding that Par’oh (Pharaoh) let the Israelis leave Mitsrayim (Exod 5:1-5).

During the Israelis’s wilderness wanderings, God appointed Aharon and his sons to be set apart and dedicated as priests (Exod 28:1-5; 29:1-46; Lev 8:1-36). Thus, Aharon became Yisrael’s first high priest. Aharon’s role as high priest was especially prominent on the annual Day of Atonement, the only day when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to purify it from the effects of Yisrael’s sins (Lev 16). Before the high priest could do so, however, he had to offer a sacrifice to atone for his own sins.

Aharon was an imperfect leader. While Mosheh was on Mount Sinay (Sinai) receiving the law from God, Aharon helped the people make an idol (Exod 32). When Mosheh returned, Aharon gave poor excuses and blamed the people. This event resulted in the death of three thousand Israelis, as well as a plague.

Aharon and his sister, Miryam (Miriam), once wrongly challenged Mosheh’s authority, resulting in a temporary state of leprosy for Miryam (Num 12). Later, when other Levites challenged Aharon’s authority, God affirmed Aharon’s role by making his staff bud with almond blossoms (Num 17). However, because Mosheh and Aharon challenged God’s authority (Num 20:1-13), they both died in the wilderness without entering the Promised Land (Num 20:22-29).
Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) has become the Great High Priest, far surpassing Aharon’s priestly authority and effectiveness (see Heb 7–10).
Passages for Further Study
Yitro (Jethro) (Re’uel (Reuel))

Yitro, also called Re’uel (Exod 2:16-18; Num 10:29), was “the priest of Midyan (Midian)” (Exod 2:16). Mosheh (Moses) rescued Yitro’s seven daughters from the rough treatment of other shepherds at a well and helped them water their flocks. At home they told their father of this surprising encounter with “an Mitsri (Egyptian).” Yitro responded gratefully by inviting Mosheh for a meal, and Mosheh proceeded to settle there. At a later point, Yitro gave his daughter Tsiporah (Zipporah) to Mosheh in marriage.

While Mosheh was still living in Midyan near his father-in-law, he encountered God at the burning bush (Exod 3:1-2). Before leaving for Mitsrayim (Egypt), Mosheh asked Yitro’s permission to go; he later sent his family to stay with Yitro during the Exodus.

When Mosheh and the Israelis (Israelites) were in the wilderness, Yitro returned with Mosheh’s family. Yitro, having heard of Yahweh’s deliverance of his people from Mitsrayim, acknowledged him as the God of all gods. He worshiped Yahweh with a burnt offering and sacrifices, thereby identifying himself with Yisrael (Israel) (18:11). In response, Yisrael’s leaders joined him for “a sacrificial meal in God’s presence” (18:12).

Yitro saw that Mosheh was overwhelmed with caring for the vast numbers of Israelis, so he gave Mosheh good administrative advice about organizing the people more efficiently and about judging disputes among the people (18:13-23). Mosheh listened to this counsel and appointed able men to assist him as leaders and judges over the people (18:24-27). Yitro returned to Midyan and seems not to have interacted further with Yisrael, but his son (Num 10:29-33) and other descendants later settled with the Israelis (Judg 1:16; 4:11).
Passages for Further Study
Par’oh (Pharaoh)

“Par’oh” is an Mitsri (Egyptian) word meaning “great house.” It refers to the royal palace and is also used as a title for the king of Mitsrayim (Egypt). During the time of Yosef (Joseph), the Israelis (Israelites) were looked upon favorably by the pharaoh. Yosef had interpreted Par’oh’s dreams, leading to his promotion as second-in-command in Mitsrayim (Gen 41:1-44). Par’oh gave Yosef’s family the best land in Mitsrayim (Gen 45:16-20), and the Israelis multiplied and flourished in Mitsrayim.

Two pharaohs appear in the book of Exodus, neither of whom had the same regard for the Hebrew people (see Exod 1:8-10). The first was king when Mosheh (Moses) was born. Out of fear, he ordered the murder of all Hebrew baby boys. Mosheh not only escaped death, but was raised by Par’oh’s daughter in the palace! This pharaoh died after Mosheh had fled from Mitsrayim (Exod 2:23).

A new pharaoh came to power, whom Mosheh and Aharon (Aaron) later confronted. This pharaoh was determined to prevent the Israelis from leaving Mitsrayim; he remained stubborn even when confronted with God’s power. The Bible describes his hard-hearted unwillingness to change (see Exod 8:32; 9:12, 34-35; cp. Rom 1:18-32).

As king, the pharaoh personified the rule of the gods over Mitsrayim, which gave him absolute authority. The plagues were God’s attacks on the false gods of Mitsrayim (see Exod 12:12). The final plague—the death of the firstborn—was an attack on Par’oh’s household. This climactic plague convinced Par’oh to let Yisrael (Israel) go, but after the Israelis left, Par’oh again changed his mind. He chased them until he had cornered them at the Red Sea. God’s rescue of the defenseless Israelis and the destruction of the powerful Mitsrim (Egyptians) at the Red Sea is among the most dramatic rescues recorded in the Old Testament. The Lord revealed himself at the Red Sea as a warrior who fought for his people (15:3).

Neither of the pharaohs in Exodus is mentioned by name, probably in keeping with Mitsri practice. However, if the Exodus took place in the 1400s BC, the Par’oh of the Exodus might have been Thutmose III (around 1504–1450 BC). If the Exodus occurred in the 1200s BC (based on an alternative chronology), this pharaoh might have been Ra’meses (Rameses) II (around 1279–1213 BC).
Passages for Further Study
Mosheh (Moses)

Mosheh was the founding leader of Yisrael (Israel) as a nation. God used Mosheh at a critical juncture in the history of his people. He was the prophet who received the law and mediated God’s covenant with Yisrael at Mount Sinay (Sinai) (Exod 19:3-6). He was also the first known writer of Scripture.

The younger brother of Miryam (Miriam) and Aharon (Aaron), Mosheh was born in Mitsrayim (Egypt) under dangerous circumstances (Exod 1:15–2:2). The Mitsri (Egyptian) pharaoh, fearing a rebellion, had decreed that all Hebrew boys be killed at birth. Mosheh’s mother, Yokeved (Jochebed), entrusted her infant son to God and set him afloat in the Nile in a reed basket. Par’oh’s (Pharaoh’s) daughter found him and took him into the palace to raise as her own child (Exod 2:3-10).

Little is known about Mosheh’s upbringing. Jewish tradition holds that he received both administrative and military training in Par’oh’s household. When he was about forty years old, he killed an Mitsri to rescue a Hebrew slave, and then he fled to Midyan (Midian) (2:11-15; cp. Acts 7:23-29). There he rescued some young women who were being harassed as they watered their flocks. Their father (Yitro (Jethro)) invited him home. Mosheh married one of the women, Tsiporah (Zipporah), and began a family as he cared for his father-in-law’s flocks.

About forty years later, God revealed himself to Mosheh in a burning bush and commissioned Mosheh to return to Mitsrayim to rescue his people from slavery (Exod 3:1–4:17). Mosheh hesitated, fearful that the Israelis (Israelites) would not accept him as their leader. So God revealed to Mosheh his covenant name, Yahweh, and assigned Aharon as Mosheh’s spokesman.

Mosheh and Aharon went to Mitsrayim and confronted Par’oh, who stubbornly resisted Mosheh’s demand that he free the Israeli (Israelite) slaves. Mosheh then announced a series of plagues, which eventually convinced Par’oh to let the Israelis leave. After they had left Mitsrayim, Par’oh changed his mind and pursued them to the edge of the Red Sea. God enabled the Israelis to cross safely to the other side by dividing the waters; the pursuing Mitsri army was destroyed when the waters closed over them.

Mosheh led Yisrael to Mount Sinay, where he had encountered God at the burning bush. God again revealed himself to Mosheh on that mountain, giving him the law (including the Ten Commandments; Exod 20:1–23:19) and directions for building the Tabernacle. But when Mosheh came down from the mountain, he found that the people had already deserted the true God by worshiping a gold calf (Exod 32). Mosheh threw down and broke the two tablets of the law and rallied the Levites to execute some of the offenders. After praying for the people, he received a new copy of the law and led the people in building the Tabernacle.

Mosheh led a grumbling, rebellious, and distrustful people through the wilderness. Even his own brother and sister challenged his leadership, using his marriage to a Kushi (Cushite) woman as an excuse (Num 12). Mosheh responded with great humility, and God affirmed that Mosheh was his spokesman and confidant.

Mosheh was a great man, but not a perfect one. When the people stretched his patience by complaining about a lack of water, Mosheh failed to follow God’s instructions and struck a certain rock rather than speaking to it (Num 20:1-13). His actions failed to demonstrate God’s holiness, and by what he said, Mosheh implied that he had brought the water by his own power (Num 20:10; cp. Ps 106:32-33). As a result, God did not allow him to enter the Promised Land.

Before his death, Mosheh delivered a final sermon, known to us as the book of Deuteronomy. The first generation of Israelis, who had come out of Mitsrayim, had died in the wilderness, so Mosheh was addressing a new generation. Mosheh renewed the covenant with this generation, reminded them of its terms, and encouraged them to obey it and serve the Lord alone.

After giving this sermon and before Yisrael entered Kena’an (Canaan), Mosheh climbed Pisgah Peak on Mount Nevo (Nebo), where he died. “There has never been another prophet in Yisrael like Mosheh, whom Yahweh knew face to face” (Deut 34:10). Only Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) surpassed Mosheh as a mediator between God and human beings (Acts 3:17-26; Heb 3).

Mosheh (Moses) is mentioned in the New Testament more than any other Old Testament figure, and he appeared at Yeshua’s transfiguration. The New Testament emphasizes his role as lawgiver and draws from Mosheh’s experiences to show patterns of life under the new covenant. Like Mosheh, Yeshua was rescued as an infant from the evil designs of a human despot (Matt 2:13-18). Yeshua’s proclamation of a new law in his Sermon on the Mount (Matt 5–7) parallels the giving of the law at Sinay and presents Yeshua as the authoritative interpreter of God’s will. The letter to the Hebrews compares Christ with Mosheh, while Paulos’s (Paul’s) letter to the Galatians and the Gospel of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) contrast the law of Mosheh with a believer’s new relationship with God (see John 1:17; Gal 3:1-5; Heb 3:5-6; 9:11–10:18).
Passages for Further Study
Eleazar

Eleazar was the third son of Aharon (Aaron), the first high priest (Exod 6:23). Eleazar’s two older brothers, Nadav (Nadab) and Avihu (Abihu), offended God by offering incense in a different way than what God had commanded (Lev 10:1-7). Because of their disobedience, God killed them. Since Eleazar was the next oldest son, he was now in line to succeed his father as high priest. He performed priestly duties during his father’s lifetime, and he helped his father and Mosheh (Moses) when some Levites rebelled because they wanted equal status with Aharon’s priestly family (Num 16:36-40).

Aharon died in the wilderness a short time before the Israelis (Israelites) entered the Promised Land. He was not allowed to enter because he and Mosheh had rebelled against God by striking the rock at Merivah (Meribah) (20:1-13). Before Aharon’s death, he, Mosheh, and Eleazar went up on Mount Hor, where Mosheh removed the priestly garments from Aharon and put them on his son (20:22-29).

After this, Eleazar served as high priest for the rest of his life, which included the time of Kena’an’s (Canaan’s) conquest. When it was time to divide the land among the tribes, Eleazar and Yehoshua (Joshua) cast the sacred lots to determine where each tribe would settle (Josh 14:1-5). When Eleazar died, he was succeeded by his son Pinhas (Phinehas), who had distinguished himself by his covenant faithfulness when Yisrael (Israel) had turned to the gods of Moav (Moab) (Num 25). Eleazar’s descendants included Tsadok (Zadok), the faithful priest who replaced Evyatar (Abiathar) (1 Kgs 2:26-27, 35; see 1 Chr 6:3-8, 50-53), and Ezra, who was instrumental in reestablishing Judea after the Exile (see Ezra 7:1-5). In Yehezkel’s (Ezekiel’s) ideal temple, only the descendants of Eleazar through Tsadok would be permitted to serve (Ezek 44:15).
Passages for Further Study
Bil’am (Balaam)

Bil’am was a diviner—a person who read signs and omens to determine the future and performed rituals to change future events (see study note on Num 22:5-6; cp. Josh 13:22). He was a diviner for hire, so when Balak, king of Moav (Moab), wanted to hire him to curse Yisrael (Israel), he was eager to get started. Even when God told him not to go, he hoped God would change his mind because he was very interested in the money (2 Pet 2:15).

Finally, God allowed Bil’am to go, but only if Bil’am agreed to say what God told him to say, and only to frustrate Balak’s purposes (Deut 23:4-5). On the road, Bil’am’s donkey stopped and refused to move because the angel of the Lord was blocking the way. The donkey could see the angel, but Bil’am was blind and foolish. Still, Bil’am was smart enough not to curse the Israelis (Israelites) when God told him to bless them, and to Balak’s great frustration, that was all Bil’am could do.

Recently, an inscription was found that mentions Bil’am son of Be’or (Beor), a diviner who had visions at night (cp. Num 22:9-12, 20). The inscription was written on a plaster wall at Deir ‘Alla, eight miles east of the Yarden (Jordan) River, not far north of where the Hebrews were camped at the time of the Bil’am incident. This nonbiblical text, dated 800–750 BC, identifies Bil’am as a “seer of the gods” and reports that the gods, whose names in the inscription are similar to Shaddai (“Almighty”; cp. Num 24:4, 16), delivered a message to Bil’am and announced judgment upon the world (cp. Num 24:15-25). The inscription provides rare extrabiblical evidence about a Bible character.

While Bil’am’s character and motives appear somewhat mixed in Numbers 22–24, chapter 25 describes how the men of Yisrael sinned by sleeping with Moavi (Moabite) women and worshiping their gods, which made God angry with his people. While Bil’am is not mentioned here, Numbers 31:16 names him as the originator of this plot. After his visions were finished, Bil’am apparently remained in Moav and kept working the angles until he found a way to damage Yisrael and get the money. The Israelis killed him a short time later (Num 31:8). Bil’am became known as a magician with bad motives (see Deut 23:4-5; Josh 13:22), a false teacher who was only interested in pay (see Neh 13:2; 2 Pet 2:15; Jude 1:11), and someone who led Yisrael into idolatry and immorality (Num 31:16; see Rev 2:14).
Passages for Further Study
Moav (Moab) and Amon (Ammon)

The Moavim (Moabites) were descended from Moav, the son of Lot and his oldest daughter (Gen 19:36-38). They settled on the high plateau immediately east of the Dead Sea. Most of Moav is gently rolling tableland divided by ravines. Even at its peak, ancient Moav encompassed a relatively small territory, but its location on the King’s Highway was strategically important (see Num 21:21-22; Judg 11:15-18). Prior to the Israelis’s (Israelites’) passage through the Transjordan, the Moavim were dominated by Sihon, the Amori (Amorite) king who ruled at Heshbon (see Num 21:13, 26). After Yisrael (Israel) defeated Sihon, King Balak of Moav feared that Yisrael might conquer his land, and Moav waged war against them (Num 22:1–25:3; Josh 24:9). From that time onward, Moav and Yisrael were often in conflict (Judg 3:12-30; 1 Sam 14:47; 2 Sam 8:2; 2 Kgs 3), but there were also periods of peace (Ruth 1:1-2) between them. A Moavi (Moabite) woman named Ruth displayed great kindness to her tragedy-plagued Israeli (Israelite) mother-in-law, No’omi (Naomi), and she came to be part of the family line that produced King David and Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus).

The Amonim (Ammonites) traced their ancestry to Amon, son of the younger daughter of Lot (Gen 19:36-38). They settled in an area of the Transjordan northeast of the Dead Sea. When the Israelis arrived in the area after leaving Mitsrayim (Egypt), God instructed them not to try to occupy Amoni (Ammonite) territory, as it had already been given to the descendants of Lot (Deut 2:18-19, 37). The Amonim helped the Moavim oppose Yisrael and were excluded from the congregation of the Lord to the tenth generation (Deut 23:3-6; Neh 13:1-2; see Num 22:1–25:3). Thereafter the Amonim were frequent enemies of Yisrael (Judg 10–11; 1 Sam 11; 14:47; 1 Chr 20:1-3; 2 Chr 20:1-24), though David seems to have allied with them for a time (2 Sam 17:27-29; 23:37).
Passages for Further Study
Yehoshua (Joshua)

Yehoshua, son of Nun, was Mosheh’s (Moses’) assistant and successor as Yisrael’s (Israel’s) leader. Yehoshua brought the young nation across the Yarden (Jordan) River into the Promised Land of Kena’an (Canaan), faithfully following God’s leadership.

Before Yisrael reached Mount Sinay (Sinai), Yehoshua led Yisrael’s warriors when Amalek attacked Yisrael (Exod 17:8-13). Shortly thereafter, he was among the twelve men Mosheh sent to scout the Promised Land (Num 13:1-16). Against popular opinion, Yehoshua and Kalev (Caleb) urged Yisrael to occupy Kena’an immediately (Num 13:22–14:9), and as a result, of the twelve spies, only they entered Kena’an (Num 14:30, 36-38).

God directed Mosheh to designate Yehoshua as his successor (Num 27:15-23; Deut 34:9). After Mosheh died, Yehoshua led Yisrael across the Yarden River (Josh 1:1-18; 3:1–4:24) to the conquest of Yeriho (Jericho) (6:1-27). When Yisrael suffered defeat at Ay (Ai), Yehoshua turned to the Lord and followed his instructions to purge Yisrael of sin (7:1-26); then Yisrael conquered Ay (8:1-29). Following God’s instructions to Mosheh (Deut 11:29-32; 27:1–28:68), Yehoshua built an altar on Mount Eyval (Ebal) (Josh 8:30-32) and read the blessings and curses of the covenant (8:33-35). Yehoshua conducted campaigns against two coalitions of Kena’ani (Canaanite) kings, a southern and a northern coalition (10:1-43; 11:1-15). Yehoshua’s victories in these campaigns opened the hill country to settlement by the Israelis (Israelites).

After supervising the allotment of territories to the tribes of Yisrael, Yehoshua received his own portion in the land of Efrayim (Ephraim) (19:49-50). He established the cities of refuge (20:1-9) and the Levitical cities (ch 21:1-45) and released the 2½ tribes that had settled east of the Yarden River to return home (22:1-9). As he grew old, Yehoshua charged Yisrael to remain faithful to God (23:1–24:28). His farewell message at Shekem (Shechem) summarized God’s dealings with Yisrael and concluded with the familiar challenge, “Choose today whom you will serve. . . . But as for me and my family, we will serve Yahweh” (24:15). Yehoshua died at the age of 110 and was buried in Timnat-Serah (Timnath-serah) (Josh 24:29-30; Judg 2:8-9).

Yehoshua demonstrated exceptional faithfulness throughout his life, except in dealing with the Givonim (Gibeonites) (Josh 9:1-27), when he neglected to consult the Lord regarding a decision. Yisrael served God faithfully under Yehoshua and the elders Yehoshua trained (Josh 24:31; Judg 2:7). Stefanos (Stephen) mentions Yehoshua in his martyr’s sermon (Acts 7:45), and the writer of Hebrews uses Yehoshua’s conquest of Yeriho as an illustration of faith (Heb 11:30). It is fitting that Yehoshua and Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) are the same name in Hebrew: Yehoshua led Yisrael into physical salvation in Kena’an; Yeshua leads all who believe in him into eternal salvation.
Passages for Further Study
Rahav (Rahab)

Rahav, a prostitute and a woman of faith, remains enigmatic centuries after her brief appearance in Yisrael’s (Israel’s) history. Because she placed her faith in Yisrael’s God and helped the two Israeli (Israelite) scouts who came to her house, her life was spared when Yisrael captured Yeriho (Jericho).

Because Rahav’s house stood on the wall of the city, Yehoshua’s (Joshua’s) scouts went there when they entered Yeriho. Rahav might have been an innkeeper as well as a prostitute; other documents from the Old Testament era record women innkeepers who were also prostitutes. If Rahav’s house was in fact an inn, it would have been a reasonable destination; Yehoshua’s scouts could hope they would not attract unwanted attention.

Rahav’s arrangement with the scouts was a stirring declaration of faith in Yahweh, Yisrael’s God (Josh 2:8-21). As a Kena’ani (Canaanite) woman, Rahav would have practiced the fertility cult of Ba’al (Baal), god of the storm and life-giving rain, and of his consort Asherah, the mother earth goddess. Yet based on reports of Yisrael’s progress toward her land, Rahav recognized that Yahweh, the God of Yisrael, is “the supreme God of the heavens above and the earth below” (2:11).

After Yehoshua’s conquest of Yeriho, Rahav married Salmon of the tribe of Yehudah (Judah); she gave birth to a son, whom they named Boaz (Ruth 4:21; Matt 1:5). Thus, Rahav was the mother-in-law of Ruth, another foreign woman adopted into Yisrael. Rahav was also King David’s great-great-grandmother. She is listed with Mosheh (Moses), David, Shimshon (Samson), and Shmuel (Samuel) as an example of faith demonstrated by good deeds (Heb 11:31; Jas 2:25). She is one of five women (including Maria (Mary)) mentioned in Matay’s (Matthew’s; Grk. Matthaios’) genealogy of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), the human family tree of God’s Son (Matt 1:5). Rahav bears especially poignant witness to the breathtaking scope of God’s grace.
Passages for Further Study
Kalev (Caleb)

Kalev stands as an inspiring example of faith in God. He was the son of Yefuneh (Jephunneh) the Kenizi (Kenizzite) (Josh 14:6; Num 32:12). The Kenizim (Kenizzites) lived in the Negev, the southern desert region of Kena’an (Canaan) (see Gen 15:18-21). Yefuneh apparently married into the tribe of Yehudah (Judah) a generation before Yisrael (Israel) left Mitsrayim (Egypt).

Kalev first appears as one of twelve spies Mosheh (Moses) sent to scout out the land of Kena’an. Upon returning, all twelve confirmed the land’s magnificence, but ten of the scouts focused on the land’s fearsome inhabitants (Num 13:31-33). Only Yehoshua (Joshua) and Kalev believed that God would enable Yisrael to conquer the Kena’anim (Canaanites) (Num 14:6-9), advising that the Israelis (Israelites) immediately take the land (Num 13:30). Although the people wanted to stone both Kalev and Yehoshua (Num 14:10), God protected them and punished the people (Num 14:11-38). God ultimately rewarded Kalev and Yehoshua for their faithfulness: Among all the adults who left Mitsrayim, they were the only ones to enter the Promised Land.

After many years in the wilderness, and after fighting many battles, Kalev received his personal inheritance in the land (Josh 14:6-15). Kalev’s faith did not diminish in the intervening forty-five years; his testimony reveals his character and rock-solid faith in God. Although Kalev was eighty-five years old, he was still strong and able to fight. Kalev acquired Hevron (Hebron), which would become his land, by driving out the giant Anakim (Anakites) who had terrified the earlier scouts (Josh 15:13-14; see Num 13:28, 33). Kalev’s city of Hevron, about twenty miles south of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (not far from Kenizi territory), later became a Levitical city of refuge (Josh 21:13; 1 Chr 6:54-57).

Kalev looked beyond serious obstacles to God’s unbreakable promise that Yisrael would occupy Kena’an. With unabated vigor, he stood ready to conquer the territory Yehoshua assigned him. Kalev’s staunch confidence in the reliability of God’s promises earned him an honored place among the faithful. Even when outnumbered by enemies, Kalev trusted God, and God richly rewarded him.
Passages for Further Study
The Pelishtim (Philistines)

The Pelishtim, situated on the southeast coastal plain of the Mediterranean, were part of a larger group of maritime immigrants from the Aegean area known by the Mitsrim (Egyptians) as the “Sea Peoples.” They settled on Palestine’s lower coastal plain around 1200 BC and established the five cities of Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, Azah (Gaza), and Gat (Gath).

Far from being unsophisticated, the Pelishtim were politically capable and technologically advanced. They were also fierce warriors. Their advances in iron technology made them an almost invincible foe (see 1 Sam 13:19-22). They were constant adversaries of the Israelis (Israelites) in the days of the judges (approximately 1350–1050 BC) and the early united monarchy (approximately 1050–970 BC). Sha’ul (Saul) eventually died in battle against the Pelishtim (1 Sam 31:1-13). David, however, vanquished them before becoming king (1 Sam 18:20-30; 19:8; 23:1-5) and continued to gain victory over them during his reign (2 Sam 5:17-25; 8:1; 21:15-22). While the Pelishtim never completely disappeared while Yisrael (Israel) was a nation (2 Kgs 18:8; 2 Chr 17:11; 21:16-17; 26:6-7; 28:18), David effectively ended this menacing threat.

In 1 Shmuel (Samuel), God used the Pelishtim to eliminate the sinful family of Eli (1 Sam 4:10-22). The Pelishtim were also God’s tool for building David’s military and political career (1 Sam 17:32-58; 18:20-30). They distracted Sha’ul when he was about to capture David (1 Sam 23:26-28), provided David with refuge from Sha’ul (1 Sam 21:10-15; 27:1-12), prevented David from having to fight his own people (1 Sam 29:1-11), and by killing Sha’ul and his sons (1 Sam 31:1-13), opened the way for David to become king. In the end, however, the Pelishtim experienced God’s judgment (see Ezek 25:15-17; Amos 1:6-8).
Passages for Further Study
Deborah

Deborah the prophet was one of the early judges of Yisrael (Israel), a woman of integrity and devotion to the Lord. As a prophet, she received divine revelation; as a judge, she arbitrated legal disputes. She could aptly be characterized as “a mother for Yisrael” (see Judg 5:7).

The time period in which Deborah lived was one of increasing moral depravity, spiritual blindness, and political fragmentation. Yisrael was doing “evil in Yahweh’s sight” (Judg 4:1), so God once again turned Yisrael over to an oppressor, Yavin (Jabin) of Kena’an (Canaan). And once again, Yisrael “cried out to Yahweh for help” (4:3).

Through Deborah, God called Barak to fight against Sisera, the commander of Yavin’s army. But Barak did not receive God’s call with enthusiasm and courage. Instead, he set a condition: Deborah must go with him. Deborah agreed, but with a cost: The glory for the victory would not go to Barak but to a woman. And so it happened: Barak defeated Sisera and his army, but the glory went to Ya’el (Jael), the woman who killed Sisera and fulfilled Deborah’s prophecy. Barak’s lack of courage and leadership contrasts with the courage and leadership of these two women. Deborah’s actions resulted in a forty-year period of peace for Yisrael (5:31).
Passages for Further Study
Gid’on (Gideon)

Gid’on, an Israeli (Israelite) judge, was the son of Yoash (Joash), from the tribe of Menasheh (Manasseh). Gid’on described his clan as the least powerful in Menasheh and himself as the least important in the clan. His story tells how God can take a weak person and use them for great purposes.

At the time, Yisrael (Israel) was being oppressed by Midyan (Midian) and had cried out to God for relief (Judg 6:6). In response, God sent a prophet to chastise them for neglecting him and worshiping other gods. He also sent his angel to call Gid’on to rescue Yisrael.

Gid’on’s first appearance is not promising. He was threshing wheat in the bottom of a winepress because he did not want the Midyanites (Midianites) to know what he was doing. When the angel of the Lord appeared to Gid’on in the winepress, Gid’on questioned why God had not rescued his people as at the Exodus. God said that Gid’on was chosen to be Yisrael’s deliverer, and that God himself would be with him. Gid’on was slow to believe, and he requested a sign. He brought an offering, and when the angel touched the sacrifice, fire came from the rock beneath it.

This sign gave Gid’on enough faith to act locally. God told him to knock down his father’s altar to Ba’al (Baal), cut down the Asherah pole, and build an altar to the Lord instead. Gid’on did what God had commanded, becoming a warrior for God against false gods.

Then the Spirit of God came on Gid’on, and he raised an army to fight the Midyanites and their allies. Gid’on was still cautious, and he asked God to give him another sign to confirm his calling. He put out a fleece on two separate nights and asked God to reveal his power by having the dew settle on the fleece and/or the ground in miraculous ways. God did so and Gid’on was now prepared to follow God’s plan.

Gid’on had great success as an army recruiter as 32,000 men responded to his call. Yet God directed him to pare down the numbers to 300 men. Gid’on led these 300 men against an overwhelming force and defeated them.

Gid’on rightly resisted the people’s call to be their ruler, but then he made an ephod from the earrings of the defeated soldiers, and the ephod became an idol (8:22-27). Gid’on, weak in faith and dependent on visible signs, eventually turned away from worshiping the invisible God and worshiped idols. Yisrael enjoyed peace during his time, but his lack of faith bore bitter fruit after his death (8:33–9:57).
Passages for Further Study
Shimshon (Samson)

Shimshon is a prime illustration of God’s using a person for good in spite of that person’s indifference and sin. Shimshon was a rescuer of Yisrael (Israel) without even trying or caring. He did not seem to care about his people, his family, or his God. All he cared about was himself. Nonetheless, God, put him in situation after situation where he brought harm to the Pelishtim (Philistines), whom God had allowed to oppress sinful Yisrael.

The first example of how God used Shimshon occurred after he told his shocked parents that he wanted to marry a Pelishti (Philistine) girl. Israelis (Israelites) were commanded not to intermarry with the people of the land (Deut 7:1-4; Josh 23:12-13; cp. 2 Cor 6:14-18), but Shimshon persisted over his parents’ objections. As he was on his way to the wedding party, he scooped honey out of a dead lion he had earlier killed. Shimshon was born a Nazirite, and Nazirites were absolutely forbidden from touching a dead body (Num 6:1-21), but Shimshon didn’t care. He then made up a riddle about the lion (Judg 14:14) and bet thirty young Pelishti men that they could not solve his riddle. The men pestered his wife into telling them the answer. As a result, Shimshon became so angry that he killed thirty Pelishti men and took their clothing to pay off the bet. God used the self-serving hero to “begin to rescue Yisrael from the Pelishtim” (13:5).

In the final, climactic story of Shimshon’s life (16:4-31), Shimshon’s lover, Dililah (Delilah), nagged Shimshon until he revealed the secret of his strength and thus betrayed his Nazirite vow. She cut his hair, and the Pelishtim were finally able to overpower him. They blinded him, tied him up securely, and loaded him with menial work. While in captivity, Shimshon’s hair began to grow again. One day, when the Pelishtim were celebrating and making fun of him, he asked to be led to the two central pillars of their pagan temple. He then prayed to God to give him the strength to kill the Pelishtim and take his own life. So he pulled the temple down on the heads of about 3,000 Pelishtim as well as himself. Even this act, however, was not done for his people or his God, but to “pay back the Pelishtim for the loss of [his] two eyes” (16:28). Even though it was all in God’s plan, the story of Shimshon makes the reader long for a better savior.
Passages for Further Study
Ruth

The story of Ruth tells of a kind and loyal woman and of the hidden providence of God, who makes all things work together for the good of those who love him (Rom 8:28). This story, part of the history that leads to the Messiah himself, starts with sadness but ends happily.

Ruth lived during the turbulent period of the judges. A foreigner from Moav (Moab), she married into an Israeli (Israelite) family from Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) when that family was living in Moav. All the men of this Israeli family died in Moav, leaving behind three widows—Ruth, her mother-in-law No’omi (Naomi), and her sister-in-law Orpah. When No’omi decided to return to her hometown of Beyt-Lehem, Ruth cast her lot with her mother-in-law. Ruth’s declaration of love, loyalty, and faith in the Lord (No’omi’s God) has few equals (Ruth 1:16-17).

As No’omi had expected, the situation in Beyt-Lehem was difficult for her and her daughter-in-law. Ruth, by her own initiative, undertook solving the problem of food for herself and No’omi through the hard and risky task of gleaning in the grain fields (2:2). She acted with modesty, grace, and courtesy, but also with determination, focus, and endurance.

With No’omi’s encouragement, Ruth then took the initiative in asking Boaz, the wealthy landowner who was supporting Ruth’s gleaning, to act as the family redeemer (3:1-9), which would include marriage. In doing this, Ruth was exercising great “family loyalty” (3:10); Ruth’s generous and diligent care for No’omi is a major theme throughout this little book. Boaz responded to Ruth’s proposal by calling her a “virtuous woman” (3:11), and she certainly embodied the characteristics of a virtuous and capable wife (cp. Prov 31:10-31, which uses the same Hebrew phrase and is placed immediately before Ruth in the Hebrew Bible).

Boaz settled the legal matters and then married Ruth. The book ends by announcing the birth of a baby boy, Oved (Obed). With this ending we see an important purpose of the book of Ruth. Oved became the grandfather of King David. The New Testament includes Ruth as one of only five women mentioned in the genealogy of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ (Matt 1:5). The everyday faithfulness of Ruth had eternal significance as God worked out his purposes through her.
Passages for Further Study
Ruth 1:4–4:13; Matt 1:5
Eli

Eli was Yisrael’s (Israel’s) chief priest at the Tabernacle at Shiloh, Yisrael’s central shrine during the period of the judges. Eli apparently descended from Itamar (Ithamar), Aharon’s (Aaron’s) youngest son (cp. 1 Kgs 2:27; 1 Chr 18:16; 24:3). Eli was sincere and devout, but he was weak in parenting his wicked sons, Hofni (Hophni) and Pinhas (Phinehas).

When Eli encountered Hannah at the Tabernacle, he accused her of drunkenness as she fervently but silently asked God for a child. Upon realizing his mistake, Eli blessed Hannah, and God answered Hannah’s prayer by giving her Shmuel (Samuel).

Shmuel “grew in favor with Yahweh and with the people” (1 Sam 2:26), but Eli’s sons “were scoundrels who had no respect for Yahweh” (2:12). They stole from the offerings and seduced women who served at the Tabernacle. When Eli reproached them, they disregarded him. God sent a prophet to denounce Eli’s weakness and his sons’ wickedness and to announce that God would withdraw the priesthood from Eli’s family (2:27-36). This oracle was confirmed when God spoke to Shmuel one night, telling him that he would soon punish Eli’s family (3:1-14). Shortly thereafter, Yisrael’s army was defeated in battle against the Pelishtim (Philistines), the Ark of the Covenant was captured, and Eli’s sons were killed (4:1-11). When Eli, who was ninety-eight years old, heard the news, he fell over backward, broke his neck, and died (4:12-18). His daughter-in-law went into labor and died delivering Eli’s grandson, named I-Kavod (Ichabod) (“where is the glory?,” 4:19-22) because the glory had departed from Yisrael.

Eli’s priestly line survived, however, until David’s reign ended. Evyatar (Abiathar) was Eli’s last descendant to serve as chief priest. Since he supported Adoniyah’s (Adonijah’s) attempt to usurp David’s throne, Shelomoh (Solomon) removed Evyatar from office and replaced him with Tsadok (Zadok) (1 Kgs 2:27).
Passages for Further Study
Sha’ul (Saul)

Sha’ul was the first king of Yisrael (Israel). He was chosen by God and the people, but he failed tremendously because he lacked confidence in himself and in God. Sha’ul was a very complex character who sometimes elicits our sympathy. He was also the source of his own problems, especially as he brought heartache and trouble into the lives of those close to him.

Sha’ul, the son of a wealthy landowner, became king unexpectedly and reluctantly.
