The people had requested a king to help them fight their battles, so they were happy with Sha’ul, who was a head taller than anyone else (1 Sam 10:23). Their military problems were overwhelming, however, and Sha’ul was not a confident military leader. Had it not been for the prophet Shmuel (Samuel) and Sha’ul’s son Yonatan (Jonathan), Sha’ul’s reign might have been marked by complete disaster.

Sha’ul offended God by taking rash vows during wartime (14:16-46) and wrongly performing sacrifices before battle rather than waiting for Shmuel (13:7b-14). He also failed to obey God’s instruction to destroy all the people and plunder of the Amalekim (Amalekites) (15:1-35). So God determined to remove Sha’ul from the kingship and sent Shmuel to anoint David. Soon Sha’ul was deeply suspicious of David, his son’s best friend and his own most loyal servant. The reluctant king became a despot, clinging to power at all costs. He spent much time and effort in pursuit of David, seeking to kill him.

Sha’ul was wounded in battle against the Pelishtim (Philistines), then fell on his own sword. His death was a result of God’s judgment. Although David had spent considerable time fleeing from Sha’ul, he honored the first king and his son Yonatan with a moving eulogy (2 Sam 1:17-27).
Passages for Further Study
Yonatan (Jonathan)

Yonatan, the oldest son of King Sha’ul (Saul), was in line to be the next king. Yet when God rejected Sha’ul and chose David, Yonatan welcomed and supported David’s rise to power (1 Sam 18:1-4; 19:1-7).

Yonatan was a magnificent military leader. He led his father’s army to victory over the Pelishti (Philistine) garrison at Geva (Geba) (13:3-4). In another daring move, Yonatan and his armor bearer attacked a Pelishti outpost by themselves; the ensuing confusion threw the Pelishti army into disarray, allowing the main Israeli (Israelite) army to attack and win the day (14:1-23; see also David’s eulogy of Yonatan, 2 Sam 1:22). Sha’ul had unwisely taken an oath that no one should eat until victory had been won. Yonatan did not know of the vow and ate some honey. When he learned of Sha’ul’s vow, Yonatan criticized it harshly, and Sha’ul would have executed Yonatan after the battle he had helped to win if the people had not intervened.

When Yonatan and David met, they quickly became friends (1 Sam 18:1-4). Yonatan expressed his deep love for David by giving him his robe, tunic, sword, bow, and belt, which may have represented Yonatan’s belief that David should be the next ruler. When Sha’ul tried to have David killed, Yonatan interceded for David and helped him slip away unharmed.

Yonatan remained with his father even after the Lord had made it clear that he had abandoned Sha’ul. As a result, Yonatan died with Sha’ul as they fought the Pelishtim (Philistines) (31:2; 1 Chr 10:2). Yonatan was a virtuous, daring, and selfless man who always spoke and acted with integrity. His love and courage helped David survive the demented attacks of King Sha’ul.
Passages for Further Study
Mikal (Michal)
Mikal was King Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) younger daughter (1 Sam 14:49) and David’s first wife (18:17-27). She played a significant role in the transition from Sha’ul’s reign to David’s.

In the ancient Near East, marriages of leading families were often politically motivated. Sha’ul baited David into a dangerous situation by promising him his older daughter, Merav (Merab), if he would fight the Pelishtim (Philistines). As a powerful warrior, David was an emerging leader in Sha’ul’s kingdom. The king should have been happy to have such an ally, but he soon grew jealous of David’s accomplishments and suspicious of his ambitions. Sha’ul hoped that David would die in the attempt, but the deal fell through. Later, Sha’ul learned that his younger daughter, Mikal, loved David (18:20), which gave the king another opportunity to bait David into fighting the Pelishtim. This time David agreed. When David returned victorious, Sha’ul could not avoid giving David his daughter in marriage. This marriage alliance helped David when he was seeking to establish his credentials with the northern tribes (2 Sam 3:13-16).

Mikal loved David early in their relationship and even deceived her father to help David escape from a plot to kill him (1 Sam 19:11-17). After David left Sha’ul’s court, Sha’ul arranged another marriage for her (25:44), but David later broke up that marriage to get her back (2 Sam 3:13-16). Mikal expressed contempt toward David when he danced joyfully before the Ark of the Covenant as it was being brought into Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (2 Sam 6:16-23). Because of her contempt for the king, Mikal was unable to bear children.
Passages for Further Study
Evyatar (Abiathar)

Evyatar was high priest during David’s reign and into Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) reign. He first encountered David before David became king. When David fled from Sha’ul (Saul), he stopped at the city of Nov (Nob). Pretending that he was acting on Sha’ul’s orders, David got food and supplies from the priests there. Sha’ul discovered what had happened and was so angry that he killed all but one of the priests; only Evyatar escaped.

Evyatar was among the first people from Sha’ul’s administration to support David. His support was formidable; he represented the priesthood of Eli’s line and brought with him the holy ephod containing the Urim and Tumim (Thummim) (Exod 28:29-30), which allowed him to seek God’s will for David during crises (1 Sam 23:1-12; 30:7-8). After David became king, Evyatar served as priest along with Tsadok (Zadok), who was not a descendant of Eli (1 Chr 6:8; 18:16; 24:3). Both served David well; during Avshalom’s (Absalom’s) rebellion, for example, they reported to David what was happening in the capital (2 Sam 15:27-37; 17:15-16).

In David’s old age, Evyatar wrongly supported Adoniyah’s (Adonijah’s) attempt to become king in his father’s place; Tsadok remained loyal to David and supported Shelomoh (1 Kgs 1:5-8). As a result, once Shelomoh was on the throne, he removed Evyatar’s priestly authority and banished him to his estate in Anatot (Anathoth) (1 Kgs 2:26-27), a village about four miles northeast of Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Tsadok became the high priest, and that role passed to Tsadok’s descendants rather than to Evyatar’s. This removal fulfilled “the prophecy Yahweh had given at Shiloh concerning the descendants of Eli” (1 Kgs 2:27; see 1 Sam 2:27-36).
Passages for Further Study
The Amalekim (Amalekites)

The Amalekim were the descendants of Amalek, a grandson of Esav (Esau) (Gen 36:12; 1 Chr 1:36). They were nomadic herdsmen; their territory in the Negev ranged from south of Be’er-Sheva (Beersheba) to the southeast as far as Eylot (Elath) and Etsyon-Gever (Ezion-geber). They undoubtedly raided westward into the coastal plain, eastward into the Aravah (Arabah) wastelands, and possibly into Arav (Arabia).

The Amalekim were staunch enemies of Yisrael (Israel). Yisrael’s first encounter with the warriors of Amalek came at Refidim (Rephidim) near Sinay (Sinai) when they attacked Yisrael (Exod 17:8-16). In this encounter, the Amalekim were defeated by Yehoshua (Joshua) and the Israeli (Israelite) army. The Amalekim later rebuffed Yisrael’s disobedient attempt to enter the Promised Land (Num 14:39-45). As a result of their enmity, Mosheh (Moses) instructed Yisrael to destroy them (Deut 25:17-19), but the Amalekim continued to inhabit the Negev (see Judg 3:12-14; 6:33; 1 Sam 14:47-48; 15:1-35). Those who survived remained Yisrael’s enemies (27:8; 30:1-20; 2 Sam 8:11-12; Ps 83:1-8). This remnant was finally destroyed during the reign of Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) (1 Chr 4:42-43). In the book of Ester (Esther), Haman (a descendant of King Agag) embodied their animosity to the bitter end (Esth 3; see 1 Sam 15).
Passages for Further Study
Shmuel (Samuel)

Shmuel lived at the end of the period of the judges and ushered in the period of kingship. He was Yisrael’s (Israel’s) last judge (1 Sam 7:6, 15-17) and was essentially considered Yisrael’s first prophet (1 Sam 3:20; Acts 3:24; 13:20). He functioned as a priest (see 1 Sam 2:18) and was a great man of faith (Heb 11:32).

Shmuel was born in response to his mother Hannah’s prayers. Shmuel’s parents traveled annually from Ramah to the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3). While at the sanctuary, Hannah, who was infertile, prayed for a son and promised to dedicate him to God for full-time service (1 Sam 1:9-11). God answered the prayer, and Shmuel was born (1 Sam 1:19-20). When Shmuel was weaned, Hannah took him to serve in the sanctuary with Eli, the high priest (1 Sam 1:24-28; 2:11).

Eli’s sons were wicked, but Shmuel served the Lord, and soon it became clear that God spoke more intimately with Shmuel than with Eli. God spoke to Shmuel to warn Eli of the coming disaster upon his family (1 Sam 3:1-18). This prophecy was fulfilled when the Pelishtim (Philistines) defeated Yisrael, killed Eli’s sons, and took the Ark of the Covenant (1 Sam 4:1-22). Later, under Shmuel’s leadership, the people repented of their sin of idolatry and succeeded in winning an important battle against the Pelishtim (1 Sam 7:3-17).

But as Shmuel grew older, it became obvious that he suffered from the same weakness as Eli before him. Shmuel’s sons were evil (1 Sam 8:1-3), and the people did not want them to assume leadership over the nation. Instead, the people requested that Shmuel appoint for them a king who could lead them in battle against their enemies (1 Sam 8:4-5). Shmuel then anointed Sha’ul (Saul) as the first king of Yisrael (1 Sam 9:1–10:24).

The transition from the era of the judges to kingship was turbulent. As priest, Shmuel prayed for the people; as prophet, he reproved Sha’ul for impatience and disobedience (1 Sam 13:5-14; 15:12-35). When God rejected Sha’ul as king, Shmuel anointed David as God’s chosen one (1 Sam 16:1-13) and protected David from Sha’ul (19:18-24).

Through prayer and perseverance, Shmuel was a faithful leader (Jer 15:1; Heb 11:32) who cherished his people’s well-being and courageously rebuked kings and elders. He led Yisrael from tribal disunity to national solidarity and established the monarchy. He presumably wrote The Record of Shmuel the Seer (1 Chr 29:29) and defined ideal kingship (1 Sam 10:25). When he died, he was mourned by all Yisrael. He was buried in Ramah, his hometown (25:1).
Passages for Further Study
David
David is one of the monumental figures of biblical history. His reign was a high point in God’s plan for Yisrael (Israel), and it had great and lasting significance.

David was born in Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) as Yishay’s (Jesse’s) youngest son; his lineage is traced back to Yehudah (Judah) (Ruth 4:18-22; 1 Chr 2:3-15; Matt 1:3-6; Luke 3:31-33). At the time of his birth, Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was occupied by the Yevusim (Jebusites), and large parts of the Promised Land were still occupied by foreign people, most notably the Pelishtim (Philistines). God would use David to complete the conquest of the land.

As a youth, David was a simple shepherd, watching his father’s sheep (1 Sam 16:11; 17:14-15). His life took an unexpected turn when the prophet Shmuel (Samuel) came to Yishay and anointed David as the next king of Yisrael. However, David’s kingship was not initiated by a coup or an assassination. In fact, David became a faithful servant to King Sha’ul (Saul). David first entered Sha’ul’s service as a musician, playing songs that soothed Sha’ul’s tormented soul (16:14-23). This service anticipated David’s role as the composer of many of the psalms. The youthful David also helped Sha’ul by famously defeating the Pelishti (Philistine) champion Galyat (Goliath) in individual combat (17:32-51). This victory anticipated David’s role as a victorious military leader.

Although David was loyal, Sha’ul grew deeply suspicious of him, and David had to flee. He was able to escape with help from Sha’ul’s own children, Yonatan (Jonathan) and Mikal (Michal). David led a virtual kingdom in exile. He had a standing army of six hundred men. The prophet Gad and the priest Evyatar (Abiathar) were also with him, providing direction and guidance from the Lord.

God’s long-suffering patience finally ran out with Sha’ul, and Sha’ul died on the battlefield. Yet it was still not easy for David to establish his rule over all Yisrael. The tribe of Yehudah immediately proclaimed him its king, but at first the northern tribes chose Ish-Boshet (Ishbosheth), a son of Sha’ul, to be their leader. Ish-Boshet was not a powerful or good leader; he only stayed in power because of the protection of his father’s military leader, Avner (Abner). However, Ish-Boshet foolishly insulted Avner, so the general helped turn the kingdom over to David.

As king over a united Yisrael, David proceeded to solidify the kingdom. He and his men captured Yerushalem from the Yevusim and made this central city his capital. He also expelled the remaining Pelishtim from the land. He then brought the Ark of the Covenant into Yerushalem. David wanted to build a permanent temple to God in Yerushalem to replace the Tabernacle. God denied this wish, but he showed his love for David by entering into a covenant with him that established his descendants as a dynasty (2 Sam 7).

David’s life soon took a turn for the worse, however (see 2 Sam 11–12). At a time when he probably should have been on the battlefield with his army, he was lounging around on the palace roof. He saw a beautiful woman named Bat-Sheva (Bathsheba) taking a bath. He wanted her, so, like a Near Eastern despot, he took her. She became pregnant, and his attempt to cover up his adultery failed. In a desperate attempt to keep things secret, he had her husband, Uriyah (Uriah), killed. But not even a great king like David can keep secrets from God, and God sent his prophet Natan (Nathan) to confront David. David repented (see Pss 32, 51), but the consequences of his actions plagued his family and the rest of his reign.

From that point on, David’s family fell apart. David’s son Amnon raped his half sister Tamar (2 Sam 13:1-14). Her brother Avshalom (Absalom) then murdered Amnon (2 Sam 13:20-29). Avshalom later created a civil war as he tried to steal the throne from his father (2 Sam 15–18). Another son, Adoniyah (Adonijah), tried to take the throne from David by having himself proclaimed king while his father was still alive (1 Kgs 1:5-10). But David was able to muster enough strength to ensure that Shelomoh (Solomon) would succeed him (1 Kgs 1:28-40). David died, Shelomoh was proclaimed king, and David’s long dynasty began (as promised in 2 Sam 7).

David’s successors seldom measured up. Only rarely did his descendants lead the nation to worship God faithfully; the united monarchy did not even outlive Shelomoh. In the centuries that followed, the descendants of David ruled only Yehudah in the south. Eventually, the kingdom of Yehudah was destroyed. Never again did a descendant of David reign as king in Yisrael.

What, then, of the promise to David that “your throne will be secure forever” (2 Sam 7:16)? The New Testament points to Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus). He was the descendant of David, and God proclaimed him the Christ, or Messiah—the anointed king (see Matt 1:1; 9:27; 12:23; Mark 10:47-48; 11:10; 12:35-37; Luke 18:38-39; 20:41-44; John 7:42; Rev 5:5; 22:16). The life and rule of David foreshadows the messianic reign of Yeshua Christ, which will last forever (see Luke 1:32-33; Rev 11:15).
Passages for Further Study
Avner (Abner)

Avner son of Ner was King Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) cousin as well as his general (1 Sam 14:49-52). Sha’ul’s armies won important battles against the Pelishtim (Philistines) under Avner’s command (1 Sam 17:1-58), and Avner ate at the king’s table with David and Yonatan (Jonathan) (1 Sam 20:24-25). Yet Yonatan and David both outshone Avner in Sha’ul’s army.

David shamed Avner on one occasion (1 Sam 26:1-25). When Sha’ul was in pursuit of David so as to kill him, he and his troops were camped in a circle with Sha’ul sleeping at the center and Avner beside him. Avishay (Abishai) and David sneaked into the camp and could have killed Sha’ul. They took some items from beside Sha’ul’s head; then, after retreating, David shouted to waken Sha’ul and Avner and berated Avner for his carelessness.

After Sha’ul and Yonatan died, Avner promoted the interests of Sha’ul’s son Ish-Boshet (Ishbosheth) (2 Sam 2:8-12) when the tribe of Yehudah (Judah) made David king. During this time, Avner was the real power in the north. When Ish-Boshet accused Avner of sleeping with one of Sha’ul’s concubines, Avner turned the northern kingdom over to David. Ish-Boshet was later murdered (4:1-12).

During the battle between Ish-Boshet and David, Avner was forced in self-defense to kill Yoav’s (Joab’s) brother Asahel, whom he did not want to kill and had warned to turn back (2:18-32). Avner was then murdered by Yoav in calculated revenge (3:22-30), an evil act that David could not prevent (see 3:38-39). David honored Avner with a eulogy, public mourning, and a state funeral (3:31-37). Later, David remembered what had happened and made certain that Yoav did not go unpunished for the murder (1 Kgs 2:5-6).
Passages for Further Study
Bat-Sheva (Bathsheba)

Bat-Sheva, wife of Uriyah (Uriah), was the daughter of Eliam (2 Sam 11:3; cp. 1 Chr 3:5) and the granddaughter of Ahitofel (Ahithophel), the king’s adviser (2 Sam 15:12; 23:34). Her husband, Uriyah, was a Hiti (Hittite) mercenary in King David’s service and was one of David’s mighty men (23:39).

One spring, David stayed home in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) while the army went to the battlefield (11:1). Resting at midday, David strolled on his roof overlooking the city and saw the beautiful Bat-Sheva taking a bath. He arranged for her to be brought to his private chambers. Then he had sexual relations with her, and she became pregnant (11:2-4).

Not wanting this scandal to become public, David arranged a cover-up: He told Yoav (Joab), the general, to have Uriyah bring back a report from the battle lines. David hoped that Uriyah would return home and sleep with Bat-Sheva, thus legitimizing her pregnancy. But Uriyah considered himself still on active duty, so he slept at the palace gate instead (11:5-13). When David asked him about this, he replied that he could not sleep with his wife while the Ark and the armies of Yisrael (Israel) were on the battlefield. This answer put David in a very bad light: Uriyah, who was not even an Israeli (Israelite), was standing ready to return to battle by avoiding intercourse with his wife (see Lev 15:16-18), while David was staying at home and trying to cover up adultery! Then David sent Uriyah back and ordered Yoav to ensure that he was killed in battle (2 Sam 11:14-25). Uriyah’s death did not keep David’s sin a secret, however. The Lord sent the prophet Natan (Nathan) to confront David, and David confessed his sin and repented (12:1-14; see Ps 51).

Bat-Sheva’s baby became sick and died, as Natan had predicted. After Bat-Sheva’s period of mourning, David brought her to the palace as his wife. David and Bat-Sheva had other children (Shimea, Shovav (Shobab), Natan, and Shelomoh (Solomon); 2 Sam 12:15-25; 1 Chr 3:5). The rest of David’s life is filled with intrigue among the different factions of his wives and children, culminating in David’s old age when Bat-Sheva sought to ensure the kingship for her son Shelomoh (1 Kgs 1:1-53).

In Matay’s (Matthew’s; Grk. Matthaios’) genealogy of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) the Messiah, both Shelomoh and Bat-Sheva appear (Matt 1:6); she is described there as “the widow of Uriyah,” a reminder of the sin that brought her into David’s family and of God’s gracious favor toward her descendants.
Passages for Further Study
Tsadok (Zadok)

Tsadok was an important transitional figure in the history of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) priesthood. Since he seemingly appears out of nowhere in the narrative of 2 Shmuel (Samuel) (8:17), some scholars suggest that he was not really born into a priestly family. However, there is no reason to doubt the biblical record that he was Aharon’s (Aaron’s) descendant (1 Chr 6:1-15, 50-53). Tsadok’s family line is traced back to Eleazar, Aharon’s son (1 Chr 6:4-8; 24:3; Ezra 7:2-5). Tsadok served alongside Evyatar (Abiathar), a descendant of Eli. Tsadok and Evyatar were priests of Yisrael under King David (2 Sam 8:17; 20:25).

When Avshalom (Absalom) revolted against King David, both Tsadok and Evyatar showed their loyalty to David by taking the Ark to him, fully prepared to share in his exile (15:24-29). Instead, David sent them to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) as his spies.

Later, when David’s son Adoniyah (Adonijah) tried to seize the aged David’s throne with the support of Yoav (Joab) and Evyatar, Tsadok wisely refrained from supporting him (1 Kgs 1:5-10). Evyatar was banished (1 Kgs 2:26-27), fulfilling the prophecy that Eli’s family would be removed from the priesthood (1 Sam 2:27-36). In this same prophecy, God said, “I will raise up a faithful priest who will serve me and do what I desire. I will establish his family, and they will be priests to my anointed kings forever” (1 Sam 2:35).

The loyal Tsadok fulfilled this prophecy and became the sole high priest under Shelomoh (Solomon) (1 Kgs 2:35). Tsadok’s descendants served as Yisrael’s priests throughout the monarchy and beyond. Azaryah (Azariah), chief priest during Hizkiyah’s (Hezekiah’s) reign, was of Tsadok’s line (2 Chr 31:10). During the Exile, Yehezkel’s (Ezekiel’s) eschatological vision of the new Temple refers to Tsadok’s priestly line (Ezek 40:46; 43:19; 44:15; 48:11). When the Yehudim (Jews) later came under Seleucid domination in the early 100s BC, the high priesthood, by then regarded as a political appointment, was taken away from Tsadok’s descendants. As a result of Yehezkel’s prophecies, Jewish groups such as those responsible for the Dead Sea Scrolls continued to await the restoration of Tsadok’s line to the high priesthood. The New Testament teaches that the office of the high priest now rests on Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ (Heb 9:11; 10:12-25).
Passages for Further Study
Avishay (Abishai)

Avishay was a powerful and successful warrior and a leader in David’s army. He was David’s nephew, a son of David’s sister Tseruyah (Zeruiah) and the brother of Yoav (Joab) and Asahel (1 Chr 2:13-16).

Avishay was completely devoted to David and quick to suggest violence against David’s enemies. When God allowed David and Avishay to penetrate Sha’ul’s (Saul’s) war camp while the troops were sleeping, Avishay wanted to assassinate Sha’ul, but David restrained him. Later, when the revolt of Avshalom (Absalom) required that David leave Yerushalem (Jerusalem), the king was cursed by Shimei, a member of Sha’ul’s family, and Avishay wanted to execute Shimei (2 Sam 16:5-9). David twice rejected that proposal (2 Sam 16:10-13; 19:18-23). The vengeful spirit of Avishay and his brothers also came out in an earlier conflict: After Sha’ul’s general, Avner (Abner), killed Avishay’s brother Asahel in self-defense, Yoav and Avishay took revenge by killing Avner (3:22-30).

Avishay was brave and very capable. He once killed three hundred soldiers in a single battle. For this, he was made leader of the Thirty, a group of especially skillful warriors surpassed only by the Three (1 Chr 11:20-21). Avishay also won a major victory over the Edomim (Edomites) (1 Chr 18:12-13). In a battle with the Pelishtim (Philistines), Avishay saved David’s life by killing the giant Yishbi-Benov (Ishbi-benob) (2 Sam 21:15-17). Avishay also led the army, and when it divided for strategic purposes, Avishay led one group while his brother Yoav led the other (10:1-19; 18:1-18). Their military efforts were usually very successful.
Though Yoav’s actions eventually led to his death, we nowhere read about the same fate befalling Avishay, who, like Yoav, was a violently impulsive military leader.
Passages for Further Study
Yoav (Joab)

Yoav was David’s nephew, the son of David’s sister Tseruyah (Zeruiah) (1 Chr 2:13-16); his brothers were Avishay (Abishai) and Asahel. Yoav became commander of David’s armies because of his bravery and military skill (2 Sam 2:18; 8:16; 11:1; 1 Chr 18:15). As the first to attack the Yevusi (Jebusite) city of Yerushalem (Jerusalem), he was awarded the commander’s position (1 Chr 11:4-9). Yoav also suppressed a rebellion among the Arameans and Amonim (Ammonites) (2 Sam 10:1-19; 1 Chr 19:8-15) and won many key battles for David against the northern army of Yisrael (Israel) under Avner’s (Abner’s) impressive command (2 Sam 2:12-32).

Yoav often acted to promote what he perceived were David’s interests. For example, he colluded with David in the death of Uriyah (Uriah) the Hiti (Hittite) to cover up the king’s adultery with Bat-Sheva (Bathsheba) (11:1-27). He persuaded David to allow Avshalom’s (Absalom’s) return to court (14:1-33), and he tried to talk David out of taking a census that provoked God’s anger (24:1-9; 1 Chr 21:1-6).

Though he was very loyal to David, Yoav sometimes acted in his own interest, and sometimes he disregarded the king’s orders. When Avner killed Yoav’s brother Asahel (2 Sam 2:23), Yoav killed Avner in revenge (3:26-30), despite Avner’s new loyalty to David (3:12-19). Later, Yoav killed his own cousin Amasa (20:8-10), who commanded Avshalom’s army (17:25), after David had appointed Amasa commander in Yoav’s place (19:13; 20:4). Yoav also killed Avshalom against David’s direct order (18:5, 10-17). He then rebuked David for grieving Avshalom’s death rather than congratulating the army (19:5-7). Yoav was ruthless, and he regained the most powerful position in David’s army (20:23; 24:2; 1 Kgs 1:19).

Yoav sealed his fate by supporting Adoniyah’s (Adonijah’s) bid for David’s throne (1 Kgs 1:5-7). David’s deathbed instructions to Shelomoh (Solomon) included having Yoav killed because of his murders of Avner and Amasa. When Shelomoh became king, he sent Benayah (Benaiah) to kill Yoav even as Yoav clung to the horns of the altar (1 Kgs 2:28-34). Yoav met the same fate that he dealt to others throughout his life, and his executioner replaced him as commander of Yisrael’s army (1 Kgs 2:35).
Passages for Further Study
Avshalom (Absalom)

Avshalom, son of David, was a handsome prince (2 Sam 14:25-26). When his sister Tamar was raped by their half brother Amnon and then discarded, Avshalom took her in (13:1-20). He might have expected David to punish Amnon, but David said nothing (13:21). For two years of suppressed rage and growing hatred (13:22), Avshalom plotted revenge. Then he murdered Amnon and fled to his grandfather, King Talmay (Talmai) of Geshur (13:23-39).

After three years, Yoav (Joab) convinced David to bring Avshalom back, but David neither punished him nor was reconciled to him. Avshalom lived in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for two years with privilege and unresolved alienation. Then he insisted on seeing the king. The two met and made at least a show of reconciliation (14:28-33). But for Avshalom, the meeting might have been a maneuver toward the throne. Afterward, he put on a public-relations campaign to undermine the people’s confidence in David (15:1-6). Eventually, Avshalom’s underhanded tactics bore the fruit he had hoped for: He launched a coup and gathered supporters in Hevron (Hebron) from all over Yisrael (Israel). By the time news of Avshalom’s conspiracy reached David, the king was unable to do anything but flee Yerushalem (15:13-37; see Ps 3).

When Avshalom arrived in Yerushalem, David’s wisest adviser, Ahitofel (Ahithophel), joined Avshalom’s side and advised him to attack quickly while David was weak. But Hushay (Hushai), David’s secret agent, advised him to gather more troops and attack with overwhelming force. This advice appealed to Avshalom’s ego, but it was fatally wrong—as both advisers knew—to give such experienced warriors as David and his mighty men time to gather their strength, develop reconnaissance, and devise a strategy. By the time Avshalom led his forces across the Yarden (Jordan) River to do battle in the forest of Efrayim (Ephraim), David and his loyal forces were well rested and under the supremely capable leadership of Yoav, Avishay (Abishai), and Itay (Ittai) from Gat (Gath). David’s men outmaneuvered Avshalom’s superior forces and routed them. Avshalom himself fled on a mule, but his long hair got caught in the branches of a tree. Yoav and his men came upon Avshalom dangling helplessly and killed him, despite David’s command that they show him mercy (18:1-18).

Avshalom’s death stunned David; his grief nearly alienated those who had risked their lives to end Avshalom’s treasonous uprising against his kingdom (18:33–19:8). For Avshalom’s part, he had good reasons to be unsatisfied with David’s rule. But rather than following his father’s example of trusting in the Lord and honoring the anointed king (1 Sam 24:5-11; 26:5-24), Avshalom instigated a rebellion that resulted in his own death.
Passages for Further Study
Shelomoh (Solomon)

Shelomoh was the third king of Yisrael (Israel), the second son of David and Bat-Sheva (Bathsheba) (2 Sam 12:13-25); he reigned forty years (971–931 BC). Shelomoh began his reign with promising confidence in God but ended his life as an idol-worshiper who destroyed his kingdom.

As King David neared death, his son Adoniyah (Adonijah) made an attempt on the throne, supported by the priest Evyatar (Abiathar) and the general Yoav (Joab) (1 Kgs 1:1-53). The kingdom had been promised to Shelomoh, however (1 Kgs 1:17; see 2 Sam 12:24-25; 1 Chr 28:4-7), so Bat-Sheva and the prophet Natan (Nathan) informed David of Adoniyah’s intentions. David immediately arranged Shelomoh’s coronation. Then David advised Shelomoh to follow God faithfully (1 Kgs 2:1-9).

Shelomoh loved God and sought his help. God asked him to choose a gift, and since he chose wisdom rather than long life, riches, or fame, God gave him all of these. Shelomoh governed wisely (1 Kgs 3:16-28), received worldwide respect (1 Kgs 4:20-34), and wrote the Song of Songs, along with most of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes. Rabbis said that these books came from three stages of his life: “When a man is young he composes songs; when he grows older he makes sententious remarks; and when he becomes an old man he speaks of the vanity of things” (Midrash Rabah (Rabbah)). He also built the Temple in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and his own palace, developed trade, and increased the wealth and security of Yisrael. His reputation for wisdom and wealth was very great, and the queen of Sheva (Sheba) traveled to Yerushalem to see him for herself (1 Kgs 10:1-29).

Unfortunately, Shelomoh made many foreign alliances and married many foreign women, beginning with the daughter of Mitsrayim’s (Egypt’s) pharaoh (1 Kgs 3:1). Shelomoh’s foreign wives turned his heart away from God and toward idols. Later in life, the wise Shelomoh became extremely foolish under his wives’ influence; he worshiped false gods and oppressed his people. So God used Yarov’am (Jeroboam) to remove a large part of his kingdom.

Nonetheless, the New Testament remembers Shelomoh’s wisdom and glory as the standard against which others are measured. Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) is the incarnation of God’s wisdom, which far surpassed that of Shelomoh (Matt 12:42; Luke 11:31).
Passages for Further Study
Yarov’am (Jeroboam) I

Yarov’am I, son of Nevat (Nebat) from the tribe of Efrayim (Ephraim), was the first king of the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel) (931–910 BC). He led the northern ten tribes into the sins that brought about the destruction of the northern kingdom.

Yarov’am began his political career by supervising Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) labor forces in the territory of Efrayim and Menasheh (Manasseh) (1 Kgs 11:26-28). Because Shelomoh had drifted away from the Lord, God determined to remove the ten northern tribes from the rule of David’s descendants. The prophet Ahiyah (Ahijah) told Yarov’am that the Lord had chosen him to lead those tribes and to give him a lasting dynasty if he was faithful (11:29-39). Shelomoh apparently caught wind of what had happened and tried to kill Yarov’am, who sought refuge in Mitsrayim (Egypt) (11:40; cp. Sha’ul (Saul) and David, 1 Sam 18:5–20:42).

When Shelomoh died, his son Rehav’am (Rehoboam) was immediately proclaimed king in Yehudah (Judah), but the northern tribes had to affirm his kingship separately. Seizing the opportunity, Yarov’am took the northern leaders to Rehav’am to seek relief from the harsh labor Shelomoh had forced on them (1 Kgs 12:1-4). Rehav’am foolishly spurned their request (12:5-14), so the north rebelled and appointed Yarov’am as its king (12:20). Thus the kingdom was divided, as God had promised.

Yarov’am did not remain committed to God, however. He worried that if his people went to the Temple in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) to worship, they would support the southern kingdom. He had no confidence in God to secure his reign, so he carried out his own plan to secure his people’s spiritual allegiance. He built two gold calf shrines, at the north and south of his kingdom (12:26-33). God was displeased with these shrines and sent a prophet to condemn Yarov’am. Though Yarov’am initially responded to the prophet’s display of divine power, the calf shrines remained intact throughout the northern kingdom’s history (931–722 BC). Yarov’am’s false religion was a key reason for the destruction of the northern kingdom in 722 BC (14:14-16; 2 Kgs 17:5-23).

Because of Yarov’am’s sins, God did not give him a dynasty (1 Kgs 13:33-34). Though Yarov’am’s son Nadav (Nadab) inherited the throne when his father died, he was assassinated—along with the rest of Yarov’am’s descendants—two years later by a usurper named Baesha (Baasha) (14:20; 15:25-31).
Passages for Further Study
Rehav’am (Rehoboam)

Rehav’am, the son of Shelomoh (Solomon) and an Amoni (Ammonite) woman (1 Kgs 14:21), was forty-one when he became king; he reigned for seventeen years (931–913 BC). He is remembered for instigating the split of Shelomoh’s kingdom and for being the first king of Yehudah (Judah), the southern kingdom.

When Shelomoh died (931 BC), Yehudah immediately proclaimed Rehav’am king. The ten northern tribes were hesitant to support him, demanding relief from Shelomoh’s harsh policies (see 12:4; 2 Chr 10:4). The king’s mature advisers urged him to agree to their requests, but he rejected their advice and foolishly listened to younger advisers, who advised him to be even tougher than his father. The northern tribes rebelled and proclaimed Yarov’am (Jeroboam), Shelomoh’s former labor official, as their king. Rehav’am went to war, seeking control against the north, but God sent the prophet Shemayah (Shemaiah) to tell him this was useless since the split was God’s judgment (2 Chr 11:1-4). So Rehav’am returned to Yehudah and fortified his boundaries (2 Chr 11:5-12).

When Yarov’am established a new apostate religion in the northern kingdom, priests and Levites streamed to the south, where they strengthened the spiritual fiber of the realm and helped to maintain Yehudah’s stability (2 Chr 11:13-17). In the end, however, Rehav’am also turned to idol worship. The people of Yehudah built high places and pagan sanctuaries throughout the land and adopted corrupt religious practices from the heathen nations around them (1 Kgs 14:22-24). God stopped supporting Rehav’am, so he was vulnerable when King Shishak of Mitsrayim (Egypt) attacked him and removed many precious items from the Temple (926/925 BC; 1 Kgs 14:25-26; 2 Chr 12:1-5). Rehav’am then replaced Shelomoh’s gold shields with bronze ones (1 Kgs 14:27), an act that represented the loss of Yehudah’s glory because of false worship.
Passages for Further Study
Ahav (Ahab)

Ahav, Yisrael’s (Israel’s) eighth king, inherited the northern kingdom from his powerful father, Omri (1 Kgs 16:27-28), and reigned in Yisrael from 874 to 853 BC. Ahav married Izevel (Jezebel), daughter of King Etba’al (Ethbaal) of Tsidon (Sidon). Under her influence, Ahav began worshiping Ba’al (Baal) instead of the Lord (16:29-33).

Ahav had several military successes. He achieved victories over the Arameans (20:1-34), and in 853 BC he led a coalition of kings against the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III and defeated him at the battle of Qarqar. However, the Old Testament reports little positive news about Ahav, who was a traitor to God. God raised up the prophet Eliyah (Elijah) to confront Ahav, Izevel, and their prophets and to reassert the supremacy of the true God (17:1; 18:1-46).

Ahav not only betrayed the Lord; he also exploited his people, as in the matter of Navot (Naboth) and his vineyard (21:1-29). In Yisrael, the people had absolute title to the land as a gift from God. When Ahav wanted to annex a vineyard from his neighbor Navot and Navot refused, he was frustrated. Izevel was familiar with another type of kingship back home: When kings wanted something, they just took it. So she helped Ahav frame Navot, who was executed on false charges. Ahav took possession of the land, but the Lord would not let him get away with it. He sent Eliyah to deliver a death sentence for Ahav and his dynasty.

Then war flared up again with Aram, and Ahav enlisted Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat), the southern king, as his ally (1 Kgs 22:2-4; 2 Chr 18:1-3). Yehoshafat still believed in the Lord, so he talked Ahav into consulting God’s prophet Mikayah (Micaiah), who prophesied that this battle would end Ahav’s life (1 Kgs 22:5-28; 2 Chr 18:4-27). Ahav tried to escape this fate by wearing ordinary armor and having Yehoshafat wear royal battle dress as a decoy, but there is no fooling God. An archer’s shot penetrated the joint of Ahav’s armor, and he died, “just as Yahweh had promised” (1 Kgs 22:38).
Passages for Further Study
Izevel (Jezebel)

Izevel, daughter of Etba’al (Ethbaal), king of Tsidon (Sidon) (1 Kgs 16:31), married King Ahav (Ahab) of Yisrael (Israel), probably to confirm a political alliance between their countries. Izevel promoted Ba’al (Baal) worship and demanded absolute rights for the monarchy.

Izevel influenced Ahav into establishing Ba’al worship in Shomron (Samaria) and setting up an Asherah pole (16:30-33). She tried to exterminate God’s prophets (18:4) and supported large groups of Ba’al’s prophets in the royal palace (18:19).

Eliyah’s (Elijah’s) confrontation with Izevel and Ahav culminated on Mount Karmel (Carmel) (18:19-40), where Eliyah challenged Yisrael to follow the true God. Following a display of God’s power, the Israelis (Israelites) acknowledged God and helped Eliyah slaughter the false prophets. When Izevel heard this, she threatened Eliyah, and he fled (19:1-3).

Later, Izevel advised her husband about how to steal a vineyard from his neighbor Navot (Naboth). When Navot wouldn’t sell it, Izevel coldly devised a plan to falsely convict Navot of cursing God and the king, and he was executed. Ahav seized the vineyard, but God sent Eliyah to pronounce judgment on Izevel and Ahav (21:20-24). Ahav soon died (22:29-40), but Izevel survived throughout her son Ahazyah’s (Ahaziah’s) reign. She was later executed when Yehu (Jehu) exterminated the ruling family, and God’s sentence against her was fulfilled (2 Kgs 9:30-37).

Izevel’s corrupt influence spread to the southern kingdom of Yehudah (Judah) when her daughter Atalyah (Athaliah) married Yehoram (Jehoram), King Yehoshafat’s (Jehoshaphat’s) son (see 2 Kgs 8:18, 26-27).

The long-standing association of her name with evil is seen in Revelation 2:20, where the name Izevel is used to label a prophetess who seduced the Christians of Thuateira (Thyatira) to commit sexual sins and eat things sacrificed to idols.
Passages for Further Study
Eliyah (Elijah)

Eliyah from Tishbeh (Tishbe) served as prophet of Yisrael (Israel) during the reigns of Ahav (Ahab) and Ahazyah (Ahaziah) (874–852 BC). His name means “my God is Yahweh,” and his ministry involved demonstrating that the Lord is the one true God and calling Yisrael back to the Lord.

Under Ahav and Izevel (Jezebel), Yisrael began worshiping Ba’al (Baal), a Kena’ani (Canaanite) fertility god of storm and rain, so God sent a drought upon Yisrael (1 Kgs 17:1). Eliyah hid until the drought ended, and he was sustained by God. During that time, he lived with a widow in Tserefat (Zarephath), a town in Izevel’s home territory of Tsidon (Sidon). The widow’s son died, but Eliyah prayed for him and he was revived (1 Kgs 17:8-24).

In the third year of drought, Eliyah challenged Ba’al’s prophets to a contest on Mount Karmel (Carmel) to demonstrate the identity of the true God (1 Kgs 18:1-40). The prophets of Ba’al called on Ba’al in vain, becoming frantic to induce him to appear, while Eliyah made fun of Ba’al. When it was Eliyah’s turn, he poured water over his sacrifice and prayed a simple, powerful prayer. Fire immediately consumed the offering. In response, the people of Yisrael worshiped the Lord and, at Eliyah’s direction, killed Ba’al’s prophets. Then Eliyah prayed for rain, and the drought ended (1 Kgs 18:41-46).

Even with such tremendous displays of God’s power, Ahav and Izevel continued to lead Yisrael astray. Izevel was furious that her prophets had been killed (1 Kgs 19:1-2). She threatened Eliyah, who fled to the desert and asked God to take his life. Instead, an angel nourished him until he reached Mount Sinay (Sinai). Eliyah complained that he was the only remaining prophet of the Lord and that his life was at risk. God encouraged him in a quiet voice, gave him good news, then recommissioned him for service (1 Kgs 19:3-18).

Eliyah was single-minded in his devotion to the true God. He had an assistant named Elisha whom he trained well. At the end of Eliyah’s earthly existence, rather than dying, he was caught up into heaven in a chariot of fire (2 Kgs 2:11-12). Elisha inherited Eliyah’s prophetic mantle and continued the task of confronting false worship in Yisrael (see 2 Kgs 2:1–9:13; 13:14-25).

The Old Testament closes with the expectation that Eliyah would return before the day of the Lord (Mal 4:5-6), an expectation that Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) the immerser fulfilled, at least in part (see Matt 11:7-14; 17:10-13; Luke 1:17). Eliyah appeared with Mosheh (Moses) at Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) transfiguration (Matt 17:1-9). In Revelation 11:3-12, one of the two witnesses seems either to be Eliyah himself or to be modeled after Eliyah. Eliyah’s life illustrates God’s kindness and the effectiveness of prayer (Luke 4:25-26; Rom 11:2-6; Jas 5:17-18).
Passages for Further Study
Arameans

The Arameans were a Semitic group, descendants of Shem (Gen 10:22-23; cp. Gen 22:20-21). Betuel (Bethuel) and Lavan (Laban) were known as Arameans (Gen 25:20; 28:1-7). Ya’akov (Jacob) lived for some twenty years with them in Aramean territory (Gen 28–31; Hos 12:12), and the people of Yisrael (Israel) remembered that their forefathers were (at least culturally) Arameans (Deut 26:5).

When the Arameans emerged into history around the time of Avraham (Abraham), they were settled around the central Perat (Euphrates), from which they spread out to the east, west, and north. By around 1100 BC, Aramean tribes had spread throughout Aram (Syria) and had expanded into northern Transjordan. They set up a number of powerful Aramean city-states, including Tsovah (Zobah) and Damesek (Damascus), that came into conflict with the Israelis (Israelites) beginning in the time of David (see 2 Sam 8:3-8; 10:6-25).

After Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) death and the division of Yisrael into northern and southern kingdoms, Aramean Damesek became a powerful and opportunistic player in the political struggles between the two states. When war broke out between Yisrael and Yehudah (Judah) in the years 890–880 BC, King Asa of Yisrael sought aid from Ben-Hadad (Ben-hadad) I of Damesek (1 Kgs 15:18-19). Roughly thirty years later, in the early 850s BC, Ben-Hadad invaded Yisrael, but Ahav (Ahab) defeated him both at Shomron (Samaria) (20:1-21) and at Afek (Aphek) the following year (20:22-34). After three years of peace between Yisrael and Damesek, hostilities broke out again in 853 BC, resulting in the battle in which Ahav was killed (22:29-37). Aramean Damesek continued to inflict losses on the kingdom of Yisrael for the next several decades (see 2 Kgs 8:28-29; 12:17-18; 13:1-7).

During this period, the Aramean city-states began feeling pressure from Ashur (Assyria). Damesek was first defeated by Ashur around 838 BC and was forced to become a tribute-paying vassal of Ashur in 803 BC. The resulting weakness of Damesek helped enable Yehoash (Jehoash) (798–782 BC) to defeat the Arameans and expel them from Yisrael’s territory around 795 BC (2 Kgs 13:14-25). Later, Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II (793–753 BC) was able to force Damesek to pay tribute to him (see 2 Kgs 14:28).

Around 738 BC the Arameans of Damesek joined forces with Yisrael to subjugate Yehudah. They captured much land, but their siege of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was unsuccessful (2 Kgs 16:5; see also 2 Chr 28:5). At this time of seeming success for Damesek, the prophets Yeshayah (Isaiah) and Amos predicted the city’s doom (Isa 8:4; 17:1; Amos 1:3-5). But rather than trust in God, King Ahaz of Yehudah turned to the Assyrians for protection, who responded to his gifts by sacking Damesek and exiling its population in 733/732 BC (2 Kgs 16:7-11). Damesek was no longer an independent city-state.

The language of the Arameans, Aramaic, eventually became the language for diplomacy and administration all over the Near East (see, e.g., 2 Kgs 18:26). During the Exile, the Yehudim (Jews) adopted the Aramaic language; portions of Ezra and Daniyel (Daniel) are written in Aramaic. Aramaic was the lingua franca from Mitsrayim (Egypt) to Hodu (India) during the Persian period and was widely spoken in Palestine in Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) day (see Mark 5:41; 1 Cor 16:22).
Passages for Further Study
Elisha

Elisha the prophet was Eliyah’s (Elijah’s) follower and successor in the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel) during the late 800s BC, a time when the leaders and people of the northern kingdom turned their backs on God and worshiped the Kena’ani (Canaanite) god Ba’al (Baal). Ahav (Ahab) and Izevel (Jezebel) were eager worshipers of this false god, as were their descendants who succeeded them on the throne. Elisha’s ministry (853–798 BC) began as King Ahav’s reign was ending; he was an important part of God’s strategy to bring down Yisrael’s idol-worshiping leaders.

Elisha started his work as a disciple of Eliyah and was the one God chose to take Eliyah’s place (1 Kgs 19:15-21; 2 Kgs 2:1-18). After Eliyah was taken into heaven, Elisha’s miracles demonstrated that God’s great power was with him.

Elisha’s miracles often involved water. He purified the putrid water of a spring near Yeriho (Jericho) (2 Kgs 2:19-22) and caused an ax head to float (2 Kgs 6:1-7). When King Yoram’s (Joram’s) water supply ran out in enemy territory, Elisha correctly predicted that an ample water supply would emerge (2 Kgs 3:4-20). Ba’al supposedly controlled water, so these signs showed that the Lord, and not Ba’al, was really in charge.

Elisha displayed God’s power by helping people in tangible ways. He helped a poor woman by miraculously causing her jars to fill with olive oil (2 Kgs 4:1-7). He predicted to a woman from Shunem that she would have a son, and he brought the boy back to life when he died (2 Kgs 4:8-37). He cured an Aramean general named Na’aman (Naaman) of leprosy (2 Kgs 5:1-19). And he provided food for people who needed it (2 Kgs 4:38-44).

Elisha was part of God’s plan to bring judgment on the northern kingdom. He anointed both Yehu (Jehu) of Yisrael and Hazael of Aram (2 Kgs 8:7-15; 9:1-13), who brought a violent end to the leaders of Yisrael who encouraged the worship of Ba’al (see 1 Kgs 19:15-18).

Elisha’s miracles anticipated Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) ministry. Yeshua also cured lepers (Matt 8:1-4), raised the dead (Mark 5:21-43; Luke 7:11-17; John 11:1-44), and miraculously provided food (Matt 14:13-21; 15:32-38). Yeshua mentioned the healing of Na’aman as a precedent for his reaching out to Gentiles, to show that God’s mercy is not restricted to Israelis (Israelites) (Luke 4:27).
Passages for Further Study
Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II

Yarov’am II, son of Yehoash (Jehoash), reigned over Yisrael (Israel) for 41 years (793–753 BC), longer than any other northern king. He followed the evil example of his (unrelated) namesake, Yarov’am I (2 Kgs 14:23-24). During his era the northern kingdom reached its greatest extent and experienced its greatest prosperity since Shelomoh (Solomon) (archaeological evidence from Yarov’am’s capital, Shomron (Samaria), suggests the opulence of Yisrael’s royal house during his reign). On a human level, an explanation for Yisrael’s newfound prosperity was that Ashur (Assyria) experienced a decline in power during this time, allowing the northern kingdom to expand. The prophet Yonah (Jonah), however, predicted this prosperity as the fulfillment of God’s promise (14:25). Even though Yarov’am’s reign came after 150 years of apostasy in the northern kingdom, God still exhibited his faithful love by offering Yisrael his mercy (14:26-27).

While the reign of Yarov’am II produced great wealth, it was not accompanied by justice. The rich landowners oppressed the less wealthy and forced small landowners to migrate from their farms to the cities. There was an increase in government corruption, economic depression, and political weakness, and Yisrael’s spiritual state continued to degenerate. God raised up prophets to challenge the leaders and people of Yisrael during this time. Amos and Hoshea (Hosea) prophesied against Yisrael’s vast corruption. Amos was particularly scathing in his attacks on the rich for oppressing the poor. He mentions Yarov’am’s impending death and the punishment that was coming upon Yisrael (Amos 7:10-17).

When Yarov’am II died, the northern kingdom rapidly declined. In the following years (753–722 BC), six kings ruled in rapid succession, and most of them were assassinated. In 722 BC, about 30 years after the end of Yarov’am II’s reign, Ashur destroyed the northern kingdom and deported its people, thus properly bringing judgment on the sins of Yarov’am II and other northern kings.
Passages for Further Study
Ahaz

Ahaz reigned in Yehudah (Judah) during a turbulent period (743–715 BC). His father Yotam (Jotham) (2 Kgs 15:32-38; 2 Chr 27:1-9) and son Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) (2 Kgs 18:1-8) were praised for their obedience to the Lord, but Ahaz was evil, even sacrificing one of his sons to false gods.

Ahaz’s reign was marked with conflict. King Pekah of Yisrael (Israel) and King Retsin (Rezin) of Aram (Aram (Syria)) wanted him to join a coalition against Ashur (Assyria), but he refused. So Pekah and Retsin turned against Yehudah and won substantial victories, which severely frightened Ahaz. Yeshayah (Isaiah) the prophet encouraged Ahaz to rely on the Lord, but Ahaz refused (Isa 7).

Revealing his lack of trust in the true God, Ahaz appealed to Tiglat-Pileser (Tiglath-pileser) III for help (2 Kgs 16:7-9). Ahaz made Yehudah dangerously dependent on Ashur, and Yehudah effectively became a vassal state. The Assyrian king subsequently defeated the Arameans in a two-year campaign (734–732 BC) and killed Retsin. He subdued Yisrael and incorporated great tracts of Pekah’s land into the Assyrian Empire (15:29).

Ahaz became an eager servant of Ashur. He adopted many religious innovations based on Assyrian models. Ahaz visited Tiglat-Pileser III in Damesek (Damascus), where he saw an Assyrian altar and sent a model of it to Yerushalem (Jerusalem), where a similar altar was built, replacing the original bronze altar (16:10-18). Several other Temple alterations also indicate Ahaz’s defection from faith in the Lord.

Ahaz illustrates why the people of Yehudah were finally exiled. He did not comport himself appropriately as a king (Deut 17:14-20), and he did not worship the Lord. Upon his death, he was succeeded by his son Hizkiyah (2 Kgs 16:20).
Passages for Further Study
Hizkiyah (Hezekiah)

Hizkiyah, who reigned from 728 to 686 BC was one of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) best kings. Hizkiyah’s father, Ahaz, betrayed the Lord, but Hizkiyah promoted true worship of God. Reversing the damage done by Ahaz, he repaired the Temple doors, had the Levites sanctify themselves, and reinstated religious ceremonies. He brought sacrifices, restored the priestly Temple service, and invited people throughout Yehudah and Yisrael (Israel) to celebrate Passover in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (2 Chr 29–30). After the celebration, he faithfully destroyed pagan worship sites.

Soon after Hizkiyah started ruling, the Assyrians under Shalmaneser V and his successor Sargon II defeated the northern kingdom, deported its inhabitants, and brought in foreign residents (722 BC). When Sargon II died in 705 BC, his son Sanheriv (Sennacherib) came to power, triggering widespread rebellion. Hizkiyah stopped paying the tribute that his father Ahaz had paid (2 Kgs 18:7; see 16:7). As a result, in 701 BC Sanheriv invaded Yehudah. Hizkiyah tried to appease the Assyrian ruler by sending a vast tribute payment, but the attempted return to servitude failed and the Assyrian forces threatened Yerushalem and mocked Hizkiyah’s reliance on the Lord (18:17-35). Hizkiyah responded with grieving and supplication. The Lord, speaking through Yeshayah (Isaiah) the prophet, assured Hizkiyah that his prayers had been heard and that Sanheriv would not conquer Yerushalem (19:1-34).

Around that same time, Hizkiyah became seriously ill (20:1-11). Yeshayah told him to prepare for death, but Hizkiyah turned to the Lord and prayed for healing. The Lord promised him fifteen more years as well as deliverance from the Assyrians. When he had recovered, Hizkiyah unwisely hosted the rebel Babylonian king Merodak-Bal’adan (Merodach-baladan) in his palace, showing him the Temple treasures and seeking support from Bavel (Babylon) rather than the Lord. Yeshayah predicted that those treasures would be carried off to Bavel (20:12-19).
After the Assyrian threat in 701 BC, Hizkiyah’s remaining years were peaceful and prosperous; he died in 686 BC and was succeeded by his son Menasheh (Manasseh).
Passages for Further Study
Yoshiyah (Josiah)

Yoshiyah, who reigned in Yehudah (Judah) from 640 to 609 BC, was a godly man, unlike his grandfather Menasheh (Manasseh) and his father, Amon. Yoshiyah “turned to Yahweh with all his heart and soul and strength, obeying all the laws of Mosheh (Moses)” (2 Kgs 23:25).

The kingdom of Yehudah was grossly idolatrous and wicked during Menasheh’s reign (697–642 BC). Despite Menasheh’s own repentance toward the end of his reign, conditions continued to worsen under his son Amon (642–640 BC), who was so bad that his own officials assassinated him, and the eight-year-old Yoshiyah was placed on the throne (21:23-24; 22:1; 2 Chr 33:24–34:1).

When Yoshiyah was sixteen, he began “to seek the God of his ancestor David” (2 Chr 34:3). From that point on, he was dedicated to purifying the worship of the people of God. At twenty, Yoshiyah began eradicating pagan places of worship, especially the despised pagan worship center at Beyt-El (Bethel). Yoshiyah fulfilled prophecy (1 Kgs 13:1-3) by destroying its altar and burning the bones of pagan priests to desecrate the site (2 Kgs 23:15-18).

When Yoshiyah was twenty-six, he organized repairs to the Temple (22:3-7). In the process, the priest Hilkiyah (Hilkiah) found the Book of the Law and read it to Yoshiyah, who was devastated by its pronouncements against apostasy (22:8-20). He then sought more fully to obey God’s instructions and to lead the people in worshiping the Lord. He celebrated Passover as the law demanded, destroyed many artifacts used in Ba’al (Baal) and sun worship, and eliminated pagan shrines in Yehudah (23:4-14). In all this, Yoshiyah was apparently supported by the prophets Tsefanyah (Zephaniah) and Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), who spoke for God during his time.

Yoshiyah was not sensitive to God’s voice on one significant occasion, however, and it cost him his life (23:29-30; 2 Chr 35:20-25). In 609 BC, Par’oh (Pharaoh) Nekoh (Neco) marched toward Karkemish (Carchemish) to reinforce the Assyrian army against Bavel (Babylon). Yoshiyah delayed Nekoh at Megidon (Megiddo), perhaps wanting to support the Babylonians. Nekoh insisted that the Lord wanted him to fight Bavel, but Yoshiyah attacked him and was killed in battle. Yoshiyah was greatly mourned by Yirmiyah and the people of Yehudah (2 Chr 35:25).

Though Yoshiyah was faithful, the people were not; once he died, his sons and successors began to turn away from the Lord. In spite of Yirmiyah’s increased efforts, the people did not repent. The turbulent years that followed Yoshiyah’s death soon ended with the destruction of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and the exile of its citizens to Bavel (605–586 BC).
Passages for Further Study
Ashur (Assyria)

Ashur was a symbol of terror and tyranny in the Near East for more than three centuries. In the biblical account, we learn about its power and ruthlessness in its treatment of the people of Yisrael (Israel) and Yehudah (Judah). But its fortune rose and fell with the strength of its leaders. Eventually, it was overpowered by those who were stronger.
Ashurnasirpal II (885–860 BC)
Ashurnasirpal II possessed all the qualities and defects of his successors to the extreme: He had the ambition, energy, courage, vanity, and magnificence of a ruthless and unrelenting empire builder.
Shalmaneser III (858–824 BC)

Shalmaneser III is well known for the Battle of Qarqar (853 BC), considered the most fully documented event from the ancient world. His invasion of Aram (Syria) was repelled by a coalition that included King Ahav (Ahab) of Yisrael and several other states. It was years before Shalmaneser was able to conquer Yisrael and Aram. King Yehu (Jehu) of Yisrael is depicted on the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III kissing the ground at his feet and offering tribute.
Repentance during the Time of Yonah (Jonah)

Sometime during the reign of King Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II in Yisrael (793–753 BC), the prophet Yonah grudgingly traveled to Nineveh to proclaim judgment (Jon 3–4). Ashur was then in decline, and as Yonah had feared, the king and people of Nineveh listened and repented of their sins. As a result, God granted them a reprieve, which lasted some 150 years.
Tiglat-Pileser (Tiglath-pileser) III (744–727 BC)

Tiglat-Pileser III usurped the Assyrian throne and began to recover and consolidate control of all Ashur’s territories. He gained the throne of Bavel (Babylon) as well, establishing Ashur firmly as the dominant military and economic power in the Near East. He demonstrated political prudence not usually found in the ruthless Assyrian monarchs. King Menahem of Yisrael (752–742 BC) paid him tribute (2 Kgs 15:19-20), as did Tsor (Tyre), Byblos, and Damesek (Damascus). Responding to an appeal from King Ahaz of Yehudah (735–715 BC) to help resist Aram and Yisrael (2 Kgs 16:5-20), Tiglat-Pileser conquered Damesek in 732 BC. (His successor, Shalmaneser V, would destroy Shomron (Samaria) in 722 BC, punctuating the end of the northern kingdom of Yisrael.)
Sanheriv (Sennacherib) (705–681 BC)

Sanheriv was occupied throughout his reign in a series of bitter wars. He is especially known in the biblical account for his campaign against Yehudah and siege of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) in 701 BC during the reign of King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) and the ministry of the prophet Yeshayah (Isaiah) (2 Kgs 18:13–19:37; Isa 36–37).
Ashurbanipal (668–627 BC)

Ashurbanipal captured No-amon (No (Thebes)) in Mitsrayim (Egypt), thereby realizing the greatest victory in Assyrian history (see Nah 3:3-10). He also established a great library in Nineveh, which was excavated in 1860. Many tablets were found, containing a vast selection of Akkadian material. This library is now one of the principal treasures of the British Museum in London. Very little is known about Ashurbanipal’s reign after 639 BC, since his annals do not extend beyond that year. However, allusions in state correspondence, commercial documents, and prayers addressed to the gods suggest that Ashur (Assyria) was becoming increasingly unstable. When Ashurbanipal died in 627 BC, his empire declined quickly.
Final Decline and Destruction

In 626 BC, Nabopolassar became king of Bavel (626–605 BC) and formed an alliance with the Madim (Medes), making it almost inevitable that Bavel would succeed against Ashur. In 612 BC their combined forces launched a final assault against Nineveh, and after three months of siege the mighty city fell (see Nah 1:8). The last of the Assyrian forces were completely destroyed by Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) (then a general in his father’s army) at the battle of Karkemish (Carchemish) in 605 BC.
Passages for Further Study
Bavel (Babylon)
Bavel, one of the world’s most ancient cities, was the center of the Babylonian civilization and is an enduring symbol for defiant human pride.

Bavel was founded a few generations after the Flood by Nimrod (Gen 10:8-10), one of history’s first powerful overlords. Bavel takes its name from Bavel, a word that means “gate of god” in the Babylonian language. Bavel was probably the location of the tower of Bavel (Gen 11:1-9), an early attempt by humanity to construct their own identity apart from the Creator. It was this proud civilization that Avraham (Abraham) and his family left when they traveled out of Ur of the Kasdim (Chaldeans) around 2000 BC. Even though Bavel was ruled by many kingdoms throughout the centuries, the city remained a cultural and religious figurehead.
Sumerian Civilization (3200–2000 BC)
The first great civilization to flourish in Bavel was Sumer, centered south of Bavel. The Sumerians invented cuneiform writing, which was used by Mesopotamian cultures for three thousand years.
The Akkadian Empire (2334–2154 BC)

To the north of Bavel, Akkadian king Sargon I (2339–2279 BC) founded the capital city of Akkad and gained political and cultural supremacy over Mesopotamia. The Akkadian Empire lasted for nearly two centuries.
First Babylonian Kingdom (1900–1600 BC)

During the period of the Akkadian Empire, Semitic-speaking nomads from Aram (Syria) called Amurru (“Amorim (Amorites)”), regarded as barbarians by the urbane Babylonians, began migrating into Bavel, where they eventually established a new Babylonian kingdom under Amori (Amorite) control. The sixth king of that dynasty was Hammurabi (1792–1750 BC), who enlarged the kingdom significantly. Bavel’s glory, however, was short-lived; the kingdom shriveled under Hammurabi’s son and lasted only another century.
Assyrian Domination (900–614 BC)

In 851 BC Assyrian king Shalmaneser III (858–824 BC) entered Bavel but treated the ancient city with respect and left its king on his throne as a vassal. A century and a half later (around 705 BC), a Babylonian vassal-king named Merodak-Bal’adan (Merodach-baladan) organized a revolution, and he sent ambassadors to King Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) of Yehudah (Judah) for support (see 2 Kgs 20:12-19; Isa 39). Ashur (Assyria) quickly crushed Merodak-Bal’adan’s revolution, and Ashur’s domination continued for another century.
Neo-Babylonian Empire (612–539 BC)

The Chaldean prince Nabopolassar seized the throne of Bavel (Babylon) (625–605 BC) and put an end to the Assyrian Empire. Under his son Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) II (605–562 BC), Bavel was master of the Near East, a city of splendor (see Dan 1–4).

Nevukadnetsar was eventually succeeded by a high diplomatic official named Nabonidus (555–539 BC), who neglected Bavel and lost its support. When Koresh (Cyrus) II of Paras (Persia) (559–530 BC) attacked the city in October 539 BC (see Dan 5:30-31 and study note on Dan 5:31), the city gave itself up without a battle. That surrender marked the end of independent Bavel.
The Symbolic Enemy of God’s People

In 1 Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) and Revelation, Romai (Rome) is personified as “Bavel the Great, Mother of all Prostitutes and Obscenities in the World” (Rev 17:5)—a dreadfully immoral center of wealth and commerce, ruling over the kings of the earth and persecuting God’s people. The kings and merchants of the earth will mourn her demise (Rev 18:9-19), but God’s people will rejoice that their oppression has ended and will worship God freely.
Passages for Further Study
Asa

Asa became the third king of Yehudah (Judah) after the split of Shelomoh’s (Solomon’s) empire into independent kingdoms. Asa succeeded his father, Aviyah (Abijah), after Aviyah’s brief kingship (913–910 BC) and reigned for 41 years (910–869 BC).

In the beginning of his reign, Asa was a good king. He opposed the worship of false gods in the land, destroyed the Asherah pole that his grandmother Ma’akah (Maacah) had set up, and removed her remaining political influence (1 Kgs 15:13; 2 Chr 15:16).

In these early days, God blessed Asa’s reign with military victory and peace. Asa forced out or defeated all who attempted to conquer, divide, or destroy Yehudah (2 Chr 14:1-8). Asa’s most astounding conquest was over an Kushi (Ethiopian) leader named Zerah, who attacked Yehudah with more than a million troops. Because of Asa’s obedience and faithfulness, God gave him a tremendous victory (14:9-15).

Unfortunately, Asa’s attitude changed toward the end of his life, and he abandoned his trust in God. Baesha (Baasha), the king of the northern kingdom, attacked Yehudah with the support of Ben-Hadad (Ben-hadad), king of Aram, and fortified the city of Ramah. Asa paid the king of Aram to change sides and support him rather than Baesha. This meant that Asa had more confidence in a foreign king than in the Lord. Worse, Asa paid Ben-Hadad with gold and silver that he had earlier given to the Temple! Asa’s power play worked, and the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel) had to leave Yehudah to stave off Ben-Hadad’s threat from the north. But the prophet Hanani rebuked Asa for his disbelief in God. Infuriated, Asa had Hanani thrown into prison (16:7-10).

For the final years of his reign, Asa became ill with a serious foot disease. “Even with the severity of his disease, he did not seek Yahweh’s help but turned only to his physicians” (16:12). Even so, when Asa died he was buried with honor in the royal tombs (16:14).
Passages for Further Study
Yehoshafat (Jehoshaphat)

Yehoshafat succeeded his father Asa to become the fourth king of Yehudah (Judah) (872–848 BC). Like Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) and Yoshiyah (Josiah) after him, Yehoshafat trusted the Lord throughout his life and worked to remove most forms of pagan worship from Yisrael (Israel) (2 Chr 17:6).

Yehoshafat continued his father Asa’s religious reforms but reversed his foreign policy. Yehoshafat discontinued Yehudah’s war with Yisrael over their boundaries (see 1 Kgs 22:2) and made an alliance with Ahav (Ahab). To confirm this alliance, he arranged for his son Yehoram (Jehoram) to marry Ahav’s daughter Atalyah (Athaliah) (2 Chr 18:1-2; 2 Kgs 8:18) and supported the north in its wars against the Arameans and Moavim (Moabites) (2 Chr 18:3-34; 1 Kgs 22; 2 Kgs 3:4-27). The prophet Yehu (Jehu) rebuked Yehoshafat for his unwise alliance with Yisrael (2 Chr 19:1-3), which resulted in his son Yehoram falling under the influence of Ahav and Izevel (Jezebel). Yehoram and his son Ahazyah (Ahaziah) turned Yehudah toward idol worship.

Yet during his reign, Yehoshafat kept the worship of the Lord pure. He closed the temples of prostitution (1 Kgs 22:46) and sent teachers of God’s law throughout the land (2 Chr 17:7-9). He also established a system of judges and admonished them to function as the Lord’s representatives so that justice might prevail (19:4-7). He appointed Levites, priests, and family heads to handle cases pertaining to religious practice and to negotiate disputes among citizens (19:8-10).

Before going to battle, Yehoshafat would insist on hearing from a true prophet of the Lord. And in one of the most stirring descriptions of war in the Old Testament, Yehoshafat preached to the army before entering a battle. As a result, God caused the armies from Amon (Ammon), Moav (Moab), and their allies to turn against each other (2 Chr 20).
Yehoshafat died when he was about sixty years old and was buried in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). His son Yehoram became Yehudah’s next king (21:1).
Passages for Further Study
Uziyah (Uzziah)

Uziyah, son of Amatsyah (Amaziah) and Yekaleyah (Jecoliah), reigned over Yehudah (Judah) for 52 years (792–740 BC; see 2 Kgs 14:21-22; 15:1-2; 2 Chr 26:1-3). He reigned as co-regent with his father from the age of sixteen for approximately 25 years. Later, when his father was assassinated, Uziyah became the sole ruler. He served as a capable, energetic, and well-organized king who pleased the Lord through most of his reign.

During most of Uziyah’s reign, Yarov’am (Jeroboam) II ruled the northern kingdom of Yisrael (Israel) (793–753 BC). Both kings were successful and brought a long period of prosperity to Yisrael and Yehudah. Uziyah successfully fought the Pelishtim (Philistines), and he built many fortifications in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and throughout Yehudah. He “sought guidance from Yahweh” (2 Chr 26:5), and as long as he did, the Lord blessed him in all his undertakings and he prospered.

Several prophets were active during Uziyah’s reign. Amos and Hoshea (Hosea) both prophesied during his life (Hos 1:1; Amos 1:1), though most of their oracles were directed toward the northern kingdom. And the prophet Yeshayah (Isaiah) received his call the year Uziyah died (Isa 1:1; 6:1).

Uziyah became proud of his many successes and had a sad downfall (2 Chr 26:16). He took upon himself the prerogatives of a priest, entered the holy area of the Temple, and burned incense. The priests tried to stop him from this sin against the Lord, but he angrily rejected their warnings. Because of his disobedience, God struck Uziyah with leprosy and he had to live out the rest of his life in seclusion. Uziyah was buried with his forefathers, but at a distance because of his leprosy (26:23).
Passages for Further Study
Menasheh (Manasseh)

Menasheh, the thirteenth king of Yehudah (Judah) (697–642 BC), had a long but notoriously wicked reign (2 Kgs 21:1-18; 2 Chr 33:1-9)—even though his father was the godly king Hizkiyah (Hezekiah) (2 Kgs 20:21).

In 697 BC, Menasheh became co-ruler with his father Hizkiyah at age twelve (2 Chr 33:1). In 686 BC, Hizkiyah died and Menasheh became sole monarch. He reigned a total of fifty-five years (2 Kgs 21:1), longer than any other king in Yehudah or Yisrael (Israel). Regrettably, he was the most wicked of all the kings of Yehudah. He rebuilt the high places for pagan worship; he encouraged the worship of Ba’al (Baal), the sun, the moon, and the stars; and he even burnt his son as a child sacrifice (2 Kgs 21:2-9; see 2 Kgs 23:10; Jer 7:31). He allowed divination and sorcery in Yehudah and “murdered many innocent people until Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was filled . . . with innocent blood” (2 Kgs 21:16; 24:3-4).

Surviving Assyrian records note that Menasheh provided men to transport timber from Levanon (Lebanon) to Nineveh for the Assyrian king Esar-Hadon (Esarhaddon) (680–669 BC), and he paid tribute to King Ashurbanipal (668–626 BC) after an Assyrian military campaign in Mitsrayim (Egypt) in 667 BC. Menasheh served Ashur (Assyria) more faithfully than he served the Lord.

Because of Menasheh’s tremendous sin, God determined to “wipe away the people of Yerushalem as one wipes a dish and turns it upside down” (2 Kgs 21:13). However, Menasheh repented late in life. The Assyrian army captured him, put a hook through his nose, and exiled him to Bavel (Babylon) (2 Chr 33:10-13). There Menasheh turned to the Lord. God heard his prayers, restored him as king, and blessed the rest of his reign as Menasheh sought to restore proper worship of God alone (33:14-17).

Sadly, Menasheh’s sins had infected the people of Yehudah (33:17), and God did not reverse his determination to judge the kingdom (2 Kgs 23:26; 24:3-4). This indicates just how seriously Menasheh had sinned. Even Yirmiyah (Jeremiah), one hundred years later, announced: “Because of the wicked things Menasheh son of Hizkiyah, king of Yehudah, did in Yerushalem, I will make my people an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth” (Jer 15:4). The destruction of Yerushalem and its Temple and the exile of Yehudah’s people followed.
When Menasheh died in 642 BC at age 67, he was buried in his own garden (2 Kgs 21:18), rather than with highly regarded leaders such as Yehoyada (Jehoiada) and Hizkiyah (2 Chr 24:15-16; 32:33).
Passages for Further Study
Koresh (Cyrus) II

Koresh II, king of Paras (Persia) (559–530 BC), founded the great Persian Empire. His father was king of Paras, a small nation that was subject to Media, and his mother was the daughter of the king of the Madim (Medes). Koresh conquered the Madim in 549 BC and combined the two nations into one. He conquered Ludia (Lydia) in Asia Minor in 547 BC, then turned to the east and brought Parthia and part of Hodu (India) into the Persian Empire. Finally, on October 29, 539 BC, Koresh conquered the city of Bavel (Babylon) and brought Bavel into his empire (see Dan 5:30-31).

After conquering Bavel, Koresh issued a decree that allowed the Jewish people to return home and rebuild the Temple in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). The part of this decree dealing with the Yehudim (Jews) has been recorded in 2 Chronicles 36:22-23 and Ezra 1:1-4. This practice is confirmed by the Koresh Cylinder, a barrel that was discovered at Bavel in 1879–82, which describes Koresh’s policy regarding conquered peoples.

Yeshayah (Isaiah) named Koresh as Yehudah’s (Judah’s) future deliverer (Isa 44:28–45:13) and even called him the Lord’s anointed (Isa 45:1, Hebrew mashiakh, “messiah”). Yisrael (Israel) regarded Koresh as called and empowered by God to free them. Koresh was not the Messiah, but what he did served as an example of what the Messiah, Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ, would later do in setting God’s people free from servitude.
Passages for Further Study
Ezra

Ezra was a priest and scribe of the high-priestly line of Tsadok (Zadok) (Ezra 7:1-5, 11-12; cp. Neh 8:2, 9). He was a leader in Yehudah (Judah) following the Yehudim’s (Jews’) return from exile. As a scribe, Ezra was not just a copyist but a disciplined student of God’s laws (Ezra 7:6) who was qualified to teach, preach, and interpret the Scriptures.

As an important official who assisted the king with Jewish affairs in the Persian Empire, Ezra visited Yerushalem (Jerusalem) around 458 BC, bringing articles for the Temple and the mission of establishing God’s laws and the laws of Paras (Persia). One of his first reforms was to confront the sin of intermarriage with pagan neighbors (9:1–10:44). Later, after the city walls were rebuilt in 445 BC (Neh 6:15), Ezra led the community to obey God’s law more fully (Neh 8:13-15).

Ezra honored God through his handling of finances. The Persian king trusted Ezra’s judgment and allowed him to ask for more money when needed (Ezra 7:15-20). Ezra gave others the responsibility for financial affairs whenever he could and required strict financial integrity (8:24-30). He identified certain financial resources as holy and belonging to God.

Ezra humbled himself before God when the people began their journey (8:21-23), when he found out about the people’s unholy marriages (9:5-15), and when he gathered those required to divorce their pagan wives (10:6). He always recognized that God’s gracious hand—not his own ability or wisdom—enabled good things to happen (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31; 9:8-9). He studied and lived by God’s Word and taught others to follow what God revealed (7:10). He was a teacher and servant-leader, not a self-important official who lorded it over other people.

Ezra’s piety and dedication, demonstrated through prayer and fasting, put his reforming zeal in proper spiritual perspective. He set the pattern for life in the postexilic Jewish community, making God’s Word and worship central priorities.
Passages for Further Study
The Madim (Medes) and Persians
The Madim (around 850–549 BC)

The early Madim left no written records. According to an inscription from Shalmaneser III of Ashur (Assyria) (858–824 BC), the Madim had settled around Ahmeta (Ecbatana), their capital (modern Hamadan, Iran), by the mid-800s BC. The Madim were renowned horse breeders, so Shalmaneser raided their territory to steal large herds of fine horses. The Madim were subject to the Assyrians until the late 600s, when they gained their independence as Ashur weakened.
The Persians (around 700–549 BC)

Around 700 BC, a small kingdom of Paras (Persia) was established under Achaemenes, who ruled around 700~675 BC. His son Teispes (675~640 BC) was under the domination of the Madim, who were gathering forces to overthrow Ashur. But trouble for the Madim later freed Teispes from their control. Cambyses (600~559 BC), son of Koresh (Cyrus) I and grandson of Teispes, married the daughter of the Median king Astuages (Astyages); their son was Koresh II (559–530 BC), who ascended the throne of Paras in 559 BC.
The Medo-Persian Empire (549–331 BC)

Koresh II fought and defeated his grandfather, Astuages of Media, in 549 BC. He made Ahmeta in Media his capital and set up his archives there (see Ezra 6:1-5). With a Persian father and Median mother, Koresh II embodied the joining of Media and Paras.

Koresh exhibited an attitude of benevolence and generosity toward defeated enemies. A capable military leader, Koresh invaded Asia Minor and defeated Croesus, king of Ludia (Lydia), and brought the Greek cities of the area into subjection. In 539 BC, he captured Bavel (Babylon) with virtually no resistance and decreed that exiled peoples could return to their homelands to rebuild their temples (see Ezra 1:1-4).

The son of Koresh, Cambyses II (529–522 BC), conquered Mitsrayim (Egypt), but the empire nearly disintegrated when he committed suicide. Cambyses was succeeded by Dareyavesh (Darius) I (521–486 BC), the son of Hystaspes, satrap of Parthia. Dareyavesh, an energetic and efficient administrator, put down internal revolts and consolidated the empire into twenty provinces, each under a satrap or “protector of the kingdom,” with inspectors (“the ears of the king”) to check on the activities of the satraps. Dareyavesh changed the principal capital of Paras to Persepolis, where a tremendous palace complex was eventually constructed. Dareyavesh was a follower of Zoroaster and a worshiper of Ahura Mazda, the principal god of Zoroastrianism, as were Ahashverosh (Xerxes) and Artahshashta (Artaxerxes) after him.
During the latter part of Dareyavesh’s reign, he suffered defeat at the hands of the Greeks at Marathon (491 BC).

Dareyavesh was succeeded by his son Khshayarsha, better known as Ahashverosh in Greek or as Ahashverosh in Hebrew. During his rule (486–465 BC), the Persian fleet was defeated by the Greeks at Salamis (480 BC).

The loss of the empire has been attributed to the cowardice of Dareyavesh III (336–330 BC), whose armies were defeated by Alexandros (Alexander) the Great at Issus in 333 BC and ultimately at Gaugamela, near modern Erbil (Arbela) in 331 BC.
Paras and the Bible

The earliest mention of Paras in Yisrael’s (Israel’s) history is in Isaiah 44:28–45:13, a predictive prophecy that was given to Yeshayah (Isaiah) more than 150 years before Koresh captured Bavel and decreed the return of the exiled Yehudim (Jews) to Yerushalem (Jerusalem).
