The rest of the biblical references to Paras occur in the later period of Old Testament history (Ezra, Nehemyah (Nehemiah), Ester (Esther)) and in the writings of the exilic and postexilic prophets (Daniyel (Daniel), Tsefanyah (Zephaniah), Hagay (Haggai)). Paras is portrayed in Scripture as a stern but usually benevolent master that generally let the Yehudim govern themselves and worship in their own way. Nevertheless, the fact that the postexilic community of Judea was under foreign rule was never far from their minds.
Passages for Further Study
Nehemyah (Nehemiah)
Nehemyah was a powerful leader of God’s people living in Judea following the Exile. Nehemyah improved the morale and strength of God’s people in the midst of difficulty.

Before Nehemyah returned to Judea, he was cup-bearer to Persian king Artahshashta (Artaxerxes) I (465–424 BC). The cup-bearer brought the king his wine (tasting it first to make sure it wasn’t poisoned) and was his trusted confidant and adviser. Nehemyah heard reports about Yerushalem’s (Jerusalem’s) sad state and, moved with compassion, he asked the king’s permission to return to Judea to help his people. The king responded favorably and made him governor of the province of Judea for twelve years to aid his fellow Yehudim (Jews) and rebuild the walls of Yerushalem (Neh 1:1–2:8).

Nehemyah had the support of the Persian king, but he faced opposition from the inhabitants of the land. These people of mixed heritage were the ancestors of the New Testament Shomronim (Samaritans). Nehemyah showed great courage and skill as he successfully helped the people of Judea rebuild the walls that protected Yerushalem.

Nehemyah had a strong personal faith, as seen by his prayers (Neh 1:4-11; 2:4) and his confidence in divine guidance and help (2:8, 18, 20). He also advocated economic justice: He rebuked a few rich Yehudim who were exploiting a food shortage by exacting high interest from their poorer relatives, and he provided an example of better conduct (Neh 5).

Nehemyah was vitally concerned about the people’s faithfulness, and he individually confronted men who had married pagan women (13:23-29). He had a strong interest in maintaining Temple worship, and he led the Jewish community to pledge support for Temple personnel and to provide offerings (10:32-39). He also reformed Rest Day observance (13:15-22).

Although there were still problems at the end of his tenure in Yerushalem (see Neh 13), Nehemyah was an effective leader who restored a national and religious identity to the Jewish settlers in a period of political and economic weakness.
Passages for Further Study
Ester (Esther)

Ester was queen of Paras (Persia) during the reign of Ahashverosh (Xerxes) I (486–465 BC). She was a woman of the Diaspora (“scattering”), descended from Yehudim (Jews) who had been scattered among the nations at the time of the Exile. Her family had not returned to the land of Yehudah (Judah), as some Yehudim had (see Ezra 1–2), but had chosen to stay in the land of Paras, like many others. Noting how important her cousin Mordekai (Mordecai) was in the Persian government makes us guess that her family had grown rich and comfortable.

Ester was an orphan and was raised by her cousin Mordekai, who became a minor official in the Persian government in Shushan (Susa). She became queen after King Ahashverosh became displeased with Queen Vashti for refusing to attend a banquet when commanded to do so (Esth 1:11-12).

After Ester’s coronation, she discreetly won Ahashverosh’s confidence by informing him of an assassination plot (2:21-23). This later enabled her to rescue her people from a massacre planned by Haman, a high official to the king. Through her wise advice and brave action, Ester exposed Haman, he was executed, and the Jewish people were rescued. The Jewish Festival of Purim was instituted to celebrate these events.
Passages for Further Study
Ahashverosh (Xerxes) I

Ahashverosh I, who reigned over the Persian Empire from 486 to 465 BC, was the son and successor of Dareyavesh (Darius) I (Hystaspes). He inherited a vast empire from his father and his maternal grandfather (Koresh (Cyrus) II), but he was unable to govern Paras (Persia) effectively due to his cruelty and instability.

Early in Ahashverosh’s reign, Mitsrayim (Egypt) and Bavel (Babylon) revolted against Persian rule. Ahashverosh crushed the revolts and kept the tax revenues flowing, but his brutal treatment of his subjects began cementing his reputation for despotism.

In the third year of his reign, Ahashverosh convened an assembly of his leaders to plan an invasion of Yavan (Greece). (The book of Ester (Esther) begins with a banquet that probably reflects that situation.) In 480 BC the legendary but ill-fated campaign to conquer Yavan began. Ahashverosh’s tyrannical cruelty is exemplified by two accounts that Herodotus records from this campaign. When he and his armies reached the Hellespont (the waterway connecting the Black Sea with the Mediterranean), his engineers built a bridge so his armies could cross, but a storm destroyed the bridge. Ahashverosh responded by beheading the engineers and whipping the water before building a stronger bridge. Later in the campaign, after he had burned Athainai (Athens), his fleet was defeated at Salamis. Ahashverosh responded by executing the admiral of the Phoenician fleet, and the Phoenicians and Mitsrim (Egyptians) deserted him. Only the Persian fleet remained, and it was defeated by the Greeks in 479 BC. Ahashverosh was forced to retreat. Afterward, Ahashverosh turned his attention to matters at home, such as massive building projects at Shushan (Susa) and Persepolis, and the events recorded in Ester.

Ahashverosh had reason to worry that assassins would try to kill him. According to Esther 2:21-23, Mordekai (Mordecai) thwarted an assassination plot, which later led to Ahashverosh publicly honoring Mordekai. After Ahashverosh was again defeated by the Greeks at the Battle of the Eurymedon in 466 BC and stripped of territory, another assassination plot by his court officials succeeded, and his reign ended ignominiously in 465 BC.
Passages for Further Study
Ezra 4:6; Esth 1:1-22
Satan

The book of Iyov (Job) includes “the satan” among the heavenly court (Job 1:6; 2:1). The Hebrew word satan refers to an adversary or an accuser in court (see Job 1–2; Zech 3:1). God sometimes appoints angels as adversaries for righteous judgment and opposition to evildoers (e.g., Num 22:22, 32, where the term satan is often translated “block”; see also 1 Kgs 22:19-23). The Old Testament hints at the accuser’s demonic character, but it was between the times of the Old Testament and the New Testament that Satan became identified with the serpent in Eden (see Wisdom of Shelomoh (Solomon) 2:24). The New Testament refers to the chief demon as “(the) Satan” (Rev 20:2), along with numerous other names such as the devil (Matt 4:1-11), the tempter (1 Thes 3:5), Beelzeboul, the ruler of demons (see textual notes at Matt 12:24; Luke 11:15), the evil one (Matt 13:19, 38; 1 Jn 2:13-14; 3:12; 5:18), Beliar (see textual note at 2 Cor 6:15), the deceiver (Rev 12:9), the great seven-headed dragon and serpent of old (Rev 12:3, 9; 20:2), a murderer, and the father of lies (John 8:44).

Satan incited David’s census (1 Chr 21:1; cp. 2 Sam 24:1), tempted and betrayed Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) (Mark 1:12-13; John 13:27), desired to test Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) as he had tested Iyov (Luke 22:31), enslaved sinners (Acts 26:17-18), and deceitfully opposed God’s people (1 Cor 7:5; 2 Cor 11:14). The adversary of God’s people will be overcome in the end, when God defeats and imprisons him (Rev 12:9; 20:2, 10).
Passages for Further Study
Yeshayah (Isaiah)

Yeshayah was a Yehudi (Judean) prophet during the reigns of Uziyah (Uzziah), Yotam (Jotham), Ahaz, and Hizkiyah (Hezekiah). He was the son of Amots (Amoz) (Isa 1:1) and was possibly related to King Amatsyah (Amaziah). He lived in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), was well educated, and had deep insight into human nature. He had a long ministry (about 740~685 BC); as Yehudah’s (Judah’s) political and religious counselor, he had access to kings and was apparently the court historian (2 Chr 26:22; 32:32). Yeshayah’s wife was called a “prophetess” (see Study Note on Isa 8:3); their sons were She’ar-Yashuv (Shear-jashub) (7:3) and Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz (Maher-shalal-hash-baz) (8:3).

Yeshayah opposed social and political evil at all levels. He censured fortune-tellers. He rebuked kings for their willfulness and indifference. He denounced wealthy, influential people who ignored their responsibilities. And he exhorted everyone to obey God’s covenant. Yeshayah opposed Kena’ani (Canaanite) idolatry and insincere religious observances (1:10-17; 29:13), proclaiming judgment and declaring that only a righteous remnant would survive (6:11-13). He foretold the coming Messiah, the peaceful prince of God’s kingdom (9:6-7; 11:1-11) who was also an obedient, suffering servant (53:3-12). The book of Yeshayah has more overtones of the New Testament than any other Old Testament book and is frequently cited by New Testament authors.
Passages for Further Study
Yirmiyah (Jeremiah)

Yirmiyah, a prophet in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) before its destruction in 586 BC, is sometimes called the “weeping prophet” because he shared his personal struggles and sorrows as he delivered God’s messages.

Yirmiyah was born in Anatot (Anathoth), near Yerushalem, during Menasheh’s (Manasseh’s) reign. His father was Hilkiyah (Hilkiah) of Benyamin (Benjamin). Yirmiyah received his calling as a prophet during the thirteenth year of Yoshiyah’s (Josiah’s) reign (627 BC). At first, Yirmiyah retreated from his call (Jer 1:6), but God assured Yirmiyah that he would tell him what to say and would guide and protect him despite opposition (Jer 1:7-8, 18-19).

Yirmiyah warned the kings and people of Yehudah (Judah) to repent in order to avoid exile. They had broken God’s covenant, primarily through idolatry (Jer 10:1-16), and as a result, they were subject to the consequences (Deut 27–28). They rejected God’s invitation to repent, so Yirmiyah later delivered messages that God’s judgment had become inevitable.

Yirmiyah was particularly hated by Yehudah’s leaders. King Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) held Yirmiyah in contempt and tried to silence him. King Tsidkiyah (Zedekiah) secretly sought Yirmiyah’s advice, but bowed to his administrators when they wanted to silence the prophet. God’s word could not be silenced, however. The promised judgment came in 586 BC: Yerushalem was sacked, the Temple was destroyed, and Yehudah’s leaders were killed or exiled to Bavel (Babylon).

Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Bavel, knew of Yirmiyah and was favorably disposed toward him (Jer 39:11-12). As a result, the captain of the Babylonian army allowed Yirmiyah to stay with the remnant in Yehudah. Yirmiyah counseled those who remained behind to submit to Bavel, even when Yehudi (Judean) terrorists killed Gedalyah (Gedaliah), the governor appointed by Bavel. The Yehudim (Judeans) rejected Yirmiyah’s advice and fled to Mitsrayim (Egypt). Yirmiyah was taken with them, and little more is ever heard about Yirmiyah. According to tradition, he was stoned to death by Jewish exiles in Tahfanhes (Tahpanhes), Mitsrayim.

Yirmiyah suffered continual rejection, imprisonment, and physical abuse during his life, but his ministry was not entirely negative. He foretold that the Exile would be temporary (25:1-14) and that God would establish a new covenant with his people (31:31-34). This promise was fulfilled in Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ (Luke 22:20).
Passages for Further Study
Baruk (Baruch)

Baruk the son of Neriyah (Neriah) was a royal scribe in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) who served as secretary for Yirmiyah (Jeremiah) the prophet. His brother Serayah (Seraiah) was a “staff officer” in Tsidkiyah’s (Zedekiah’s) administration (Jer 51:59-64). Baruk’s family evidently ranked highly in the administration of Yehudah (Judah).

In the fourth year of King Yehoyakim (Jehoiakim) of Yehudah (605 BC), God instructed Yirmiyah to record the messages he had given to Yisrael (Israel), Yehudah, and the other nations (36:1-3). Yirmiyah sent for Baruk, who wrote the prophecies down (36:4) and read the words to the people (36:8-19). When the message reached Yehoyakim, he destroyed the scroll and called for Baruk’s and Yirmiyah’s arrest (36:21-26). But they had gone into hiding, where Yirmiyah repeated the prophecies and Baruk again wrote them down (36:27-32).

At about that time, God gave Baruk a personal message through Yirmiyah (Jer 45). Baruk might have been troubled about the loss of career prospects or personal comfort resulting from his association with Yirmiyah. God comforted Baruk with an assurance of protection and instructed him not to seek “great things” for himself, because the promise of Yehudah’s destruction was certain.

When Yerushalem was destroyed in 586 BC, Baruk stayed with Yirmiyah and the others who remained in the land. Apparently Baruk was viewed as influential: The rebel leaders wanted to go to Mitsrayim (Egypt) and when Yirmiyah warned them against it (Jer 42), they accused Baruk of persuading Yirmiyah. The leaders did not listen but took Baruk and Yirmiyah with them to Mitsrayim (43:1-7). We do not know how, when, or where Baruk died. One tradition records that he was taken to Bavel (Babylon) when Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) invaded Mitsrayim. It is also possible that Baruk died in Mitsrayim.

Although God warned Baruk not to pursue great things, and he seemed to die without honor, his legacy might in fact be the book of Yirmiyah, which he clearly had a hand in producing—a book that warns of judgment and eloquently expresses the hope for the new covenant (31:31-34).

In 1975, a clay impression (bulla) formed from a scribe’s seal was found with the words “[Belonging to] Berechiahu, son of Neriahu, the scribe” (Berechiahu is the long form of the name Baruk). Each scribe and government official had a unique seal bearing his name, with which he would seal documents to verify their authenticity—the ancient equivalent of a signature. The seal would be pressed into soft clay to form an impression (bulla), which was affixed to the signed document. The bulla of Baruk dates from the time of Yirmiyah and Baruk; other bullae that were found include the names of several other individuals in Yirmiyah (e.g., “Gemaryah (Gemariah), son of Shafan (Shaphan),” 36:10-12, 25; Yishmael (Ishmael), 40:7–41:10). Most scholars have concluded that the Baruk bulla was in fact formed by the seal of Baruk, Yirmiyah’s scribe. These bullae, seemingly insignificant artifacts of an ancient civilization, provide independent historical verification of some of the details of Yirmiyah’s account.
Passages for Further Study
Yehezkel (Ezekiel)

Yehezkel, a priest and prophet, was born around 623 BC. He was probably raised in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), and he was married (24:16-18). He went into exile in Bavel (Babylon) with Yehoyakin (Jehoiachin) in 597 BC, where he lived by the Kevar (Kebar) River. He was called to be a prophet in Bavel on July 31, 593 BC (1:1). All that we know of his personal life is from the book named after him.

Yehezkel often reinforced his prophetic words with strange actions, such as illustrating his message about the dire lack of food in the final siege of Yerushalem by eating food cooked over dung (4:12). Another time, he lay motionless for 430 days, one day for each year of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) and Yehudah’s (Judah’s) sin (4:4-7). When Yehezkel’s wife died suddenly, he was forbidden to mourn her in public (24:16-18); her death was a solemn warning of what would happen in Yehudah (24:15-27). Yehezkel’s strange actions were designed to grab people’s attention.

At first, Yehezkel’s messages were rejected, but his prophecies were later vindicated as they began to come true and the nation was purged of idolatry. His teaching emphasized holiness, purity, resurrection, and the ritual law. His message of hope encouraged the exiles to remain faithful during the dark hours of their captivity, and after their return it kept them looking toward a greater fulfillment.

The circumstances of Yehezkel’s death are unknown, and he is not mentioned elsewhere in the Old Testament. The New Testament has over sixty references to Yehezkel’s prophecies, mostly in the book of Revelation. Yehezkel’s prophetic vision extended beyond his immediate future to the final judgment and the great hope of heaven.

Daniyel (Daniel)

Daniyel provides a stirring example of faith, wisdom, and endurance under difficulty and oppression. His life and prophecies affirm that God is in control and will have the final victory despite apparently dominant evil forces.

Daniyel was a young man of Yehudah’s (Judah’s) royal family when the Babylonian army first attacked Yerushalem (Jerusalem) in 605 BC (Dan 1:3). Daniyel was deported to Bavel (Babylon) with Azaryah (Azariah), Hananyah (Hananiah), and Mishael. King Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) trained these young men, among others, to serve in his growing empire. Daniyel and his friends were the brightest and healthiest of the students, so they assumed important positions in Nevukadnetsar’s court.

Daniyel’s court career lasted nearly seventy years (see Dan 1:21). He quickly established a reputation for intelligence and absolute fidelity to God. When Nevukadnetsar had a troubling dream, God revealed its meaning to Daniyel, who explained it to the king (Dan 2). Later, Daniyel interpreted a second dream about the king’s pride (Dan 4). Daniyel urged Nevukadnetsar to repent, but he did not. As a result, Nevukadnetsar became temporarily deranged (Dan 4:28-37).

Daniyel always treated the Babylonian king respectfully, and Nevukadnetsar had high regard for Daniyel, whose character and behavior led Nevukadnetsar to worship the Lord (though not exclusively). Daniyel’s faithfulness and prudence encourage later readers in similarly hostile cultures.

Later, Belshatsar (Belshazzar), vice-regent of Bavel, profaned the sacred vessels from the Yerushalem Temple during a banquet (539 BC). A disembodied hand suddenly wrote the words “Mene, Mene, Tekel, and Parsin” on the palace wall, which Daniyel interpreted as forecasting Bavel’s imminent end. That same night, Belshatsar was killed by Persians who captured the capital (Dan 5:1-31).

Under Dareyavesh (Darius) the Madi (Mede) (539 BC), Daniyel became an administrator of the realm (Dan 6:2). Daniyel’s capable management infuriated political enemies, who persuaded Dareyavesh to pass a decree forbidding worship of anyone but the king, under penalty of being cast into a lions’ den. To preserve his religious integrity, Daniyel violated the law, but he was miraculously unscathed by the lions. Thereafter he was restored to his office (Dan 6:17-28). Daniyel’s later visions date from around this time (Dan 10:1, 4).

Daniyel’s prophecies are difficult to understand in detail, but their message is clear: Evil forces are now in power, but God is in control and will save his people. Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) and New Testament authors cited Daniyel, often using his imagery when speaking of the end times (e.g., cp. Dan 7:1-9 and Rev 13:1-10; Dan 7:13 and Rev 1:7; Dan 9:27 and Matt 24:15). Daniyel had no doubt that God Most High would be victorious.
Passages for Further Study
Nevukadnetsar (Nebuchadnezzar) II

King Nevukadnetsar II reigned over Bavel (Babylon) from 605 to 562 BC. He secured and extended the empire of his father, Nabopolassar (626–605 BC). Beyond the scriptural record, many ancient Babylonian documents report Nevukadnetsar’s accomplishments.

In 626 BC, Bavel, like Yehudah (Judah), was under the domination of Ashur (Assyria), but in that year Nabopolassar began a revolt that would change the world. In 612 BC, the Babylonians captured Nineveh, Ashur’s capital, and again defeated the Assyrians at Haran in 609 BC. By the time of this battle, Nabopolassar’s son Nevukadnetsar played a leading role in the army. In 605 BC, Nevukadnetsar defeated the remnant of the Assyrian army at Karkemish (Carchemish); this victory also pushed the Mitsrim (Egyptians) back within their borders. In the same year, Nabopolassar died and his son became king.

Following his victory at Karkemish in 605 BC, Nevukadnetsar conquered Aram (Syria) and surrounding areas, including Yehudah. In that year, Nevukadnetsar besieged Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for the first time (2 Kgs 24:1; 1:1-2). He took away a number of the Temple vessels and some of the leading young citizens of Yehudah, including Daniyel (Daniel) and his three friends. Nevukadnetsar captured Yerushalem again in 597 BC (2 Kgs 24:10-17). He later besieged Yerushalem in 588 BC and destroyed the city and Temple in 586 BC, exiling most of the remaining people (2 Kgs 25:1-21).

A detailed and interesting personal description of Nevukadnetsar is found in Daniyel. He brought Daniyel and his friends to Bavel in order to educate them in the ways of Bavel, but God used Daniyel to teach Nevukadnetsar about himself. After being humbled for his great pride (Dan 4:28-33), Nevukadnetsar acknowledged the Lord’s sovereignty and power (4:34-37), though he probably never worshiped the true God exclusively.

The Son of Man

The Hebrew and Aramaic idiom “son of man” simply means “human being.” But the majestic yet humble figure in Daniel 7:13-14, who is “like a son of man”—meaning that he looked like a man—also appears to be much more. His exact identity is not specified, but his role is clear: The Most High has appointed him to rule an eternal, universal kingdom that will be over all other nations. He also represents his own people, the holy people of the Most High. They will also share in this son of man’s kingdom over all peoples and nations (see 7:22).

The scene surrounding this son of man indicates his divine characteristics. That he comes “with the clouds of heaven” (7:13) indicates his heavenly origin (cp. Ps 68:4; 97:2; Nah 1:3). The Lord God covered himself with a cloud in the book of Exodus (Exod 19:9). God’s people will be caught up into the clouds (1 Thes 4:17) when Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) returns as he was received into a cloud at his ascension (Acts 1:9). This son of man receives his kingdom with humility and holiness, not arrogantly grasping after it. He is thus opposite in character to the “little horn” (Dan 7:8).

Yeshua identifies himself with this Son of Man (Matt 24:30; 26:24; Mark 13:26; Luke 21:27; John 12:34; see also Acts 7:56; Heb 2:6; Rev 1:13; 14:14). Revelation 1:7 likewise yokes this figure with Yeshua Christ, the one who was pierced for our sins. God the Father has given Yeshua all authority and power to rule over all things (Dan 7:14; Matt 28:18) and to win people from all the nations and kingdoms of the world (Matt 28:19-20). God’s purpose in calling Avraham (Abraham) was to make a great nation through his people and to bless all nations through him (Gen 12:1-3). Yeshua fulfilled this promise.
Passages for Further Study
The Greeks

Greek civilization played a major role in the ancient world, and Greek culture was a primary influence on the world into which Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) was born and in which the New Testament was written.
Mycenaean Civilization (1450–1200 BC)

The Mycenaeans lived during the “heroic age” that Greeks later immortalized in the epics of Homer. Their civilization was centered at Mycenae, about thirty miles south of the site of Korinthos (Corinth). The Mycenaeans traded extensively and were successful in war. The Greek gods and myths familiar from later literature have their roots in Mycenaean Yavan (Greece). Mycenaean documents were written in Linear B, a syllabic script.

Mycenaean civilization ended violently around 1200 BC at the hands of Dorian Greek invaders. The several hundred years which followed have been called the “Greek Dark Ages”—Linear B usage ceased, and there are no written records.
Archaic Age, City-States (850–546 BC)

Eventually Greek towns and villages began organizing into city-states that controlled entire areas. This era also saw a rise of cooperation and a shared sense of identity among the Greeks; for example, the first Olympic games were held in 776 BC.

As trade with the surrounding world increased, the Greeks made contact with the Phoenicians and adopted their script. Homer wrote the Iliad and Odyssey, chronicling the shared memories and myths of the earlier Mycenaean civilization and their gods.

Many of the city-states looked to a dictator (Greek tyrannos, “tyrant”) to provide political stability. In many places there was also a written constitution that provided a basis for authority in law. Athainai (Athens), for its part, developed an oligarchy led by the Areios Pagos (Areopagus) Council. Later, Solon, an Athainaios (Athenian) statesman, instituted reforms and created the context in which democracy bloomed in later decades.
Persian Wars, Classical Period (546–336 BC)

In 546 BC, the Greek colonies in Asia Minor fell under the rule of Koresh (Cyrus) the Great of Paras (Persia). Ionia unsuccessfully attempted to revolt around 500 BC, prompting Dareyavesh (Darius) I to invade the Greek mainland in 492 BC. In the wars that followed, Greek forces were badly outnumbered, but they often outmaneuvered the Persians with superior skill and strategy. In the Battle of Marathon in 490 BC, the Greeks soundly defeated the Persians. Ten years later, the Persian army under Ahashverosh (Xerxes) famously crossed the Hellespont while the vast Persian fleet sailed into Greek waters. The Persians burned Athainai, but in the end the Greeks were victorious, and Ahashverosh withdrew.

After the Persian Wars ended, Athainai was rebuilt and entered into a remarkable period of greatness. Pericles led Athainai to establish a full democracy. Vast buildings were erected on the Acropolis. Athainai became wealthy, and Athainaios sea power grew. It was a golden age of spectacular achievement in art, thought, literature, and architecture.
Makedonian (Macedonian) Empire, Hellenistic Civilization (336–146 BC)

Filippos (Philip) II of Macedon, with ambitions of empire, overwhelmed Athainai and No (Thebes) in 338 BC and united Yavan into the Makedonian Empire. After Filippos was assassinated in 336 BC, his son Alexandros (Alexander) took his place. Alexandros brutally destroyed a rebellious No in 335 BC, then set out to conquer Bavel (Babylon) and Paras, which he did with lightning speed (cp. Dan 8:5-8). When Alexandros suddenly died in 323 BC, his vast territories were divided among four generals. After a period of conflict, three major divisions emerged: Mitsrayim (Egypt); Asia Minor, Aram (Syria), and Bavel; and Makedonia (Macedonia) and Akaia (Achaia).

Alexandros’s conquest spread Greek culture and influence around the ancient world. The resulting conflict between Greek culture and Youdaismos (Judaism) eventually contributed to the Maccabean revolt in Judea in the 160s BC.
Roman Rule (168 BC–AD 330)

Romai (Rome) expanded its power and influence into Yavan (Greece) beginning in 198 BC. In 168 BC, Romai defeated the Makedonians (Macedonians) at the battle of Pydna, and in 148 BC, Romai annexed Makedonia as a province. Then, in 146 BC, Romai destroyed Korinthos (Corinth). Yavan was now firmly in the grip of Romai, as it continued to be until Constantine made Byzantium the capital of the Roman Empire in AD 330. Greek culture and Roman rule formed the context for the earthly life of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) and the beginning of Christianity.
Passages for Further Study
Hellenistic Kingdoms

During the 300 years following the death of Alexandros (Alexander) in 323 BC, Greek kings continued to rule in the lands he conquered, and Hellenistic religion, culture, and values expanded across civilization. Hellenism provided a context for both Jewish and Greek learning to flourish. But Hellenism also came into conflict with Jewish faith, causing a time of great tribulation for the Yehudim (Jews), especially in the 160s BC. Greek culture eventually combined with Roman rule to set the stage for the coming of the Messiah, as Daniyel (Daniel) foresaw. The history of this era is accurately portrayed in several of Daniyel’s prophecies (see 7:6; 8:8-14, 21-26; 11:4-45).
Successors (Diadochoi), 323–301 BC
After Alexandros died suddenly in 323 BC, a struggle for power and dominance ensued among several of his top generals (Greek diadochoi, “successors”).

Ptolemaios (Ptolemy) I was one of Alexandros’s strongest and most capable Makedonian (Macedonian) generals. He became satrap of Mitsrayim (Egypt) in 323 BC, the year of Alexandros’s death, and he successfully ruled Mitsrayim until his death in 285 BC.

Antigonus was a leading general in Alexandros’s army and served as the energetic regent of a large portion of Alexandros’s empire. In 315 BC, Antigonus invaded Aram (Syria) and Palestine, but his bid to reunite the empire failed and he was killed in battle in 301 BC.

Seleukos (Seleucus) I, another of Alexandros’s top generals, became satrap of Bavel (Babylon) in 321 BC. When he heard of Antigonus’s plans to reunite the empire, he fled for protection to Ptolemaios in Mitsrayim in 316 BC. After regaining control of Bavel (315 BC) and Aram (312 BC), he ruled until his death in 281 BC.
Lusimakos (Lysimachus) was satrap of Thrace and Bithunia (Bithynia) (in Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey) following the death of Alexandros.

Cassander was satrap of Makedonia (Macedonia) until 294 BC. The son of Antigonus, Demetrios (Demetrius) I, then gained control of Makedonia and Akaia (Achaia), founding the Antigonid dynasty that ruled there until the Romans took control of Yavan (Greece) after the Battle of Pydna in 168 BC.
Alexandros’s empire was thus divided into four kingdoms ruled by Makedonian Greeks: Mitsrayim, Bavel and Aram, Makedonia and Akaia, and parts of Asia Minor.
Throughout the 200s BC, the Ptolemies and the Seleucids fought several wars for control of the strategic territory of Palestine. The history of this conflict is accurately portrayed in Daniel 11.
Ptolemies, 323–30 BC

Ptolemaios I and his descendants (the “king of the south” in Dan 11) ruled Mitsrayim for nearly three hundred years. After Ptolemaios I took control of Judea in 319 BC, he resettled some Jewish people in Alexandria, which became a large and important Jewish community as well as a center for both Jewish and Hellenistic learning and scholarship (the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, was created in Alexandria during this era). Even though the Ptolemies were worshiped as gods and spread Greek culture in Mitsrayim, they were generally tolerant of the Yehudim (Jews) and their monotheistic culture. The dynasty of the Ptolemies ended at the death of Kleopatra (Cleopatra) VII when Romai (Rome) took control of Mitsrayim in 30 BC.
Seleucids, 321–64 BC

Seleukos I and his descendants (the “king of the north” in Dan 11) ruled Aram (and, for a time, Bavel) until the Roman general Pompey annexed Aram in 64 BC. The Seleucids, like the Ptolemies, propagated both Hellenistic culture and the worship of rulers in the areas they controlled; but they were less tolerant of the Yehudim’s non-participation than the Ptolemies were. After the Seleucid king Antiokos (Antiochus) III gained control of Judea around 200 BC, he gave positions and power to Yehudim who assimilated. His son, Antiokos IV, harshly persecuted the Yehudim, executing those who kept the Rest Day or copies of the Torah or who would not worship at the altar of Zeus that he erected in the Temple in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (note Daniyel’s (Daniel’s) mention of the “sacrilegious object that causes desecration,” Dan 11:31). This persecution provoked the revolt of the Jewish priest Matityah (Mattathias) and his sons, who gained semi-autonomy for the Jewish state for nearly one hundred years under the leadership of their descendants (the Hasmoneans).
Passages for Further Study
Zerubavel (Zerubbabel)

Zerubavel, a Babylonian-born Yehudi (Jew), relocated to Judea in 538 BC as governor of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) under Persian rule. Koresh (Cyrus), the king of Paras (Persia), had declared that Yehudim (Jews) captured and exiled from Yehudah (Judah) might return to their homeland; Zerubavel led one of the first groups of returning exiles.

Zerubavel came to Judea with the mission of rebuilding the Temple, and he began by constructing the altar. Sacrifice could begin again once the Holy Place was restored. However, the community of Judea soon ran into opposition from the people in the land, who effectively shut down construction. The Yehudim were distracted from the project until the preaching of Hagay (Haggai) and Zekaryah (Zechariah) encouraged them to begin working again. Zerubavel was instrumental in leading and organizing the Temple rebuilding effort, which took about six years (520–515 BC).

Exuberant hope surrounded Zerubavel, who was a direct descendant of King David (1 Chr 3:1-19). Zekaryah and Hagay both describe Zerubavel in messianic terms as the one chosen by God to bring restoration to Yisrael (Israel) (Hag 2:21-23; Zech 4:6-7). But Zerubavel soon disappears from the biblical narrative without explanation. This early governor of Judea was not the Messiah. Rather, Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ, one of Zerubavel’s descendants (Matt 1:12), would assume that glorious position.
Passages for Further Study
Antiokos (Antiochus) IV

Antiokos IV is the most important of all the Seleucid rulers as far as the biblical literature is concerned and is known as one of the cruelest tyrants of all time. He was an enthusiastic believer in the Olympian god Zeus and hoped to unify his territories by spreading Hellenistic culture, law, and religion. In so doing, he came into violent conflict with the Yehudim (Jews) in Judea.

Antiokos IV, born in 215 BC with the name Mitredat (Mithradates), was a son of Antiokos III but was not the designated heir of the Seleucid kingdom. After the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BC, Mitredat went to Romai (Rome) as a hostage to guarantee payment of his father’s debts to Romai. His brother, Seleukos (Seleucus) IV, then began to reign in 187 BC, but Mitredat used intrigue to get himself released from bondage and when his brother was murdered, he usurped the Seleucid throne, becoming Antiokos IV. He called himself Epifanes (Epiphanes), which means “god manifest.” But his unstable temper led critics to use the pejorative nickname Epimanes, which means “manifestly insane.”

Antiokos’s drive for Hellenization and his need for finances created a ripe environment for him to sell the Jewish high priesthood to the highest Hellenizing bidder. He sold the office twice, first to Yason (Jason) in 174 BC and then to Menalaus (who offered a higher bid) in 171 BC.

Antiokos wanted to gain control of Mitsrayim (Egypt), so in 169 BC he invaded. Meanwhile, Yason seized control of Yerushalem (Jerusalem), attempting to take back the high priest’s office. Yason failed, but Antiokos smelled insurrection, so on his return from a successful campaign in Mitsrayim he attacked Yerushalem, killed and enslaved thousands, and plundered the Temple. The following year, Antiokos again attacked Mitsrayim, but this time Roman forces came to Mitsrayim’s aid, and Antiokos was stopped outside Alexandria. There he was humiliated by the Roman legate Popilius, who famously drew a circle around him and forced him to make a decision to surrender before leaving the circle.

In 167 BC, a maddened Antiokos sent troops to massacre the male population of Yerushalem and enslave the women and children. By Antiokos’s edict, Youdaismos (Judaism) was made illegal under pain of death, and Yehudim were forced to participate in pagan sacrifices. He evidently thought that destroying the Jewish nation would secure his borders and strengthen his Hellenization program. Instead, it had the opposite effect: Open rebellion broke out later that same year in the village of Modein near Yerushalem. When the king’s representative came to Modein to enforce the edict banning Youdaismos, a Jewish priest named Matityah (Mattathias) killed him and then fled with his followers to the surrounding hills. This sparked the Maccabean rebellion, in which Matityah’s sons gained control of Yerushalem and cleansed the Temple in 164 BC. They eventually achieved semi-independence for Judea.

Antiokos was already considered insane by many, but the success of the Maccabees and Antiokos’s inability to suppress the Jewish revolt drove him further into madness. He withdrew to Paras (Persia) where he died in 164 BC.
Passages for Further Study
Maccabees

The Maccabees (meaning, “hammers”) successfully led a revolt against Antiokos (Antiochus) IV in response to his persecution of the Yehudim (Jews). They and their descendants (called Hasmoneans) ruled Judea for nearly a hundred years and helped form Jewish society as we see it in the time of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus).
The Maccabean Revolt (166–142 BC)

When Antiokos IV made the practice of Youdaismos (Judaism) punishable by death in 167 BC, many Yehudim acquiesced, while others passively resisted and paid with their lives. Soon, more active resistance arose. When a representative of Antiokos IV came to the town of Modein to require the Yehudim to perform a pagan sacrifice, a priest named Matityah (Mattathias) killed him and then said, “Everyone who is zealous for the law of Mosheh (Moses) and wants to obey the covenant, follow me!” (1 Maccabees 2:27). He then fled to the mountains with his sons and some other followers.

Matityah, who was very old, soon died, but before his death, he appointed his son Yehudah (Judas; Grk. Yudas) to lead the revolt. Yehudah was a tactical genius and charismatic commander. He, his brothers, and their followers succeeded in defeating Seleucid attacks and liberating most of Judea. After gaining control of Yerushalem (Jerusalem), Yehudah and his band of rebels immediately set about to cleanse the Temple and restore the daily sacrifices, so that daily worship could be resumed. This restoration and rededication was then memorialized in the Festival of Dedication or Lights (Hanukkah). Yehudah opposed the appointment of a Hellenistic high priest and sought additional political freedom. He defeated the Seleucid army that was dispatched to put down the uprising, but the Seleucid king responded by sending a much larger army. Most of Yehudah’s men deserted, and Yehudah was killed in the battle of Elasa (160 BC).

After Yehudah was killed, the Maccabees regrouped under his younger brother Yonatan (Jonathan), who was a skilled politician and commander. Over the next few years the Maccabees regained control of Judea once more. Yonatan secured the high priesthood and allied himself with Romai (Rome). But the Seleucid general Trufon (Tryphon) tricked him, took him hostage, and murdered him in 143 BC.

Another brother, Shim’on (Simon), followed Yonatan as leader of the Maccabees. In 142 BC, Shim’on extracted a treaty from Seleucid king Demetrios (Demetrius) II, whereby Judea became independent. Shim’on retained the office of high priest, and it became a hereditary position for his family. Shim’on was assassinated by his son-in-law in 135 BC.
Hasmonean Rule (142–63 BC)

The rule of Matityah’s son Shim’on marks the transition from the Maccabean rebel movement to the Hasmonean dynasty, named for Matityah’s great-grandfather Asmoneus. Shim’on’s descendants ruled Judea for close to a hundred years. This era saw the increasing Hellenization of Jewish political leadership. At the same time, the Farisaios (Pharisees) gained popularity as they sought to preserve orthodox Youdaismos. Meanwhile, separatist groups such as the Essenes removed themselves completely from Jewish society. Toward the end of this period, the struggle for control between two brothers, Aristobulos (Aristobulus) and Hurkanos (Hyrcanus) II, led to political instability and provided Romai an opportunity to bring peace and assert control.
Roman Rule (beginning 63 BC)

In 63 BC, the Roman general Pompey marched on Yerushalem, and Judea became a tributary to Romai. Judea then entered a period of relative peace. With the end of Hasmonean rule, the stage was set for the coming of a new and strong religious leader for the Jewish people, the long-awaited Messiah.
Herodes (Herod) the Great

Herodes the Great was the Roman-appointed king of Judea (37–4 BC) at the time of Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) birth (Matt 2:1; Luke 1:5). He was a strong military leader, a brilliant politician, and a cruel tyrant. Born into an Idumean (Edomi (Edomite)) family with links to the Romans, he rose to power by gaining Roman favor and retained it by cruelly suppressing his opponents.

Herodes was known for his large building projects. His greatest accomplishment was the rebuilding and beautification of the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) Temple, begun ~20 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.8.1), making it one of the most magnificent buildings in the ancient world. He also built Kaisareia (Caesarea) and made it the Roman headquarters in Palestine. Herodes earned the title “the Great” because of his reputation as a great builder.

Herodes was also known for his family troubles and his brutal treatment of those who opposed him or whom he considered threats. He murdered two of his wives and three of his own sons when he suspected them of plotting against him. Kaisar (Caesar) Augustus once said that he would rather be Herodes’s swine than his son (a play on words in Greek since the two words sound alike—hus, huios). When Yeshua was born toward the end of Herodes’s reign and Herodes heard him referred to as a future “king,” Herodes attempted to have him killed also. Unable to locate the boy, Herodes ordered the massacre of all the boys less than two years old in the Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) area (see Matt 2:1-20)—an act typical of his ruthlessness and paranoia.

Though Herodes gained the title “king of the Yehudim (Jews),” the Jewish people never accepted him as a legitimate king because he was not from the line of David and because he was an Edomi (a descendant of Esav (Esau)) rather than a Yehudi (Jew).

The Farisaios (Pharisees)

The Farisaios were one of three major Jewish sects, along with the Saddoukaios (Sadducees) and the Essenes. The Farisaios comprised a non-political lay movement within Youdaismos (Judaism). They arose from the hasidim (pious ones), who opposed the syncretizing (combining together) of Greek culture and religion with Youdaismos in the second century BC.

The Farisaios attempted, by rigorous examination of the details of the Old Testament law, to make the law accessible and practical to people seeking to be obedient Yehudim (Jews). They taught strict adherence to the law, not only the written law of Mosheh (Moses) (torah), but also the oral traditions which they claimed Mosheh had passed down to them. Their goal was to defend the written law against any possible infringement. They were God-fearing and law-abiding people. They were known for passing their interpretations from generation to generation by word of mouth, establishing an oral tradition concerning legal matters. They made the law applicable by extracting from it specific guidelines for many possible situations. They argued that if the law were obeyed by all, the nation would be purged of sin and God would establish his Kingdom over all the nations. This gave their concern for obedience a goal in the future. The traditions of the Farisaios developed into the rabbinic writings known as the Mishnah and the Talmud.

Although the Farisaios were small in number, their influence on Yisrael (Israel) was widespread (see Matt 15:12-14; see also Josephus, War 2.8.14; Antiquities 13.10.5). The primary influence of the Farisaios was in the local meeting hall communities, while the Saddoukaios were more influential in the worship at the Temple in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and in the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council.

Unlike the Saddoukaios, the Farisaios had a strong belief in the resurrection of the dead (see Acts 23:6-8). After the destruction of Yerushalem in AD 70, the Farisaios provided leadership and direction for the people of Yisrael.

Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) often came into conflict with the Farisaios, accusing them of hypocrisy and of elevating human rules over God’s righteous standards. Yeshua opposed the Farisaios because they were leading people away from God’s plan for redemption. They were the theological shepherds of Yisrael, but Yeshua castigated them as hypocrites for their perversions of doctrine and practice (see Matt 23). And the Farisaios were antagonistic toward Yeshua, rejecting both him and his work, largely because of his shocking disregard of their traditions (see e.g., Matt 15:1-20).

Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios) (Levi)
Matay was a tax collector for the Romans and became one of Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) twelve apostles. According to early tradition, he was the author of the Gospel of Matay.

Though he is called Matay in all the lists of the apostles (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13), he is referred to as Levi—his other name—in two of the accounts of his calling (Mark 2:14-15; Luke 5:27-29; cp. Matt 9:9-10). His father was named Halfay (Alphaeus) (Mark 2:14), but there is no certainty that he is the brother of Ya’akov (James) the son of Halfay (the two are not linked in the lists of the apostles, as the other pairs of brothers are).

Yehudim (Jews) who collected taxes for the Romans were generally considered despicable sinners by their fellow Yehudim. They profited from working for the occupying forces and engaged in legalized extortion. Thus it is significant that Yeshua called a tax collector to become one of his followers. When Yeshua was criticized by the Farisaios (Pharisees) for accepting Matay’s invitation to his home for dinner, and for eating with tax collectors and other disreputable sinners, Yeshua used the occasion to teach the importance of compassion. He emphasized that it was precisely for such sinners—not those who considered themselves righteous—that he had come (Matt 9:9-13; Mark 2:14-17; Luke 5:27-32). Matay responded immediately to Yeshua’s call, leaving everything behind to follow Yeshua (Luke 5:28). The implication is that he never turned back to tax collecting or his former way of life.

Matay’s Gospel, written for his fellow Yehudim, gives us a Jewish perspective on the life and teachings of Yeshua, and it includes topics of special interest for those from a Jewish background. His Gospel was the most popular Gospel in the early church, which is probably why it occurs first in the canonical sequence.

Shim’on (Simon) Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros)

Shim’on Kefa was the most prominent of the twelve apostles. After Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) death, he became the primary spokesman for the early Christians in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and was the apostle primarily responsible for evangelizing the Yehudim (Jews) (Gal 2:7-8).

The Hebrew name Shim’on (transliterated in English as “Shim’on”) was probably his original name. Kefa is the transliteration of an Aramaic name given him by Yeshua, meaning “rock”—translated in Greek as Petros (English “Kefa”; see Matt 16:17-18; John 1:42).

Though Beyt-Tsayda (Bethsaida) was Kefa’s hometown (John 1:44), he later lived in Kafarnaoum (Capernaum). He was married (1 Cor 9:5), and at one point, when visiting Kefa’s home, Yeshua healed Kefa’s mother-in-law (Matt 8:14-15; Mark 1:29-31; Luke 4:38-39).

Originally fishermen, Kefa and his brother Andreas (Andrew) were among the first to be called by Yeshua to be disciples, together with Ya’akov (James) and Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes), their fishing partners (Matt 4:18-22; Mark 1:16-20; cp. Luke 5:1-11; John 1:35-51). They were ordinary, minimally educated working men (Acts 4:13).

Kefa’s name occurs first on every list of the twelve apostles (Matt 10:2; Mark 3:16; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13). Together with the brothers Ya’akov and Yohan, Kefa was part of an “inner circle” of disciples who were with Yeshua on certain special occasions—the healing of Yair’s (Jairus’) daughter (Mark 5:37; Luke 8:51), Yeshua’s transfiguration (Matt 17:1-2; Mark 9:2; Luke 9:28-29), and Yeshua’s prayer in the garden (Matt 26:37; Mark 14:33).

Kefa was bold and impulsive (Matt 26:33; Mark 14:29; Luke 5:8; 22:33; John 13:36-37; 21:7), and the first of the disciples to confess his belief in Yeshua as the Messiah (Matt 16:15-16; Mark 8:29; Luke 9:20). He reproved Yeshua when Yeshua spoke of his coming death—a notion that did not fit Kefa’s view of the Messiah—and was in turn rebuked by Yeshua for it (Matt 16:21-23; Mark 8:31-33). However, Yeshua spoke of Kefa as a key person he would use to build the church (Matt 16:18-19).

Kefa surreptitiously entered the courtyard of the high priest when Yeshua was taken there for interrogation. But when challenged by people who recognized him (partly because of his Galili (Galilean) accent), he vigorously denied all knowledge of Yeshua (26:69-75; Mark 14:66-72; Luke 22:54-62)—as Yeshua had said he would, in spite of Kefa’s insistence that he would never do so (Matt 26:33-35; Mark 14:29-31; Luke 22:31-34). Kefa immediately felt deep remorse.

After the news of Yeshua’s resurrection, Kefa was one of the first to run to the tomb to see if it was true (John 20:3-7), and he appears to have been the first of the Twelve to whom the risen Yeshua showed himself (Luke 24:33-34; 1 Cor 15:5). Much of Yeshua’s conversation recorded in John 21 was with Kefa, whom Yeshua encouraged to “feed my sheep” (John 21:15-17).

Following the coming of the Holy Spirit on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:1-13), Kefa quickly emerged as the primary spokesman for the early Christians. From that point on, as recorded in Acts 2:14–12:25, he played a crucial role in the spread of the gospel in Judea, boldly preaching to the crowds (Acts 2:14-41; 3:12-26), healing people (Acts 3:1-11; 5:12-16; 9:32-43), and—even under arrest—speaking fearlessly to the authorities (Acts 4:1-20; 5:26-32). Twice he miraculously escaped from prison (Acts 5:18-25; 12:6-11). He also exercised leadership in the administrative affairs of the quickly growing community of disciples (Acts 5:3-11).

Kefa was the first to bring the Good News to Gentiles (Acts 10:1-48; see Matt 16:18). And he played a key role in the Yerushalem council concerning Gentile converts, arguing that Gentiles should not be compelled to observe the law of Mosheh (Moses) but should be accepted on the basis of their faith in Christ alone (Acts 15:7-11). Later, however, when visiting Antiokeia (Antioch), he was inconsistent on this point—resulting in a rebuke from Paulos (Paul) (Gal 2:11-16).

Other than his taking his wife with him on at least some of his mission trips (1 Cor 9:5), few details are known about Kefa’s (Peter’s; Grk. Petros’) later life and missionary work. (He may have spent time at Korinthos (Corinth); see 1 Cor 1:12; 3:22). Widespread early tradition says that Kefa was crucified—like his Lord, just as Yeshua had predicted (John 21:18-19)—in Romai (Rome) during Nero’s persecution of Christians in AD 64–65. The reliability of the tradition that he was crucified upside-down is less certain.

Kefa was likely the source of the material recorded by Markos (Mark) in his Gospel, which Markos probably learned while he was assisting Kefa in his evangelistic work in Italia (Italy) near the end of his life. Kefa is also traditionally understood to be the author of 1 Kefa (written from Romai—“Bavel (Babylon),” 1 Pet 5:13) and 2 Kefa.

In the New Testament, Kefa stands as a reassuring example of Christ’s forgiving grace for those who know they’ve failed him—and of the way Christ can graciously restore and use such people for his glory, in spite of their failings.

The Saddoukaios (Sadducees)

The Saddoukaios were made up of the priestly class (in contrast to the lay movement of the Farisaios (Pharisees)). The Saddoukaios probably lived in the vicinity of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and controlled the Temple system (Acts 4:1-2; 5:17). They were powerful aristocrats and mediators between Romai (Rome) and Yisrael (Israel) (see Josephus, Antiquities 13.10.6; War 2.10.5). They did not have great favor or influence with the people (Josephus, Antiquities 18.1.4). The term Saddoukaios probably derives from Tsadok (Zadok), the high priest during the reigns of David (2 Sam 8:17; 15:24; 1 Kgs 1:8) and Shelomoh (Solomon) (1 Kgs 1:32-48); both words have the same Hebrew root. The earliest historical reference to the Saddoukaios occurs during the reign of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Hurkanos (Hyrcanus) (135–104 BC), a descendant of the Maccabees (Josephus, Antiquities 13.10.6), but it is clear from this account that they had already existed for some time.

Their theological views are often contrasted with those of the Farisaios (Acts 23:8; see also Acts 4:1-2). The Pentateuch had primary authority for the Saddoukaios. They rejected the oral tradition so cherished by the Farisaios. Also in contrast with the Farisaios, the Saddoukaios did not believe in the resurrection of the dead (see Matt 22:23-33), angelic beings (see Acts 23:8), or the concept of final judgment. The Farisaios, by contrast, were so committed to belief in the resurrection that they sided with Paulos (Paul) against the Saddoukaios when he was on trial for disturbing the Temple (Acts 23:6-10).

Despite their differences, the Farisaios and Saddoukaios united with a single front against Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus). If the Farisaios opposed Yeshua because he made light of their oral traditions, the Saddoukaios opposed Yeshua because he affirmed the supernatural world of angels and demons and appealed to a final judgment and resurrection.

With the destruction of the Temple in AD 70, the Saddoukaios disappeared from the scene. They left no written records. Since all our information about the Saddoukaios comes from their opponents, we have a limited idea of what they were really like.

The Jewish High Council

The high council of Jewish aristocrats in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) was endowed with considerable power in governing the Jewish people. It is traditionally called the Sanhedrin, a transliteration of the Greek word sunedrion (“council”).

According to Jewish tradition, the Sanhedrin dates from Mosheh’s (Moses’) choice of seventy elders (Num 11:16), but the earliest datable reference is found in Josephus (Antiquities 12.3.3) from the time of Antiokos (Antiochus) the Great (223–187 BC). The Sanhedrin probably emerged from a self-governing body of leaders under the Persians (see Ezra 5:5-10; Neh 2:16). The high council was controlled by the priestly class under the leadership of the high priest, though these priests were influenced to various degrees by Roman rulers and the Farisaios (Pharisees). Herodes (Herod) the Great exercised a particularly heavy hand over the affairs of the Sanhedrin.

The Sanhedrin managed the internal legal and religious affairs of Youdaismos (Judaism), including judicial decisions not resolved in lesser courts (called “local sanhedrins”), criminal justice and arrests (see Acts 9:1-2), and official (though unenforceable) decisions regarding Jewish matters. Though the Sanhedrin could not of its own accord put tried criminals to death (John 18:31), apparently it could do so with the support of Roman officials.
The destruction of Yerushalem in AD 70 eliminated the high council as the ruling body of Youdaismos.

Herodes (Herod) Antipas

Herodes Antipas, sixth son of Herodes the Great, was ruler of Galil (Galilee) and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39, during the life of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus). His jurisdiction included the regions where Yeshua and Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) the immerser concentrated their ministries.

Following the example of his father, Herodes Antipas founded cities. Sepphoris, his first project, was the largest city in Galil. It was Antipas’s capital city until he built Tiberias, named in honor of the reigning emperor, Tiberios (Tiberius) (AD 14–37). The city Tiberias was on the western shore of the Sea of Galil. Antipas completed the city in AD 23 and made it his capital.

Herodes Antipas offended many Yehudim (Jews) by divorcing his wife and marrying Herodias, the wife of his half brother, Herodes Filippos (Philip). Antipas’s marriage to Herodias was in violation of the law of Mosheh (Moses) (Lev 18:16; 20:21) because Herodes’s brother Filippos was still alive. When Yohan the immerser spoke out strongly against this illegal marriage, Antipas imprisoned him (Mark 6:17-18); Herodes was afraid Yohan’s denunciation would lead to a political revolt (Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.2). Later, at a banquet, Herodias’s daughter pleased Herodes with her dancing, evoking a rash promise from him to give her anything she wanted. Herodias took the opportunity to have Yohan beheaded (Matt 14:1-12).

It was obvious to Antipas that Yeshua’s ministry was even more remarkable than Yohan’s (see Mark 6:14-16; Matt 14:1-2; Luke 9:7-9), but he was reluctant to use force to bring about a meeting, for fear of arousing the people against him. Yeshua, for his part, was openly critical of Herodes Antipas (Mark 8:15; Luke 13:31-33).

When Yeshua was finally arrested, Pilatos (Pilate) could find no fault in Yeshua, so he sent him to Herodes Antipas, who was in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) for Passover. Pilatos may also have been attempting to reconcile himself to Antipas. Their relationship had been rather strained since the Galili (Galilean) massacre (Luke 13:1), and because Pilatos had brought votive shields to Yerushalem that bore the image of Tiberios and were considered blasphemous by the Yehudim (Philo, On the Embassy to Gaios (Gaius) 299–304). When Yeshua was brought before Antipas, Herodes only mocked him and sent him back to Pilatos (Luke 23:6-11). The main political accomplishment of the incident was that Herodes and Pilatos were indeed reconciled (Luke 23:12).

Herodes Antipas was later defeated in war by King Aretas, whose daughter he had divorced. (Yehudim interpreted this defeat as an act of divine judgment.) He was then deposed by Emperor Gaios in AD 39 and sent into exile, in response to accusations from Herodes Agrippas (Agrippa) I of Antipas’s conspiracy against Romai (Rome).

Yehudah (Judas; Grk. Yudas) Iskariot (Iscariot)
Yehudah Iskariot is infamous for betraying Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) to the authorities (Matt 10:4; Mark 3:19; Luke 6:16).
The meaning of the name “Iskariot” is uncertain; it might refer to a village named Keriyot (Kerioth). He is not the same person as Yehudah son of Ya’akov (James) (Luke 6:16; John 14:22).

Among the apostles, Yehudah Iskariot came to be known as greedy; he carried the money bag and had the reputation of stealing from it (John 12:4-6). The money offered him as a bribe by the leading priests later convinced him to betray Yeshua (Matt 26:14-16; Mark 14:10-11; Luke 22:3-6).

Yeshua called Yehudah himself a devil (John 6:70-71) and predicted the betrayal (Mark 14:18-21). The devil put the idea of betrayal into Yehudah’s mind, and Satan “entered” him at the time of the betrayal (Luke 22:3-4; John 13:2, 27). Yehudah led a group of soldiers and officers to the garden of Gethsaimanai (Gethsemane) in the middle of the night, where he found Yeshua and betrayed him with a prearranged signal, a kiss of greeting (Mark 14:43-46). Later, Yehudah was apparently overcome by remorse for betraying an innocent man, and he hanged himself (Matt 27:3-10; Acts 1:18-19).

Yeshua clearly understood Yehudah’s betrayal as part of God’s plan for redemption: It brought about the death of the Messiah as the ultimate sacrifice for sin (Matt 26:24, 53-54; Mark 14:21; Luke 22:22; John 17:12). Even though Yehudah served God’s plan, his tragic end was clearly deserved (Acts 1:24-25). It would have been better for Yehudah if he had never been born (Matt 26:24; Mark 14:21). Yehudah’s fate soberly warns those who are apparently followers of Yeshua but have never committed themselves to him personally (cp. Heb 6:4-6).
