Pontios (Pontius) Pilatos (Pilate)

Pontios Pilatos was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36, including the time of Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) death in AD 30 or 33. Pilatos gave the official order for Yeshua to be crucified.

As the governor of Judea, Pilatos was in control of all the Roman occupation forces as well as the Temple and its funds. He was the only one who had the authority to execute criminals (see John 18:31), so the Jewish authorities were compelled to bring charges before Pilatos in order to have Yeshua executed (Mark 15:1-4).

Pilatos was sometimes abusive as governor. He appropriated Temple funds to construct a thirty-five-mile aqueduct for Yerushalem (Jerusalem), provoking a major protest. In response, Pilatos had soldiers infiltrate the crowds in disguise and beat the offenders to death with clubs (Josephus, War 2.9.4; Antiquities 18.3.2). Another time, Pilatos murdered some Galilim (Galileans) “as they were offering sacrifices at the Temple” (Luke 13:1); this incident might have estranged him from the Galili (Galilean) ruler Herodes (Herod) Antipas. Pilatos also tried to bring images of Kaisar (Caesar) into Yerushalem for worship. Later (AD 36), Pilatos slaughtered pilgrims who followed a Shomroni (Samaritan) false prophet, an event that led to his dismissal by the emperor Tiberios (Tiberius) in the same year.

Each Gospel records Pilatos’s role in the death of Yeshua (Matt 27:11-26; Mark 15:1:1-15; Luke 23:1-25; John 18:28–19:16; see also Acts 3:13; 4:27; 13:28; 1 Tim 6:13). After interrogating Yeshua, he was convinced that Yeshua had done nothing deserving of death, so he tried to return the case to the Jewish authorities. When they resisted, he tried to pass Yeshua to Herodes Antipas for judgment—but he, too, refused the case. Pilatos finally tried appealing to a traditional Roman custom of freeing a prisoner on Passover. Meanwhile, his wife had been deeply troubled by a dream about “that innocent man” (Matt 27:19). But the clamor of the crowd became threatening, and the Jewish leaders began insinuating that Pilatos was not taking Yeshua’s threat to Romai (Rome) seriously. Pilatos yielded to Jewish pressure. He ordered that Yeshua be whipped and then crucified, with the title “King of the Yehudim (Jews)” posted on a sign over his head—but only after strenuously objecting and declaring himself to be innocent of the guilt of such an unjust death (Matt 27:18-25; Mark 15:14; Luke 23:4, 13-23; John 18:38); 19:4-16. Pilatos’s attitude toward Yeshua stands as a testimony that Yeshua posed no threat to the Roman government but only to the Jewish leadership. This may have been a helpful point for later Christians who were portrayed as a threat to Romai.

Shortly after Yeshua’s death, Pilatos gave special permission to Yosef (Joseph) of Arimathaia (Arimathea) to take the body of Yeshua from the cross and bury it (Matt 27:57-61; Mark 15:42-46; Luke 23:50-53; John 19:38-42). He also gave permission to the Jewish authorities to seal the tomb to make sure no one would steal the body or make false claims about Yeshua coming back to life (Matt 27:62-66).
Little is known of Pilatos after his dismissal in AD 36; Eusebius reports that Pilatos committed suicide during the reign of Caligula, AD 37–41 (Eusebius, Church History 2.7).
Passages for Further Study
Maria (Mary), Mother of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus)

Maria, the wife of Yosef (Joseph), was the virgin mother of Yeshua. Lukas (Luke) tells us that as a young girl in Nazaret (Nazareth), Maria was betrothed to Yosef, a local carpenter. Before the marriage took place, an angel announced to her that she would become pregnant by the power of God’s Spirit and give birth to the Son of God (Luke 1:26-35). Maria responded to this extraordinary message in simple faith, humbly submitting herself to God’s will (Luke 1:38; see also Luke 1:46-55). Shortly thereafter, the message was confirmed by her relative Elisheva (Elizabeth; Grk. Elisabet), who spoke of Maria as the most blessed of all women (Luke 1:39-45). Maria’s miraculous bearing of the Son of God was viewed as a fulfillment of prophecy (Isa 7:14).

Yeshua’s birth took place in unusual circumstances, when Yosef took Maria to Beyt-Lehem (Bethlehem) to register for an official Roman census. The child was born in a stable because no other lodging was available (Luke 2:1-7). Some time later, Maria and Yosef fled to Mitsrayim (Egypt) to save the child from Herodes’s (Herod’s) massacre of young boys in the Beyt-Lehem area (Matt 2:13-18). When they returned, they resettled in Nazaret to raise their family (Matt 2:19-23). After Yeshua’s birth, Maria apparently gave birth to several other sons and daughters (Matt 13:55-56; Mark 6:3). It is likely that Maria herself told Lukas the details of Yeshua’s birth and the unusual events associated with it (see Luke 2:51).

When Yeshua was twelve years old, he stayed in the Temple during a family trip to Yerushalem (Jerusalem). Maria and Yosef rebuked him for staying behind when they departed, but they did not understand Yeshua’s response (Luke 2:41-51). Early in Yeshua’s public ministry, Maria encouraged him to do a miracle at a wedding in Kana (Cana) (John 2:1-11). Later, when she and Yeshua’s brothers went to see Yeshua, he said that his disciples were his “real family” (Matt 12:46-50; Mark 3:31-35; Luke 8:19-21).

When Yeshua was crucified, Maria was among the women looking on (cp. Mark 15:40, 47; John 19:25). As Yeshua was dying, he asked Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes), the “disciple he loved,” to take care of Maria as his own mother (John 19:26-27). After Yeshua’s death and resurrection, Maria was apparently a member of the believing community; she is listed among those who were praying together when the Spirit came on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 1:14).
God chose Maria to bring his Son, the Savior, into the world. For all Christians, she is a model of humble and obedient submission to God’s will.
Passages for Further Study
Ya’akov (James), Son of Zavday (Zebedee)

Ya’akov, son of Zavday and brother of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes), was one of the twelve apostles, and he was among the first to be killed as a follower of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus). His mother was possibly the sister of Maria (Mary), the mother of Yeshua, which would make him Yeshua’s cousin (cp. Matt 27:56; Mark 15:40; 16:1; John 19:25). His name usually occurs before that of Yohan, which may suggest that Ya’akov was the older of the two. He should not be confused with Ya’akov, son of Halfay (Alphaeus) (see Luke 6:15) or Ya’akov, brother of Yeshua.

Ya’akov and Yohan were fishermen like their father (Matt 4:21; Mark 1:19); they fished with Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) and Andreas (Andrew), another pair of brothers who became disciples (Luke 5:10). They were among the first that Yeshua called to be his disciples, and they left everything, including their father, to follow him (Matt 4:22; Mark 1:20; Luke 5:11). Yeshua called them “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17), which might imply that they had vehement personalities (see Luke 9:54), though the exact connotation is unclear.

Ya’akov and his brother Yohan were among those closest to Yeshua. With Kefa, they formed an inner circle of trusted disciples who accompanied Yeshua on special occasions, as when he healed Yair’s (Jairus’) daughter (Mark 5:37; Luke 8:51), conversed with Eliyah (Elijah) and Mosheh (Moses) on a mountain (Matt 17:1-3; Mark 9:2-4; Luke 9:28-30), and agonized in prayer in the garden (Matt 26:37; Mark 14:33). At one point, the two brothers provoked the indignation of the other disciples by asking for special positions of privilege in the coming Kingdom (Matt 20:20-28; Mark 10:35-45; cp. Luke 22:24-27).

Perhaps because of Ya’akov’s prominence among the disciples, Herodes (Herod) Agrippas (Agrippa) had him killed soon after Yeshua’s death, which pleased the Jewish leaders (Acts 12:1-3) and fulfilled Yeshua’s prediction about his drinking the bitter cup that Yeshua drank (Matt 20:23; Mark 10:38-39).

Ya’akov was an ordinary working person whom Yeshua called to be his disciple. His willingness to leave everything he knew—work, family, and home—to follow Yeshua in simple trust, and eventually to die for him, makes him a model of committed discipleship.
Passages for Further Study
Marta (Martha), Maria (Mary), and Eleazar (Lazarus; Grk. Lazaros)

The sisters Marta and Maria lived with their brother Eleazar in Beyt-Ania (Bethany), near Yerushalem (Jerusalem); Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) loved and spent time with this family. Marta and Maria are mentioned only in the Gospels of Lukas (Luke) and Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes), while Eleazar appears only in Yohan (this Eleazar is not Eleazar the beggar from Luke 16:19-31).

Lukas’s account of these two sisters (10:38-42) focuses on the contrast between Marta and Maria. When Yeshua visited their home, Marta was busy in the kitchen and became upset with her sister for not helping her prepare the meal. Yeshua defended Maria’s desire to simply sit and learn from him as the most important thing.

Yohan’s Gospel relays Yeshua’s act of raising Eleazar from the dead (John 11:1-44). When Yeshua arrived in Beyt-Ania, four days after Eleazar had died, the sisters expressed their dismay that Yeshua had not come in time to heal their sick brother, and Yeshua was deeply moved by the weeping of Eleazar’s family and friends. He went to the tomb and ordered Eleazar to come out. To everyone’s astonishment, he did so, bound in the cloths he had been buried in. This amazing miracle exemplifies Yeshua as the giver of eternal life (John 11:25-26). Ironically, this act of restoring Eleazar’s life also galvanized the Jewish leaders to bring about Yeshua’s death because so many people were responding to Yeshua’s miracles (John 11:47-53; 12:10-11).

Soon thereafter, when the family invited Yeshua to their home for a celebration meal, Maria poured a bottle of extremely expensive perfume on Yeshua. When people criticized her for what they considered an extravagant waste, Yeshua defended her action, saying that it anticipated his coming death (John 12:1-8; cp. Matt 26:6-13; Mark 14:3-9).
Passages for Further Study
Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) the immerser

Yohan the immerser was a fiery open-air preacher who called people to repent and be baptized. Yohan worked in the role of Eliyah (Elijah), to prepare people for the coming of the Messiah (Mal 4:4-5; Matt 11:14; 17:12; Mark 9:13).

Yohan’s birth, like that of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), was miraculous. His parents were elderly and had been unable to have children (Luke 1:5-25). His mother, Elisheva (Elizabeth; Grk. Elisabet), was a relative of Maria (Mary), Yeshua’s mother (Luke 1:36), so Yohan was related to Yeshua. The two miraculous births around the same time signaled the beginning of God’s redeeming work.

Yohan was filled with the Holy Spirit from birth and devoted his life to preparing people for the coming of the Lord (Luke 1:15-17). Living in the desert (Luke 1:80), he began preaching when he was about thirty years old. Dressed like a prophet and subsisting on desert food (locusts and wild honey, see Matt 3:4; Mark 1:6), he called everyone to repent and be baptized (Matt 3:1-2; Mark 1:4; Luke 3:1-3). He even castigated the religious leaders who came to hear him (Matt 3:7-10).

Though Yohan reluctantly baptized Yeshua (Matt 3:13-17), he considered Yeshua his superior, the one who would “baptize with the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33; Matt 3:11; Mark 1:7-8; Luke 3:16; cp. John 3:23-30). He encouraged his followers to become Yeshua’s disciples—and many did, including Andreas (Andrew) (1:35-40), Apollos (Acts 18:24-26), and the twelve disciples at Efesos (Ephesus) (Acts 19:1-7).

Herodes (Herod) Antipas received harsh judgment from Yohan because of Herodes’s unlawful marriage to Herodias, his brother Filippos’s (Philip’s) wife. To please Herodias, Herodes imprisoned Yohan and then beheaded him (Matt 14:3-12; Mark 6:17-29; Luke 3:19-20). Yohan’s imprisonment marked the beginning of Yeshua’s public preaching (Matt 4:12; Mark 1:14).

Shortly before his death, Yohan seemed to be confused about Yeshua and sent messengers from prison to ask him if he really was the Messiah. Yeshua did not do what most people anticipated the Messiah would do. Rather than bringing judgment and a visible kingdom, he brought forgiveness, healing, and a spiritual kingdom. To reassure Yohan, Yeshua spoke of the miraculous things God was doing through him (Luke 7:18-23).

Yohan remained faithful to his calling throughout his life, consistently preaching repentance and the judgment of God, even to people who had no desire to hear it. Yeshua referred to Yohan as one of the greatest servants of God who had ever lived (Matt 11:2-19; Luke 7:18-35), the end of a long line of prophets anticipating the coming of the Kingdom of God (Luke 16:16). Yohan stood on the threshold of the new age, proclaiming its coming to all who would hear.
Passages for Further Study
Nikodemos (Nicodemus)

Nikodemos was a highly respected Jewish Farisaios (Pharisee) (John 3:1), one of the prominent members of the high council, who appears to have become a convert of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus). He is mentioned only in the Gospel of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes).

Intrigued by the authority of Yeshua and the miracles he was doing, Nikodemos went to see him secretly, at night, in an attempt to discover who he really was. Yeshua challenged him with the need to be born again if he wished to be in the Kingdom of God (John 3:1-8). The Gospel does not give us Nikodemos’s response.

Later, however, in opposition to his colleagues on the Jewish high council, he strongly argued that Yeshua should be given a fair trial (John 7:50-51). After Yeshua was crucified, he bought seventy-five pounds of expensive perfumed ointment for his burial, took it to the tomb, and assisted Yosef (Joseph) of Arimathaia (Arimathea) in burying him (John 19:39-42). Thus, Nikodemos appears to be an example of a Farisaios who came to believe in Yeshua and was willing to express that commitment publicly after his death.
Passages for Further Study
Shomronim (Samaritans)

Shomron (Samaria) was a geographic region north of Judea centered around the ancient city of Shekem (Shechem) (Sukar (Sychar) in the New Testament was located at or near the site of Shekem). After Yisrael (Israel) was conquered in 722 BC and the cities of Shomron and Shekem were destroyed, this region was repopulated with people from throughout the Assyrian empire (2 Kgs 17:21-41). These inhabitants introduced countless pagan practices, making the religious impurity of the land infamous. In time, the monotheism of Youdaismos (Judaism) prevailed, but with significant modifications: The Shomroni (Samaritan) scriptures were limited to the Pentateuch, and their worship was centered on a new temple on Mount Gerizim above Shekem.

The Shomronim also had a long history of conflict with the Yehudim (Jews), beginning after the Yehudim’s return from exile (see Ezra 4:1-5; Neh 4:1-23). Alexandros (Alexander) the Great and later Greek generals made Shekem an important base, knowing that they could find sympathetic, anti-Jewish allies there. The Yehudim destroyed Shekem in 128 BC and burned the Shomroni temple on Mount Gerizim. The Shomronim returned the favor in AD 6–9 when they desecrated the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) Temple by scattering human bones from a cemetery during one Passover. By Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) day, smoldering tension existed between Judea and Shomron.

Yehudim in the time of Yeshua therefore avoided traveling through this land whose people they perceived as hostile and impure. When Yeshua traveled through Shomron and met a Shomroni woman, all of the fraught tensions of this relationship are in view. A first-century reader would barely expect Yeshua and the woman to acknowledge each other, much less speak. Yet Yeshua reached beyond his ethnic identity to call even a Shomroni woman of ill-repute to believe.
Passages for Further Study
Jewish Leaders

Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) experienced numerous conflicts with Jewish leaders throughout his public ministry. These opponents viewed themselves as defending the Temple and its sacrifices or the meeting hall and its teachings. In Yeshua’s final week in Yerushalem (Jerusalem), these debates intensified (see Matt 23) and contributed to the case against him.

When Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) wrote his Gospel, Christians were being persecuted by local Jewish meeting halls, and the language of those conflicts spilled over into Yohan’s Gospel (see Acts 14:19; 1 Thes 2:14; cp. Gal 1:13-14). The Greek term translated “Jewish leaders” could be literally translated as “Yehudim (Jews).” But the word took on this technical meaning to refer to the Temple leadership who confronted Yeshua, judged him, and orchestrated his crucifixion (see John 1:19; 2:18; 5:9-18; 9:18-22). This is important because the New Testament—particularly Yohan’s Gospel—has often been seen as anti-Semitic. But the truth is that Yeshua, who was himself a Yehudi (Jew), did not wrestle with “Yehudim” in general. His antagonists were the “Jewish leaders”—the brokers of religious power in first-century Yerushalem.
Passages for Further Study
Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes), Son of Zavday (Zebedee)

Yohan, brother of Ya’akov (James) and son of Zavday, was one of the twelve apostles. Early tradition identifies him as the author of the Gospel of Yohan, the Letters of Yohan, and the book of Revelation.

Yohan and his brother Ya’akov were among those closest to Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) (Mark 5:37; 9:2; 13:3; 14:33). His mother, Salome, might have been a sister of Maria (Mary), the mother of Yeshua (cp. Matt 27:56; Mark 15:40; 16:1; John 19:25). Yohan’s name usually occurs after Ya’akov’s, which suggests that Yohan was younger. Ya’akov and Yohan were fishermen like their father (Matt 4:21; Mark 1:19). They fished with Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) and Andreas (Andrew), another pair of brothers who became disciples (Luke 5:8-10). They were among the first whom Yeshua called as disciples, and they left everything to follow him (Matt 4:22; Mark 1:20; Luke 5:11; cp. John 1:35-40). Yeshua named them “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17), which might imply that they were loud or short-tempered (see Luke 9:54). At one point, the two brothers evoked the indignation of the other disciples when they asked for special positions of privilege in the coming kingdom (Matt 20:20-28; Mark 10:35-45; cp. Luke 22:24-27).

Yohan is understood to be the unnamed “disciple Yeshua loved” and “another disciple” mentioned in the Gospel of Yohan (John 13:23-25; 18:15-16; 19:26-27; 20:2-10; 21:20-24). He may have been the unnamed disciple of Yohan the immerser, who, together with Andreas, became an early follower of Yeshua (John 1:35-40).

Yohan’s name occurs three times in Acts; each time he was working with Kefa (Acts 3:1-11; 4:1-23; 8:14-25). Paulos (Paul) referred to him as one of the “pillars” of the church in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Gal 2:9).

The most widespread tradition about Yohan’s later life is that he moved to Efesos (Ephesus), where he eventually became the bishop of Asia Minor, lived to an old age, and died peacefully in the company of friends. His Gospel provides a profound portrait of Yeshua, and his letters provide a moving depiction of the Christian life (1–3 Yohan).
Passages for Further Study
Hanan (Annas; Grk. Hannas) and Kayafa (Caiaphas; Grk. Kaiafas)
Hanan and Kayafa were both spoken of as high priests during the time of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), and they were instrumental in getting Yeshua condemned to death.

Hanan was the Jewish high priest around AD 6–15. But even after he was officially deposed by the Roman procurator of Judea, he retained considerable power and influence in the Jewish high council and was still spoken of as “high priest” fifteen to twenty years later (Luke 3:2; Acts 4:6)—perhaps because of the Jewish view that high priests retain their position for life. Five of his sons and his son-in-law Kayafa became high priests after him. According to the Gospel of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes), when Yeshua was arrested, he was brought to Hanan for his initial interrogation before he was turned over to Kayafa for the official trial (John 18:13-24).

Kayafa was the official Jewish high priest around AD 18–36. He worked closely with his powerful father-in-law, Hanan. Kayafa had argued in the high council that it would be better for Yeshua to be sacrificed than for the entire nation to be destroyed (John 11:49-50). These prophetic words were given to him by God because of his role as high priest (John 11:51-52). At the trial of Yeshua, Kayafa tore his robes at Yeshua’s claim to be the Son of God and urged the high council to condemn him for blasphemy (Matt 26:57-66).

Not long after the execution of Yeshua, the Jewish authorities became increasingly disturbed over the rapidly growing numbers of believers in Christ. Hanan and Kayafa actively involved themselves in the interrogation of Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) and Yohan over their healing a crippled beggar and their preaching about the resurrection of the dead (Acts 4:5-7).
Passages for Further Study
Toma (Thomas)

Toma, also known as “the Twin,” was one of the twelve apostles (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). He is remembered most for his unbelieving response to Yeshua’s (Jesus’; Grk. Yesus’) resurrection.

Nothing is known of how Yeshua first met and called Toma to be his disciple. The only personal accounts of Toma are found in the Gospel of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes). Toma voiced his willingness to follow Yeshua, even if it meant death (John 11:16); he openly told Yeshua that he didn’t understand what he was saying (John 14:5); and he was one of the seven disciples who returned to fishing after the resurrection, when Yeshua appeared to them (John 21:2).

When Yeshua first appeared to his disciples after his death, Toma was not present. When Toma heard the report from the others, he did not believe it, insisting he would have to see the evidence of the crucifixion on Yeshua’s body with his own eyes and feel it with his own hands (John 20:19-25). A week later, when Yeshua once again appeared to the disciples, he specifically addressed Toma, telling him to examine the marks of the nails and the spear on his body and challenging him to believe and not be skeptical (John 20:26-27). Toma’s response represents one of the strongest statements of Yeshua’s deity in the New Testament and serves as the culmination of the Gospel of Yohan’s portrayal of Yeshua: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

Later tradition speaks of Toma working as a missionary in the East: in Parthia (Eusebius), Paras (Persia) (Jerome), and Hodu (India) (Acts of Toma). The Mar Thoma church on the west coast of Hodu traces its roots back to the early missionary work of Toma. The historical reliability of these accounts is uncertain.

Toma’s name is also unreliably linked to several later apocryphal writings: the Acts of Toma, the Infancy Gospel of Toma, the Epistle to the Apostles, the Apocalypse of Toma, the Book of Toma the Athlete, and especially the Gospel of Toma, a Gnostic collection of Yeshua’s sayings.
Passages for Further Study
Barnabas

Barnabas is presented in Acts as a model Christian leader. A native of Kupros (Cyprus), Barnabas was active in the Yerushalem (Jerusalem) church and demonstrated unselfish generosity in meeting the needs of the poorer members of that community (Acts 4:32-37). His given name was Yosef (Joseph), but he was nicknamed Barnabas (“Son of Encouragement,” 4:36), which indicates his character. He was a suitable person to give a fair and open-minded assessment of the new work in Antiokeia (Antioch) (11:19-22). Barnabas perceived God’s blessing there and “encouraged the believers to stay true to the Lord” (11:23). His sterling character was clear in his transparent goodness, abundant faith, and Spirit-filled life and work (11:24). The Holy Spirit chose Barnabas and Sha’ul (Saul) for a special work (known to us as the first missionary journey), and they were sent out by the church at Antiokeia (13:1-3).

Barnabas’s wisdom is evidenced in his earlier trip to Tarsos (Tarsus) to find Sha’ul (11:25). Barnabas had been impressed by the boldness of Sha’ul’s preaching as a new Christian in Damesek (Damascus) and had taken him to the apostles, providing a vital introduction for a man who was under suspicion for his previous unrelenting attacks against believers. Through Barnabas’s intervention, Sha’ul obtained needed contact with the original apostles, received their acceptance, and preached fearlessly in Yerushalem until he was forced out of the city (9:26-30). Barnabas’s trip was successful, and for a full year the two worked together in the Antiokeia church, drawing large crowds (11:26).

Barnabas was an impressive figure (note his reception in Lustra (Lystra) as Zeus, 14:8-18). He was Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos’s (Mark’s) cousin and mentor and played a major role in giving Yohan Markos a second chance to make good as a Christian leader after he had abandoned an earlier mission (15:36-40).

Barnabas knew peer pressure, and he gave in to it on one occasion even though he knew better (Gal 2:11-13). Barnabas wasn’t perfect, but he was a “Son of Encouragement,” to many and a generous, unselfish man who fostered growth in others and in the church.
Passages for Further Study
Stefanos (Stephen)
Stefanos was an exemplary early Christian who, as a result of the boldness of his witness, was arrested and killed by the Jewish authorities. He is known as the first Christian martyr.

Stefanos was one of seven men chosen to help administer the distribution of food to needy Christians in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Acts 6:1-6). He was the most prominent of the seven and is singled out as a man “full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (6:5). Manifesting the grace and power of God in an unusual measure, he did miraculous things (6:8) and proved to be a bold and effective evangelist and defender of the faith (6:9-10). His witness was so powerful, he was soon arrested by the authorities and brought before the high council for interrogation (6:9-12).

When witnesses accused Stefanos of speaking against the sacred Temple and the law of Mosheh (Moses) (Acts 6:13-14; cp. Mark 13:2; John 2:19; 4:21), he defended himself before the Jewish high council (Acts 7:1-53). He spoke of Yisrael’s (Israel’s) long history of resisting God and his servants—first Mosheh and now the Prophet whom Mosheh had predicted (7:51-53). The Jewish authorities, infuriated by Stefanos’s bold accusations, dragged him outside the city and stoned him to death (7:54-60). As he died, Stefanos prayed that they might be forgiven (7:60).

Stefanos’s bold witness gave rise to the first wave of persecution of the early Christians (8:1-3). But this persecution resulted in the Good News spreading even wider as the believers fled Yerushalem and proclaimed the message of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) everywhere they went (8:4; 11:19-21). Stefanos’s martyrdom thus marks the beginning of the spread of the Good News beyond the borders of Judea.

Stefanos’s life reminds us of the determined opposition that a faithful Christian witness can provoke. A bold testimony for Christ may be costly (see Rev 2:10, 13), but there is no insuperable barrier to the growth of the church (see Matt 16:18; Acts 8:1-4).
Passages for Further Study
Filippos (Philip)

Filippos was one of the first to take the Good News of Christ to those outside the borders of Judea. Well respected among the early Christians, he was one of seven men chosen to administer the food-distribution program for needy believers in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Acts 6:1-6). Filippos was a strong and effective evangelist in the power of the Spirit.

When Christians were forced to flee Yerushalem following the death of Stefanos (Stephen) (8:1-5), Filippos carried the Good News of Christ north to the ethnically mixed city of Shomron (Samaria). There he performed many miraculous healings and exorcisms, and people responded eagerly to his message (8:5-8). Many men and women were baptized, including a notorious sorcerer named Shim’on (Simon) (8:9-13). Then, directed by an angel, Filippos traveled southwest from Yerushalem toward Azah (Gaza) (8:26). There, directed by the Spirit, he met the treasurer of Kush (Ethiopia), who was returning home after visiting Yerushalem (8:27-28). When the Kushi (Ethiopian) asked Filippos to help him understand Isaiah 53, Filippos told him the Good News about Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) (Acts 8:30-35), then baptized the man by the roadside (8:36-38). Filippos was then suddenly taken away by the Spirit of God to the town of Azotos (Azotus) (8:39-40), where he again preached the Good News. He traveled through all the coastal towns until he came to the large Roman city of Kaisareia (Caesarea) on the coast, where he evidently settled down (8:40; 21:8-9).

Many years later, Paulos (Paul) spent a night in Filippos’s home in Kaisareia (21:8). By this time Filippos was known as Filippos the Evangelist. He had raised four unmarried daughters, all of whom had the gift of prophecy (21:9).

Filippos exemplifies early Christian evangelists, whom the Holy Spirit empowered and guided to authenticate their witness (see also 1:8; 3:4-8; 5:12-16; 6:8; 10:9-20; 13:2; 16:6-10; 19:11-12; 20:22-23). Filippos submitted to the power and guidance of the Spirit, and God used him to take the Good News to those beyond the borders of Judea.
Passages for Further Study
Paulos (Paul) (Sha’ul (Saul))

Paulos was a leading persecutor of the early Christians who later became an apostle of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) Christ, the most illustrious of the early Christian missionaries, and the great apostle to the Gentiles. He has done more to shape Christianity than any other individual except Christ himself. We know about him from Lukas’s (Luke’s) account of his conversion and ministry in Acts and from the thirteen letters bearing his name in the New Testament.

Paulos was born in Tarsos (Tarsus) to Jewish parents who were Roman citizens (which enabled him to also acquire Roman citizenship) and grew up in a traditional Jewish home. A tentmaker (or leatherworker) by trade, he was educated as a Farisaios (Pharisee) by the well-known rabbi Gamliel (Gamaliel) in Yerushalem (Jerusalem). He became active in the violent persecution of Christians as a young man (Acts 22:3-5). But through a life-changing, personal revelation of the resurrected Yeshua (9:3-6; 22:6-10), he was radically converted. He then dedicated the rest of his life to proclaiming Yeshua as Savior and Lord throughout the Mediterranean world (see Gal 1:11-16). His dedication and hard work, especially among Gentiles (to whom he was specifically called), resulted in the founding of scores of churches during the first century. Most of his letters were written to these churches.

Paulos’s belief in Yeshua as the Jewish Messiah set him apart from his Jewish contemporaries. His vision of Yeshua brought him to the realization that Yeshua’s death and resurrection bring righteousness and life-transforming power to those who believe in him. Paulos no longer understood righteousness in terms of the careful observance of the law of Mosheh (Moses), but as a gift from God to those who put their trust in Christ, the Savior who died for their sins (Rom 4:1-8). And he was convinced that this gift is for Gentiles as well as Yehudim (Jews).

Paulos’s thirteen letters deal with a wide range of issues, such as salvation and what Christians believe about Christ (Romans, Galatians, Ephesians, Colossians), specific problems in the church (1 Corinthians), the nature of Christian life and community (Ephesians, Colossians), and questions about Paulos’s own authority as an apostle (2 Corinthians, Galatians). Some of his letters are intended to encourage young believers who are suffering for their faith (Philippians, 1 Thessalonians) or to correct false teachings (Galatians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians). Still others are written to individuals, giving specific advice related to their life and ministry (1–2 Timotheos (Timothy), Titos (Titus), Filemon (Philemon)). Together, these thirteen letters reveal much about the life of the earliest Christians and the problems they faced, and about Paulos’s own grace-centered understanding of the Christian faith and life.

Paulos’s letters, with their strong focus on Christ, reflect his all-consuming passion for Christ and his twin convictions that (1) salvation is given only to those who put their faith in Christ as Savior (Gal 2:16), and (2) every part of a believer’s life is to be devoted to serving Christ as Lord (Rom 14:7-9; 2 Cor 5:15). Of all the New Testament writers, it is Paulos who spells out most clearly what salvation is (Rom 1–8) and gives us the fullest picture of the Christian life and Christian community. Paulos’s letters also highlight the power of the Holy Spirit in believers’ lives (Rom 8:9-13; Gal 5:16-25; cp. Gal 2:20; Col 1:27). He encourages believers to pursue the high standard of a life that is truly like Christ (Rom 8:30; Eph 4:13, 15; 5:1-2). Believers are to live a life of love (1 Cor 13:1-13; Eph 5:2) and fully submit to Christ. Paulos, more than any other New Testament writer, shows us how and why Christians must always find their deepest roots and motivation in the grace of Christ (Rom 12:1-2). For Paulos, the whole of a believer’s life—and indeed, the entire universe—is centered in Christ and Christ alone; everything finds its true meaning only in relation to him (Col 1:15-20; 2:6–3:4).

Lukas’s account of Paulos’s missionary life, which spans a period of perhaps thirty years, begins with Paulos’s preaching in Damesek (Damascus) shortly after his conversion (around AD 32–35) and ends with his imprisonment in Romai (Rome) (AD 60–62). But the Pastoral Letters (1 Timotheos—Titos) appear to be dated to a later time, and reliable later traditions affirm that Paulos was released from prison (around AD 62) and continued his missionary activity. He was later rearrested, and after a lifetime of suffering as an evangelist for Christ, he was finally killed in Nero’s persecution of Christians around AD 64–67. Paulos’s desire, not only to suffer as Christ suffered but also to die as Christ died, was thus fulfilled—with the sure hope of one day being resurrected, just as Christ was resurrected (Phil 3:10-11).
Passages for Further Study
Herodes (Herod) Agrippas (Agrippa) I

Herodes Agrippas I was Herodes the Great’s grandson, Herodes Antipas’s nephew, and Herodias’s brother. Agrippas I ruled the whole of Palestine for a short time following the death of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), during the very early days of the Christian movement (AD 41–44).

While at school in Romai (Rome), Agrippas lived a wanton life, incurring many debts. At one point he stated that he wished his friend Gaios (Gaius) Caligula were emperor rather than Tiberios (Tiberius). This was reported to Tiberios, who imprisoned him. He remained in prison until Tiberios’s death six months later.

Upon Caligula’s accession to the throne, he rewarded Agrippas by releasing him and giving him Filippos (Philip) the Tetrarch’s territories and the northern part of Lusanias’s (Lysanias’) territory as well as the title of king. This title aroused the jealousy of Herodias, and Herodes Antipas (her husband) was both critical and jealous of Agrippas. Agrippas responded by accusing Antipas of conspiracy and orchestrating Antipas’s banishment. Agrippas then acquired all of Antipas’s territories and property (AD 39).

When his friend Caligula died in AD 41, Agrippas curried the favor of the new emperor, Klaudios (Claudius), whereupon Klaudios added Judea and Shomron (Samaria) to Agrippas’s domain—territory once ruled by his grandfather, Herodes the Great.

Agrippas was an active persecutor of the early Christians. He is remembered for killing the apostle Ya’akov (James) and having Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) arrested—acts which gained him the favor of the Yehudim (Jews) (Acts 12:1-4). The Yehudim, for their part, liked him more than any of the other Herods. Agrippas died suddenly in AD 44 shortly after his subjects hailed him as a god (Acts 12:20-23; see also Josephus, Antiquities 19.8.2; 19.9.1; War 2.11.5).
Passages for Further Study
Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) Markos (Mark)
Yohan Markos, writer of the earliest Gospel (the Gospel of Markos), was an assistant of three early missionaries—Barnabas, Paulos (Paul), and Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros).

Markos was taken along as an assistant by Barnabas and Paulos on their first missionary journey. However, for unknown reasons, he left them to return to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) before the trip was completed (Acts 12:25; 13:4-5, 13). Because of this, when Barnabas wanted to take him along on the second trip, Paulos flatly refused. The sharp disagreement that resulted broke the team apart: Barnabas took Markos (his cousin) with him, while Paulos chose Silas, and the two pairs went their separate ways (15:36-41).

Later, it appears that Paulos and Markos were reconciled and that Markos once again served as his assistant. In Colossians, Paulos refers to him as a coworker and suggests that he may soon be sending him to visit the church in Kolossai (Colosse) (Col 4:10; see also Phlm 1:24). Still later, when Paulos was awaiting execution in prison in Romai (Rome), he asked Timotheos (Timothy) to bring Markos with him, for he thought Markos would be helpful to him in his ministry (2 Tim 4:11).

Markos also appears to have assisted Kefa when Kefa was engaged in missionary work in Italia (Italy) near the end of his life. In one of Kefa’s letters, he speaks endearingly of Markos as his “son” who is with him (1 Pet 5:13). Early Christian tradition speaks of Markos as Kefa’s “interpreter” and indicates that it was from Kefa himself that Markos got the information for his account of the life and words of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) (Eusebius, Church History 3.39.16). Generally considered to be the earliest of all the Gospels, Markos’s Gospel was almost certainly one of the key sources used by Matay (Matthew; Grk. Matthaios) and Lukas (Luke) when they later wrote their own Gospels. For this reason, Markos’s Gospel is one of the most influential of all the early Christian writings.

Markos’s story reminds us that God can overcome human failings and restore rocky relationships for the sake of Christ and the Good News. Early failures do not disqualify a person from a life of effective service and even lasting significance.
Passages for Further Study
Ya’akov (James), Brother of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus)

Ya’akov, one of Yeshua’s brothers (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3; Gal 1:19; cp. Jude 1:1), became the recognized leader of the church in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) shortly after Yeshua’s resurrection. He is traditionally recognized as the author of the book of Ya’akov.

Though Yeshua’s brothers were initially skeptical of his claims (John 7:2-5), they later became believers (Acts 1:14). Ya’akov’s personal encounter with the resurrected Yeshua (1 Cor 15:7) might have helped convince him. Two of Yeshua’s brothers (Ya’akov and Yehudah (Jude; Grk. Yudas)) are known to have played significant roles in the early Christian community. Ya’akov quickly rose to the position of leader of the church in Yerushalem. At the council in Yerushalem, Ya’akov was instrumental in getting the Jewish church leaders to accept Gentile believers without requiring that they be circumcised—a decision of major importance for Paulos (Paul) and the early mission to Gentiles (Acts 15:13-21). Paulos visited Ya’akov in Yerushalem after his third missionary trip (Acts 21:18), just as he had done earlier, following his conversion (Gal 1:19).

Like most Jewish Christians, Ya’akov continued to observe the law of Mosheh (Moses). He emphasized the need for believers to observe certain key laws when among Yehudim (Jews) (Acts 15:20-21; 21:18-25). Ya’akov acknowledged the validity of Paulos’s missionary calling and emphasis on salvation by faith alone (Gal 2:6-9), but many Jewish Christians did not. These Jewish believers—whom Paulos does link with Ya’akov on one occasion (see Gal 2:12)—demanded that Gentile converts be circumcised and observe the law of Mosheh in order to join the Christian community.

Ya’akov’s Jewish background is reflected in his letter, which is full of wise, practical advice for living, much of it in line with the traditional wisdom teaching of Jewish Scripture. One paragraph of his letter (Jas 5:1-6) reads very much like the work of the Old Testament prophets (e.g., cp. Amos 5:21-24; 6:1-7).
Ya’akov, titled “the Just” by his contemporaries, was apparently put to death for his faith by Jewish priests in Yerushalem (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9; Eusebius, Church History 2.23.4–18).
Passages for Further Study
Lukas (Luke)

Lukas, a Gentile medical doctor who became a convert and trusted assistant of Paulos (Paul) in his missionary work, wrote both the Gospel of Lukas and the Acts of the Apostles—roughly one-quarter of the New Testament.

Though we know very little about Lukas’s background, he seems to have first encountered Paulos and his preaching in western Asia Minor, where he became a convert. Leaving his home, he devoted his life to the service of Christ and the Good News as a dedicated assistant of Paulos. Paulos speaks of him warmly as “the beloved doctor” and one of his faithful “coworkers” (Col 4:14; Phlm 1:24). Lukas is the only Christian who faithfully remained with Paulos when Paulos was awaiting execution in Romai (Rome) (2 Tim 4:11). And he is the only Gentile to have his writings included in the New Testament.

Accompanying Paulos on his last trip to Yerushalem (Jerusalem), Lukas probably acquired the information for his Gospel and the early part of the book of Acts from people he interviewed in Judea while Paulos was imprisoned there for two years. Having talked extensively with people who heard and saw Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus), and having carefully studied what others had written about him, Lukas then wrote his own careful account of Yeshua’s life and teachings (see Luke 1:1-4).

When Paulos was sent by ship to Romai to have his case tried there, Lukas accompanied him. While Paulos was under house arrest, awaiting his trial, Lukas might have used the time to write the book of Acts. The first fifteen chapters provide a chronological account of the earliest missionary work as told to him by the early followers of Christ—and probably by Paulos himself. But beginning at Acts 16:10—the point at which Lukas joined Paulos’s team—he provides a direct eyewitness account. In Acts, Lukas emphasizes the way the Holy Spirit empowered and guided the early missionaries in their witness (see Acts 1:4-5, 8). The book ends with Paulos still under house arrest in Romai (28:30-31).

We are indebted to Lukas for many unique passages including his account of Yeshua’s birth, descriptions of Yeshua’s ministry to women, many words about Yeshua caring for the poor, and the only comprehensive account of the first thirty years of Christian missionary activity—all carefully documented. Through Lukas’s writings we gain a much deeper appreciation of the crucial work of the Holy Spirit in the ministry of Yeshua and the early missionaries.
Passages for Further Study
Priskilla (Priscilla) and Akulas (Aquila)

Priskilla and Akulas were a Christian couple with whom Paulos (Paul) lived and worked during his early days in Korinthos (Corinth). They were later active in Christian ministry and instrumental in bringing Apollos to a true understanding of Christ. They made a habit of opening their home in hospitality to other Christians.

Paulos first met Priskilla and Akulas in Korinthos, where they had recently arrived as a result of Klaudios (Claudius) Kaisar’s (Caesar’s) deportation of all Yehudim (Jews) from Romai (Rome) (AD 49). Paulos became acquainted with them and, because they were tentmakers (or possibly leatherworkers) like he was, Paulos lived and worked with them during his first year and a half in Korinthos (AD 50–52; 18:1-3).

When Paulos left Korinthos, he took Priskilla and Akulas with him and left them in Efesos (Ephesus) (18:18-19) while he returned to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) and Antiokeia (Antioch). Later, when Apollos came through Efesos, enthusiastically preaching about Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) in the meeting halls, Priskilla and Akulas took him aside and explained to him more fully the truth of Christ. As a result of their training, Apollos went on to become a powerful evangelist and Christian apologist (18:24-28).

Later, Paulos speaks of their home as a meeting place for Christians in Efesos, and he sends their greeting with his own to the church in Korinthos (1 Cor 16:19; cp. 2 Tim 4:19). Still later, it seems they returned to Romai (presumably after the relaxation of Klaudios’s edict), for they are the first of many to whom Paulos sends his greetings when he writes to the church in Romai (Rom 16:3-5). Here, too, their home became a meeting place. It is clear that Paulos felt a close bond of friendship with them and that he regarded their work for Christ highly—he speaks of them as “my coworkers in the ministry of Christ,” and he refers to a time when they even risked their lives for him.

Priskilla and Akulas are examples of early Christians who, in the course of their daily work, were bold in bearing witness to Christ and active in ministering to his people—in this case, as a married couple dedicated to the service of Christ. The fact that Priskilla’s name often occurs first (which was unusual for the time) might say something about the strong role she played in the couple’s witness and ministry.
Passages for Further Study
Apollos

Apollos was a Hellenistic (Greek-speaking) Yehudi (Jew), well versed in Scripture, who became a strong evangelist and Christian apologist. A native of Alexandria in Mitsrayim (Egypt), where there was a large Jewish community, Apollos apparently came under the influence of Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) the immerser’s followers. He then became a bold and enthusiastic preacher of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) in Jewish meeting halls, though he knew nothing of Christian baptism.

When Priskilla (Priscilla) and Akulas (Aquila) heard Apollos preach in Efesos (Ephesus), they invited him to their home and explained the way of Christ to him more fully. With the encouragement of the believers in Efesos, who recognized his God-given gifts and ministry, Apollos then traveled on to Akaia (Achaia) (i.e., Korinthos (Corinth)). There he greatly helped the believers as an effective defender of the Good News in public debate with the Yehudim (Jews), boldly demonstrating that Yeshua is the Messiah predicted in Scripture (Acts 18:24-28).

A dynamic communicator, Apollos was popular with some of the Christians in Korinthos because of his intellectual style and his powerful speaking abilities. As a result of his powerful ministry, some in Korinthos were more drawn to Apollos than to Paulos (Paul) (1 Cor 1:11-12). Paulos’s defense of himself and his simple, unimpressive way of preaching the Good News may have been precipitated by comparisons that people were making between him and Apollos. Significantly, Paulos nowhere criticized Apollos himself. He called Apollos a fellow servant and was grateful for the follow-up work he had done—Apollos watered the seed that Paulos had planted, and God blessed the work of both (1 Cor 3:5-9; 4:1). Rather, Paulos criticized the shallow perspectives and divisiveness of those drawn to Apollos for superficial reasons (see 1 Cor 1:10-12; 3:3-4; 4:6-7).

Perhaps Apollos’s reluctance to return to Korinthos from Efesos (1 Cor 16:12) was due to concern over the divisions that resulted from his ministry. Yet Paulos encouraged him to return there at some point. Several years later, when Apollos was ministering on the island of Kraitai (Crete), Paulos encouraged Titos (Titus) to make sure Apollos’s needs were met as he set off to an unknown destination for further missionary service (Titus 3:13). Apollos, with his strong intellectual gifts and powerful speaking abilities, had a significantly different approach and style from that of Paulos, yet both men proved effective and useful in the service of Christ.
Passages for Further Study
Herodes (Herod) Agrippas (Agrippa) II

Herodes Agrippas II, son of Herodes Agrippas I, succeeded his father as king and ruled in Palestine AD 50–100, eventually controlling approximately the same area as his great-grandfather, Herodes the Great. Agrippas II was in control of the Temple treasury and could appoint the high priest. He was not popular among Yehudim (Jews) on account of his incestuous relationship with his sister Bernike (Bernice). The Romans consulted him on religious matters, which is probably why Festos (Festus) invited him to hear the apostle Paulos’s (Paul’s) defense at Kaisareia (Caesarea) (AD 59, 25:13–26:32).

In May AD 66, the Jewish war against the Romans began (Josephus, War 2.14.4). When Agrippas’s attempt to quell the revolt failed, he became a staunch ally of the Romans throughout the entire war (AD 66–70). During this time Nero committed suicide, the new emperor Galba was murdered, and Vespasian became the emperor. After pledging his allegiance to the new emperor, Agrippas associated himself with Titos (Titus), Vespasian’s son, who was the general in charge of the war (Tacitus, History 5.81). After the fall of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Aug 6, AD 70), Agrippas was probably present to celebrate the destruction of his own people.

In AD 79 Vespasian died and Titos became emperor. Little is known of Agrippas’s rule after this, except that he wrote to the historian Josephus, praising him for The Jewish War, and he purchased a copy of it (Josephus, Life 65; Against Apion 1.9.47–52).

Although the Talmud implies that Agrippas II had two wives (Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 27a), Josephus gives no indication that he had any wives or children. He died around AD 100, and his death marks the end of the dynasty of the Herods.
Passages for Further Study
Romai (Rome)
In the first century AD Romai was both a cosmopolitan city and a mighty empire that had brought peace and stability to the Mediterranean world.
The Founding and Early Growth of Romai
Romai was founded, according to tradition, in 753 BC on the Tiber River in Italia (Italy) by a Latin-speaking agricultural tribe. A loose association of chieftains comprised the earliest Senate.

Around 600 BC the Etruscans from central Italia invaded the territory of Romai and became its rulers. They constructed numerous works, including the forum, which became the social, commercial, and political center for the city, and a temple for Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva. Romai was now linked by roads to the Etruscans in the north, to the Greek trading cities in the south, to the sea to the west, and to the inland highlands to the east.
The Roman Republic

When Romai’s kings became autocratic, the Latin population rebelled. In 509 BC, Romai established a “republic,” an oligarchy of the powerful families who controlled the Senate. The small city-state steadily gained control of the region, expanding their influence across the Mediterranean. In 273 BC they made a treaty with the Ptolemies of Mitsrayim (Egypt). They expanded into North Africa, defeating the rival city-state Carthage in the course of the three Punic Wars (264–146 BC), and pressed on into Spania (Spain). Romai’s many conquests brought enormous wealth.

With geographical expansion came social changes in Italia. Between 200 and 100 BC, rich landowners bought out small independent farmers, who subsequently drifted into Romai, landless and unemployed. Huge, overcrowded slums appeared alongside the vast wealth and magnificent buildings. The foundations of the republic were cracking under the strain of popular discontent.
The Beginning of the Empire: Yulios (Julius) and Octavian

During this time of social and political upheaval, Yulios Kaisar (Caesar) pursued an ambitious and tumultuous career which sought to centralize power in his own person. Senators who favored the old republic assassinated him in 44 BC, but their action ultimately backfired: Yulios’s grandnephew and heir, Octavian, became a senator, consul, and the commander-in-chief in 43 BC with the support of the Senate. The Senate also deified Yulios in 42 BC. After Octavian defeated Markos (Mark) Antony and Kleopatra (Cleopatra) in 31 BC and took control of Mitsrayim, the Senate gave him the titles Augustus (“illustrious”) and Princeps (“first citizen”) in 27 BC, and Octavian began to call himself “son of a god” because of Yulios’s divine status. The form of a republic survived, but the reality of a divine emperor had arrived.
Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) and the Birth of the Church

“When the right time came, God sent his Son” (Gal 4:4). The change into an empire brought peace and stability, a pax Romana (“Roman peace”) that lasted well into the 100s AD. Many observers have noted that Roman rule during the first century AD provided the ideal setting for the spread of Christianity. The borders were secure and the roads were good, making travel relatively trouble-free. Roman laws and customs protected the rights of its citizens (see, e.g., Acts 16:35-40; 22:24-29). Youdaismos (Judaism) was protected, and the Romans viewed Christianity as a sect within Youdaismos (see, e.g., Acts 25:13-19). As a result, the Romans largely rejected complaints against Christians on religious grounds (see, e.g., Acts 19:23-41). Christians were free to proclaim the Good News about Yeshua, and many people of all nationalities became followers of Christ.
The Changing Status of Christianity

This favorable situation began to change in the time of Nero. Nero blamed Christians for the fire that destroyed a good part of Romai (Rome) in AD 64, and he proceeded with the first large-scale persecution of Christians. The overt persecution ceased in AD 66, but Christianity was no longer viewed as a sect of Youdaismos and lost its protected status. It later became imperial policy to require people to burn incense to the emperor—those who refused were usually either Yehudim (Jews) (who were protected) or Christians (who were not). As a result, from the time of Domitian (AD 81–96) to Galerius (AD 305–311), Christianity was officially illegal, punishable by death, and persecuted to varying extents depending on the zeal of those in power. Thus for over two hundred years Romai drank “the blood of God’s holy people who were witnesses for Yeshua” (Rev 17:6).
Passages for Further Study
Nero

Nero became emperor of Romai (Rome) in AD 54 at the age of 17 after his mother poisoned her husband, the emperor Klaudios (Claudius). Nero enjoyed performing in the limelight and was a sexually depraved and profligate man. Yet the early years of Nero’s reign were stable and competently administered by his advisers, the prefect Burrus and the Stoic philosopher Seneca. Nero’s debauched character would have been well known when Paulos (Paul) wrote to the Romans around AD 57 to “submit to governing authorities” as having been “placed there by God” (Rom 13:1).

Nero’s worst actions came after he arranged his mother’s murder in AD 59 (the same year in which Paulos appealed to Kaisar (Caesar), Acts 25:11). In AD 62 he banished and then executed his wife, married his lover, and forced Burrus and Seneca into retirement. In AD 64 a fire devastated a large area of Romai. At the time, Nero was away from the city, but many people believed the rumor that Nero had set the fire himself. Nero found a scapegoat in Christians, whom he charged with the crime. Christians were widely seen as hostile to civil society and thus deserving of punishment, even if few believed that they had started the fire; they were “convicted not so much of arson as of hatred of the human race” (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). The ensuing persecution of Christians in Romai was intense; it is likely that Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) and Paulos were executed in Romai at this time.

In AD 66 a Jewish revolt broke out in Kaisareia (Caesarea). Nero dispatched his general Vespasian to squelch the revolt, taking no interest in the affairs of state. He spent the next two years doing performances in Yavan (Greece), leaving the responsibility of governing to a Roman prefect. Because of the opposition he encountered from leading governors in France, Spania (Spain), and Africa on his return to Romai, Nero committed suicide in AD 68, exclaiming at his death, “What an artist dies with me!” He was the last and worst emperor of the line of Yulios (Julius) Kaisar. (See also the study notes on Rev 13:3, 11, 18; 17:8, 10-11.)
Passages for Further Study
The Roman Church

The details of the founding of the church in Romai (Rome) are not known with certainty. There was a large Jewish population in Romai, and some Yehudim (Jews) from Romai were present in Yerushalem (Jerusalem) on the day of Pentecost at the birth of the church (Acts 2:10). The most likely explanation, then, is that some of these Yehudim converted to Christianity and took the Good News about Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) the Messiah to Romai, where a Christian community was born from within the meeting halls of Romai. It is unlikely that Kefa (Peter; Grk. Petros) founded the Roman church or that he was present in Romai by the time Paulos (Paul) wrote to the Roman Christians around AD 57; otherwise, Paulos would certainly have greeted him. Consequently, Paulos wrote this letter to help ensure that the Roman church had apostolic involvement in their faith. He never wrote to the churches of Judea, founded by the other apostles, but only to churches that either he had founded (e.g., Korinthos (Corinth), Galatia) or to those that had no direct apostolic involvement (e.g., Kolossai (Colosse), Romai).

In time, the Jewish Christians in Romai would have been pushed out of the meeting halls by the non-Christian Yehudim, as happened elsewhere. By the time Paulos wrote to the Roman church, they were meeting as separate house churches in private homes (Rom 16:5, 10-11, 15). There were no centralized edifices, and it is uncertain whether the whole body of believers in Romai met together.

When Klaudios (Claudius) expelled the Yehudim from Romai (around AD 49), the Jewish Christians were also forced to leave, among whom were Priskilla (Priscilla) and Akulas (Aquila) (Acts 18:2). In the absence of the Yehudim, the Roman church would have become Gentile in character. When the Yehudim returned (probably shortly after the death of Klaudios in AD 54), there were no doubt questions—if not conflicts—among the Jewish and Gentile Christians. Paulos may have written Romans to settle such controversies among this mixed group of Yehudim and Gentiles worshiping Christ in the same city.

As is evident from Romans 16, Paulos already had many friends in the Roman church. In the spring of AD 60, roughly two years after writing Romans, Paulos had the opportunity to go to Romai—a desire he had repeatedly expressed (Acts 19:21; Rom 1:13-15). He spent two years there under house arrest awaiting his first trial before Nero, “boldly proclaiming the Kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Yeshua Christ” (Acts 28:30-31).
Passages for Further Study
Korinthos (Corinth)

Korinthos was one of the oldest cities of Yavan (Greece), with evidence of settlement going back to at least 3000 BC. Its prime location along both east-west and north-south trade routes enabled it to become a center of commerce and trade, and it reached the height of its strength and power between 800 and 600 BC. When in the mid-100s BC the Roman military machine began a relentless march to forge a vast empire, Korinthos led the Hellenic League to oppose Roman dominance in Yavan. They were no match for the Romans, and in 146 BC Korinthos was completely destroyed, its men executed, its women and children sold into slavery. Korinthos lay in ruins for a century.

In 44 BC Yulios (Julius) Kaisar (Caesar) established a Roman colony at Korinthos. The colony attracted a mixed group of Italians, freedmen (freed former slaves) from Romai (Rome), and dispossessed Greeks. With great industry and ingenuity the new inhabitants quickly reestablished the city as a prosperous center for trade, commerce, and industry. By the time Paulos (Paul) came to Korinthos, it was a bustling cosmopolitan city with a population of almost 700,000, including many wealthy people, and many others who were struggling to become so. Korinthos attracted tradespeople from all over the world, though its reputation also grew as a center of luxury, indulgence, and vice. Korinthos had a reputation for promiscuity and prostitution, so much so that the verb “Corinthianize” meant having immoral sex. The church in Korinthos struggled with sexual immorality (1 Cor 5:1-13; 6:12-20).

Korinthos was also prominent because of the Isthmian Games, which dated from 523 BC and occurred every two years. Competition centered on three kinds of events: equestrian, gymnastic, and musical. By the New Testament period, the games included chariot racing and other Roman spectacles in addition to the traditional Greek competitions. In an allusion to these athletic contests, Paulos mentioned both running and boxing (1 Cor 9:24-26). The winners of the games were national heroes. The prize for winning the games was a wreath made of myrtle, olive, or pine branches, plus the additional benefits of a stipend from the state, remission of taxes, and special benefits for the champion’s children.

As in most Roman cities, marble temples dominated the landscape; participation in the worship of the gods and their feasts was a prominent part of life in Korinthos. These pagan feasts were another major issue that the Korinthios (Corinthian) church wrestled with (8:1–10:33).

A large colony of displaced Yehudim (Jews) also developed in the city, many of whom may have arrived after the emperor Klaudios’s (Claudius’) edict expelling Yehudim from Romai (see Acts 18:2). When Paulos traveled to Korinthos on his second missionary journey, he met Akulas (Aquila) and Priskilla (Priscilla), who became his close friends and co-workers (Acts 18:1-3). Paulos stayed at Korinthos for over a “year and a half, teaching the word of God” (Acts 18:11).

The church of Korinthos, born in such a hothouse of paganism and promiscuity, went through serious birth pangs. Their troubles provide, through Paulos’s letters to them, a rich collection of solutions to the practical issues of Christian life and community.

Efesos (Ephesus)

Efesos stood at the crossroads of both north-south and east-west trade routes and was well known as the “guardian” of the temple of Artemis (Acts 19:35). It was founded by Ionian Greeks around 1044 BC on a natural harbor where the Cayster River emptied into a gulf of the Aegean Sea (the site of the ancient city is now well inland). The city came under Roman rule in 41 BC. At the time of the apostles, Efesos was a wealthy city, a commercial and religious hub, and thus the most important city of the Roman province of Asia.

The worship of Artemis in Efesos was nearly as ancient as the city itself. The temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, was a key to the wealth and commerce of Efesos, because the worship of Artemis brought many pilgrims to Efesos and provided many commercial opportunities for idol makers and other vendors of goods and services.

When Paulos (Paul) arrived on his third missionary journey in AD 53 (Acts 19), Efesos had been a city continuously for over a thousand years and was deeply devoted to its patron goddess and her temple. As Paulos’s message began to gain more adherents, Christianity threatened the pagan temple and the commerce it produced for the makers of idols. The ensuing riot almost cost the apostle Paulos his life (Acts 19:24, 28-31).

The church of Efesos became strong under Paulos’s teaching and leadership, and churches in the surrounding communities were founded by people who had learned from Paulos in Efesos (e.g., Kolossai (Colosse); see Colossians Book Introduction, “Setting”). But Paulos warned the leaders of the Efesos church that they would be troubled by false teachers (Acts 20:29-31).

The apostle Yohan (John; Grk. Yoannes) is thought to have settled in Efesos around AD 70; from there he was exiled to the island of Patmos (Rev 1:9), where he wrote Revelation (probably in the AD 90s). At that time, the commendable love and good works of the Christian community described in the letter to the Ephesians had been largely abandoned (Rev 2:4). Irenaeus records that, after Yohan’s exile on Patmos, the apostle returned to live in Efesos and lived there until the end of his life during the time of the emperor Trajan (AD 98–117). According to tradition, Maria (Mary) the mother of Yeshua (Jesus; Grk. Yesus) also finished her days on earth in Efesos under Yohan’s care (see John 19:25-27).

The temple of Artemis was burned by the Goths in AD 262, and Artemis was no longer influential among the Ephesians when the third ecumenical council was held in Efesos in AD 431, thus illustrating the truth of Paulos’s message that “handmade gods” like Artemis “aren’t really gods at all” (Acts 19:26).

Filippou (Philippi)

Filippou was a minor village of Thrace until about 357 BC, when Filippos (Philip) II of Macedon, the father of Alexandros (Alexander) the Great, conquered the site and rebuilt it. He named the village after himself, fortified it as a military stronghold, and exploited the nearby gold mines. Filippou gained worldwide fame in 42 BC as the site where the imperial armies of Octavian and Markos (Mark) Antony defeated the republican generals Brutus and Cassius, the assassins of Yulios (Julius) Kaisar (Caesar). The victory opened the way for the emergence of the Roman Empire under the rule of Octavian Augustus.

Many veterans from the war of 42 BC and other battles settled in Filippou. When Paulos (Paul) came to the city, it still reflected its Roman military heritage. Situated on the Egnatian Way, it was a prominent stop on that great military highway connecting the Adrias (Adriatic) Sea with the Aegean Sea. It possessed distinct civic pride as a Roman colony (enjoying numerous privileges, such as tax exemption) and promoted Latin as its official language. Its government was modeled on the municipal constitution of Romai (Rome), and the inhabitants viewed themselves as Romans (see Acts 16:21).

Paulos visited the city on his second missionary journey, and the account of Acts gives detailed attention to this visit (Acts 16:12-40). The narrative frequently refers to the city’s Roman heritage: Not only does Paulos successfully employ his Roman citizenship in his defense (Acts 16:37-39), but the city magistrates bear the dignified Latin title praetor (given in its Greek translation, stratēgos—Acts 16:20-22, 38). There also appears to have been a small Jewish community there. The church began with believing Jewish women who met outside the city because there was no meeting hall. Later, they convened in the home of an important woman convert named Ludia (Lydia) (Acts 16:14-15, 40). Lukas (Luke) apparently stayed in Filippou when Paulos departed for Thessalonikai (Thessalonica) (cp. Acts 16:12, 40) and later rejoined Paulos at Filippou when Paulos passed through on his third missionary journey several years later (Acts 20:6). Paulos wrote a cordial letter to the church at Filippou during one of his imprisonments.

Timotheos (Timothy)

Timotheos traveled with Paulos (Paul) for much of his missionary career and was one of Paulos’s best-loved and most trusted assistants. Two of Paulos’s last letters were written to Timotheos at a time when Timotheos was providing leadership for the church in Efesos (Ephesus), near the end of Paulos’s life.

Timotheos had a devout mother and grandmother (2 Tim 1:5), and he was highly respected by the Christians in his hometown, Lustra (Lystra), and in nearby Ikonion (Iconium). He joined Paulos’s missionary team on Paulos’s second missionary journey. Paulos speaks of prophetic words that confirmed Timotheos’s selection. Timotheos also received a special gifting for service through the laying on of the hands of the elders and of Paulos (1 Tim 1:18; 4:14; 2 Tim 1:6). Out of deference to the Yehudim (Jews) in the area, Paulos had Timotheos circumcised (Acts 16:1-3).

Over the next fifteen years, Paulos sent Timotheos on special assignments to several different churches (Acts 19:22; 1 Cor 4:17; 16:10-11; Phil 2:19-23; 1 Thes 3:1-6; 1 Tim 1:3; see also Acts 17:14-15; 18:5). Paulos included Timotheos’s name as coauthor of several of his letters (2 Cor 1:1; Phil 1:1; Col 1:1; 1 Thes 1:1; 2 Thes 1:1; Phlm 1:1). It is clear that Paulos had a close relationship with Timotheos and held him in high regard (see Rom 16:21; 1 Cor 4:17; 1 Thes 3:2; 1 Tim 1:2; 6:11; 2 Tim 1:2). As Paulos neared the end of his life and awaited his sentence in prison, he longed to see Timotheos (2 Tim 1:3-4). Of all Paulos’s coworkers, Timotheos especially is commended for his selfless concern for Christ and his people (Phil 2:20-22).

In Paulos’s second letter to Timotheos (2 Timotheos), written shortly before Paulos was killed, he encouraged Timotheos to be bold and fearless in his proclamation of the Good News, willing to suffer for Christ (2 Tim 1:8; 2:1-3; 4:1-2, 5)—a strong word to one who might have been timid by nature (see 2 Tim 1:6-7). Timotheos himself seems to have become a prisoner later on (Heb 13:23).

Timotheos was exemplary in the way he faithfully served the cause of Christ behind the scenes, devoting himself selflessly and with single-minded focus to the work of Christ and the people of Christ wherever help was needed. He serves as a reminder that believers should seek to become strong and effective witnesses for Christ.

Titos (Titus)

Titos was a Gentile convert who served as one of Paulos’s (Paul’s) trusted assistants. One of Paulos’s last letters was addressed to him, when Titos was helping to consolidate the church at Kraitai (Crete). Titos is an example of the Gentile converts who were so deeply touched by the Good News of Christ that they left their homes and devoted their lives to assisting Paulos in the proclamation of the Good News.

We know nothing about Titos’s background or conversion; his name is not mentioned in Acts. We first hear of him as a Gentile believer who accompanied Paulos and Barnabas to Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (Gal 2:1). Significantly, Paulos emphasized that Titos was not compelled to be circumcised (Gal 2:3).

Later, as a trusted member of Paulos’s team, Titos was sent on special assignments. He was the one sent by Paulos to Korinthos (Corinth) to deal with a difficult situation there (apparently carrying the demanding letter mentioned in 2 Cor 2:4, 9; 7:8-9). This task required both tact and strong leadership (Titos’s personality seems to have been stronger than Timotheos’s (Timothy’s); see 1 Cor 16:10-11; 2 Cor 7:13-15; 2 Tim 1:6-7). When Titos returned to Paulos with good news (2 Cor 7:6-7, 13-15), Paulos sent him back to Korinthos carrying the letter we call 2 Corinthians to encourage the believers to complete their money-raising project for the poor believers in Yerushalem. It was an assignment he eagerly accepted because of his love for the Christians in Korinthos (2 Cor 7:15; 8:6, 16-17). Paulos speaks of him as a person of integrity and as one who is similar to Paulos himself (2 Cor 8:23; 12:18).

A few years later, following Paulos’s first trial in Romai (Rome) and subsequent release, Paulos left Titos on the island of Kraitai to help consolidate the church. While Titos was there, Paulos wrote his letter to Titos, giving him advice on choosing church leaders and encouraging him to teach and model godly behavior. Paulos then asked Titos to meet him at Nikopolis (Nicopolis) (in Akaia (Achaia)), where Paulos hoped to spend the winter (Titus 3:12). Later, shortly before Paulos was killed in Romai, he wrote that Titos had gone to Dalmatia (along the Adrias (Adriatic) coast, northwest of modern-day Yavan (Greece)), probably for ministry there (2 Tim 4:10).
The church historian Eusebius refers to an early tradition that Titos eventually settled on Kraitai, serving as the bishop there until he was quite old (Eusebius, Church History 3.4.6).

Roman Emperors (27 BC–AD 96)

Augustus (Octavian) (27 BC–AD 14) Became the first Roman emperor after defeating Marc Antony at the battle of Actium (31 BC); ruled with wisdom and good administration; given the title “Augustus” (27 BC), initiating emperor worship. See Luke 2:1.
Tiberios (Tiberius) (AD 14–37) Augustus’s adopted son and chosen successor; a wise and humble ruler; appointed Pontios (Pontius) Pilatos (Pilate) as governor of Judea. See Luke 3:1; John 19:12.

(Gaios (Gaius)) Caligula (AD 37–41) Son of Augustus’s general Germanicus, nicknamed Caligula (“Little Boot”) for his military attire; went insane, squandered the treasury, ruled as a despot, and was assassinated.

Klaudios (Claudius) (AD 41–54) Tiberios’s nephew, proclaimed emperor by the Praetorian Guard after Caligula’s death; friend of Herodes (Herod) Agrippas (Agrippa) I; ended the persecution of Yehudim (Jews) in Alexandria; later expelled Yehudim from Romai (Rome) (around AD 49); married Nero’s mother Agrippina, who poisoned him. See Acts 18:2.

Nero (AD 54–68) Adopted by Klaudios and succeeded him; spent time on pleasure; appealed to by Paulos (Paul) (who instructed the Roman Christians to submit to Nero); later murdered his wife and mother; first persecutor of Christians. See Acts 25:11; Rom 13:1-7.

Vespasian (AD 69–79) Successful legate (general) and son of a tax collector; began the Jewish War by invading Galil (Galilee) (AD 67); as emperor reformed Romai’s finances, reorganized the armies, and ruled with a reputation for justice; began the construction of the Colosseum; died of illness.

Titos (Titus) (AD 79–81) Son of Vespasian; finished the Jewish War with the destruction of Yerushalem (Jerusalem) (AD 70); as emperor completed the Colosseum, gave disaster relief after the eruption of Mount Vesuvius (AD 79) and a fire in Romai (AD 80); died of a fever.

Domitian (AD 81–96) Younger son of Vespasian who grew up in Titos’s shadow and coveted power; as emperor was a capable administrator, rebuilt damaged parts of Romai, proclaimed himself divine, and extorted new taxes; relentlessly persecuted Christians in later years; was assassinated.
